[(Kant, 1784)](https://users.manchester.edu/facstaff/ssnaragon/online/texts/318/kant%2C%20enlightenment.pdf)

## 9.10 Self-Interest and the Burden of Justification

### 9.10.1 Scrutiny Before Reliance

\noindent A company can gain from a practice while customers bear costs that the company does not fully internalize. The company may also control the interface, the outcome definitions, and the evidence presented to outsiders. These features justify demanding substantiation before relying on a claim of customer benefit. A material stake supplies a reason for scrutiny. When an interest threatens judgment owed to another person or a professional purpose, it also creates a conflict of interest in the sense developed in §9.45. A finding of wrongdoing requires evidence about the particular practice.

Institutional safeguards can be designed to remain effective under private-interest pursuit. *Of the Independency of Parliament* treats that assumption as a principle for designing checks on power and distinguishes the political maxim from a factual claim that every person is dishonest. The institutional question is whether the arrangement remains acceptable when participants pursue their separate interests. Applied to marketing, this asks whether customers retain meaningful protection when managers respond strongly to sales targets. The application extends the argument about political institutions to commercial governance. [(Hume, 1741)](https://davidhume.org/texts/emp/ip)

A commercial application appears at the end of Book I, chapter XI of *The Wealth of Nations*: proposals for commercial regulation made by merchants and manufacturers warrant particularly careful scrutiny because their interests can diverge from the public's. This argument supports examining the incentives and evidence behind an interested party's proposal. The argument concerns proposals for laws and regulation; applying it to a transaction requires a separate assessment of the relevant incentives and evidence. [(Smith, 1776, chapter XI, concluding discussion)](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3300/3300-h/3300-h.htm)

The resulting principle for a marketing decision is demanding: when a firm controls a practice and materially benefits from it, the firm should substantiate claims of customer benefit with evidence that can be examined independently. Customers should not have to infer safety or benefit from the firm's incentives, and an absence of complaints need not satisfy the burden when complaining is costly or discouraged. This ethical and institutional recommendation leaves legal burdens of proof to the applicable jurisdiction and proceeding.

### 9.10.2 What Would Discharge the Burden?

\noindent The burden must be connected to a claim that could be supported or refuted. For a cancellation process, the firm could supply evidence on completion, understanding, subsequent charges, and outcomes for customers who sought to leave. For a personalized recommendation, it could show how the objective corresponds to customers' stated purposes and how a person can revise it. For a claim about environmental performance, it could provide the relevant scope, denominator, and supporting records. Independent examination need not involve disclosing identifiable customer records; controlled access and reproducible aggregates can address different parts of the evidentiary problem.

![A material stake changes the scrutiny of evidence; a verdict follows the evaluation of the practice.](../figures/M09_burden_justification.png)

The sequence separates the reason for scrutiny from the conclusion reached after scrutiny. Commercial incentives raise questions about measurement, selective disclosure, and omitted outcomes. Evidence then supports acceptance, a narrower claim, redesign, or rejection. A process that always reaches rejection regardless of the evidence has ceased to be a critical evaluation.

The standard can also be asymmetric. When the firm receives the gains, controls the information, and imposes a substantial or difficult-to-reverse risk on customers, it is reasonable to require stronger evidence before deployment than before continuing a small, reversible pilot. That recommendation depends on a stated judgment about the consequences of acting and waiting. It does not turn uncertainty into proof of harm. The analyst should identify the information needed, the feasible alternative, and the condition under which the restriction can be relaxed.

Consider a retention experiment that reports only revenue. Withhold acceptance of its customer-benefit claim until the relevant customer outcomes are supplied. If independent evidence then shows that an easily refused offer improves informed choice and produces no material deterioration in the specified outcomes, the original objection must be revised within that scope. If the additional revenue depends on preventing an expressed refusal, the evidence supports rejecting that feature. The recommendation changes because the evidence distinguishes the mechanism.

## 9.11 Confucian Perspectives on Marketing Conduct

### 9.11.1 Righteousness and Profit

\noindent Confucian texts ask what kind of person and relationship a practice develops, alongside what it produces. In the *Analects* 4.16, the contrast between righteousness and gain concerns the grounds on which a person judges an action. In 4.5, wealth and status remain desirable, but their pursuit is constrained by the proper way of obtaining them. These passages support evaluating the means and responsibilities of profit seeking. They do not require treating every profitable exchange as a moral failure. [(Confucius, n.d.)](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3330/pg3330-images.html)

The opening of the *Mencius*, 1A.1, challenges a ruler who frames the discussion around advantage to his state. Its warning is that competition for advantage at every level can damage the relations on which political order depends. Benevolence and righteousness provide an alternative basis for judgment. The commercial application is that a firm cannot settle its responsibilities simply by showing that a practice raises its own return. The interests of customers, employees, suppliers, and affected communities require consideration. This extends a political argument to a contemporary organization. [(Mencius, 2016)](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/265d73a0-6bfa-45df-92ff-4e7d3f8be4b1/content)

For a recommendation system, the question is whether the service helps the customer pursue a worthwhile purpose while sustaining a trustworthy relationship. A firm could profit by offering relevant information, reliable support, and a product the customer continues to value. It could also increase immediate revenue by exploiting confusion. The fact that both strategies can be profitable makes the criterion of judgment consequential.

### 9.11.2 Trustworthiness and the Responsibilities of a Role

\noindent The *Analects* places weight on trustworthiness, including in its discussion of government in 12.7. Its account of the rectification of names in 13.3 concerns the relation between language, social roles, and proper conduct. A role is associated with standards of performance. Calling someone a trustworthy adviser does not supply the conduct that warrants that description. These ideas can inform a contemporary examination of how marketing labels create expectations. [(Confucius, 2015)](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/bitstreams/d1f62d31-9082-41d0-999f-4c3efa0c8857/download)

A platform that calls a paid placement a recommendation should examine what customers understand that description to mean. If users infer that the ranking serves their goals while the rule principally favors an undisclosed payment, the claimed role and actual conduct diverge. Likewise, a customer-care team whose only rewarded outcome is preventing cancellation may face incentives inconsistent with the service its name promises. Clear labeling is one response; aligning responsibilities, rewards, and actual conduct addresses the underlying relation.

Confucian role ethics does not simply duplicate the account of autonomy as rational self-legislation (Kant, 1785). It emphasizes cultivated dispositions, relationships, and responsibilities within social roles. Historical Confucian roles also contain hierarchies that require critical examination when applied to contemporary customers and organizations. A modern application should state why the proposed responsibility is justified and how affected people can challenge its interpretation. Calling a manager benevolent cannot make unilateral control over a customer's goals self-justifying.

### 9.11.3 Remonstrance, Reciprocity, and Learning

\noindent The *Analects* 13.23 distinguishes harmony from mere agreement, and 14.22 connects service to a ruler with truthful challenge. Applied to a marketing team, these ideas support a responsibility to raise a material objection even when the proposal is commercially attractive. Harmony need not require an analyst to suppress evidence that the team's preferred metric conceals customer harm. The organizational question is whether disagreement can be voiced and considered without being treated as disloyalty.

Reciprocity in *Analects* 15.24 encourages examination of how one treats others. In marketing, it can motivate asking whether an offer, disclosure, or cancellation process is one the decision maker could reasonably accept from the customer's position. Different customers have different resources and purposes, so the manager's own tolerance for inconvenience is insufficient. Perspective taking should lead to inquiry about affected people, including those who face language, accessibility, or financial constraints.

The conjunction of learning and reflection in *Analects* 2.15 also fits AI-assisted analysis. Accumulating generated explanations without examining them leaves the learner dependent on assertions. Reflection without engaging evidence can become speculation. A useful learning exercise requires the student to compare a generated argument with the source, inspect its premises, and revise a conclusion when the evidence warrants it. In this contemporary application, learning supplies the evidence and reflection examines whether the proposed conclusion follows from it.

### 9.11.4 Moral Beginnings and Cultivated Conduct

\noindent Confucianism contains substantial internal disagreement. The account of moral beginnings in *Mencius*, including compassion in 2A.6, emphasizes capacities that can be developed. The chapter on human nature in *Xunzi* emphasizes the disorder that can follow unchecked desires and the importance of learning, ritual, and deliberate effort in producing good conduct. The differing conceptions of human nature should not be reduced to a single slogan about whether all people are good or bad. [(Mencius, 2016)](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/265d73a0-6bfa-45df-92ff-4e7d3f8be4b1/content); [(Xunzi, 1999, chapter 23, Columbia selection)](https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/main_pop/ps/ps_china-xunzi-human-nature.htm); [(Goldin, 2025)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/xunzi/)

The emphasis on deliberate cultivation supplies a response to reliance on goodwill alone: ethical conduct requires sustained formation and practices that direct behavior (Xunzi, 1999). In a firm, a contemporary application would examine what employees repeatedly learn to notice, what the reward system encourages, and how the organization handles a truthful report of an unwanted outcome. Ritual propriety, often rendered *li*, concerns patterned social conduct and cultivation; it should not be equated mechanically with a compliance checklist. The word for profit or benefit, also commonly romanized *li*, is a different Chinese word.

For the subscription case, a Confucian evaluation can examine whether the customer-care role is performed faithfully, whether a refusal is treated with respect, and whether the company sustains a relationship worthy of trust. A Kantian evaluation emphasizes the principle of action and treatment of the customer as an end. The institutional argument (Hume, 1741) asks how the process behaves under strong private incentives. The perspectives can support the same redesign for different reasons. Keeping those reasons explicit permits disagreement and avoids presenting distinct philosophical traditions as interchangeable.

## 9.12 Decisions That Can Withstand Criticism

\noindent A decision memorandum should begin with the action and the reason for it. For the subscription case, a supportable recommendation could retain an optional offer while making cancellation immediately effective when requested. Its justification would distinguish the measured commercial effect, the customer's stated objective, the relevant ethical principle, and the applicable legal requirements. If the firm's gain depends on preventing an understood refusal, increased revenue cannot by itself answer the ethical objection.

Consider three further decisions. A retailer wants to display a personalized discount based on past purchases. Assess whether the offer changes the feasible options, conceals material terms, or interferes with refusal. A product team wants to replace a nutrition objective with a click objective because clicks are easier to optimize. Identify the customer purpose and the missing connection between that purpose and the metric. An advertiser wants to describe one improvement as evidence of a company-wide transition. Specify the population, denominator, and time horizon needed to support the broader claim.

For each decision, formulate the strongest defensible argument in favor of the practice, the most consequential objection, and the premise that separates them. State what evidence would alter the recommendation. A critical conclusion can endorse a practice, narrow its claim, improve its design, or reject it. Its strength comes from the reasons and evidence that survive examination.

## 9.13 Reading Path

\noindent Begin with the introduction to the Transcendental Dialectic and the *Prolegomena*, §§50–54. Read the third antinomy alongside the distinction between appearances and things in themselves. The appendix on the regulative use of ideas explains the constructive role of reason. The interpretive account of the critique of metaphysics [(Grier, 2022)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-metaphysics/) provides an interpretive guide. Read the *Groundwork*, second section, separately for the universal-law and humanity formulations; these introduce the ethical principles used to evaluate the action, alongside the Dialectic's examination of the inference.

The [categorized research collection](../../01_Resources/15_Marketing_Dialectics/README.md) links the primary texts, scholarly interpretations, marketing research, and industry cases. It identifies full texts, excerpts, versions, and remaining access gaps. The two ASA decisions, the advertising-measurement study, and the subscription-interface research supply contrasting empirical and institutional settings for assessing the scope of a marketing argument.

For scrutiny of interested claims, read the opening paragraphs on institutional checks (Hume, 1741) and the conclusion to Book I, chapter XI of *The Wealth of Nations* (Smith, 1776). For Confucian perspectives, compare *Analects* 2.15, 4.5, 4.16, 12.7, 13.3, 13.23, 14.22, and 15.24 with *Mencius* 1A.1 and 2A.6 and the discussion of human nature (Xunzi, 1999). The resource guide distinguishes the original settings, translation choices, and proposed marketing applications.

## 9.14 AI Experimentation and the Choice of an Objective

A marketing manager can use past experiments to generate more effective messages, estimate how different customers respond to prices, and choose a policy for future deployment. The commercial question concerns the action that improves the firm's outcome. The ethical question concerns the reasons for choosing that action and its treatment of the people affected. Increasing the precision of the first answer can increase the importance of the second. A firm that learns to extract value more accurately needs a correspondingly clear account of which forms of extraction are permissible.

Four applications offer distinct settings for examining that relationship: language generation informed by email experiments (Angelopoulos et al., 2026), personalized pricing and the distribution of surplus (Dubé and Misra, 2021), decisions under uncertainty about future conditions (Farrell et al., 2026), and selection of segments and treatments (Zhang and Misra, 2025). Their findings and objectives must be evaluated separately. The [research guide](../../01_Resources/16_AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/01_Research/README.md) identifies the versions, reading locations, and commercial settings.

### 9.14.1 Learning from Experimental Comparisons

The *Causal Alignment* approach trains a language model using higher- and lower-performing messages from the same historical experiment. In 36 new campaigns involving approximately 283 million email impressions, its human-assisted workflow produces about 32% higher mean click rates than unassisted human experts. Table 2 averages campaigns equally. The paper retains human selection and describes screening against unsupported claims and omitted information. The experiment measures link clicks; it supplies no corresponding causal estimate of customers' informed benefit. [August 2026 author version, Sections 4–5 and Appendix B](https://leekevin.io/caLM.pdf).

A within-campaign comparison can remove confounding due to a shared audience and context when assignment is randomized. Reusing those comparisons as training labels then inherits the definition of success in the original outcome. If a useful explanation and an obstructive appeal both increase clicks, the click label alone does not distinguish their reasons. Human review can impose an additional standard, but the reviewer needs authority and evidence to apply it. Review by a person rewarded for commercial performance does not automatically represent the interests of recipients.

Appendix A also describes steering emotional valence, including fear. An accurate warning can help a customer deliberate. An invented threat or false deadline can distort that deliberation. The ethical distinction depends on the content, its truth, the circumstances, and the recipient's opportunity to assess it. The appearance of an emotional category in a method establishes a capability; it does not establish that the deployed campaigns used deception.

### 9.14.2 Pricing, Profit, and Customer Surplus

The personalized-pricing study concerns prospective employers purchasing recruiting services. Its model projects a 19% profit gain from personalization relative to the optimized uniform price, alongside a 23% decline in total customer surplus in the June 2021 version. More than 60% of customers benefit under that comparison. The later field test uses a different uniform benchmark and capped personalized prices. Its rounded realized revenue means imply about a 10.1% advantage for personalization. Consumer surplus is calculated through the demand model. [NBER revision, Sections 4–5](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w23775/w23775.pdf); published as *Journal of Political Economy* 131(1), 2023.

These results expose an economically meaningful conflict: a policy can increase profit and benefit a majority while reducing the sum of customer surplus. The incidence of gains and losses therefore matters alongside their aggregate. A claim that every customer loses would misstate the evidence. Equally, the fact that a majority gains supplies no automatic justification for how a losing minority is treated. The authors examine alternative welfare weights and the consequences of restricting data. That analysis creates a basis for criticism of particular objectives and policy choices.

The benchmark also matters. A price increase from an initially low uniform price combines the exercise of previously unused market power with the effect of personalization. A comparison with an already optimized uniform price isolates a different change. The model's forecast and the later experiment use different price policies, so their percentage gains answer different questions. Neither comparison is an experiment in emergency pricing of household necessities.

### 9.14.3 Robustness and Segmentation

The *Robust A/B Decisions* approach ranks policies using an ambiguity-adjusted value of the chosen outcome. It evaluates deployment decisions using 552 advertising experiments. Its distinction between statistical significance and an economic decision is useful, as is its concern about changing deployment conditions. A robust commercial payoff still requires an independently justified objective. Protecting the firm against an unfavorable shift in customers does not by itself protect customers against an unfavorable policy. [September 2026 version, Sections 1–3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07633).

The *Coarse Personalization* approach chooses a limited set of treatments and assigns customers to them. In its application, five segments recover over 99.5% of the estimated incremental profit under full personalization. The paper discusses fairness and stability as practical concerns. A smaller treatment menu can simplify oversight; the number of segments alone does not establish that the assignment principle is justifiable. Customers in a single segment may still face an objectionable use of data. [June 2025 revision, introduction and application](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05793v4).

## 9.15 Pricing Policy: What Conduct is Being Evaluated?

Price discrimination means that different buyers face different prices for comparable offerings in an economically relevant sense. Dynamic pricing changes prices with conditions. Personalized algorithmic pricing conditions a quoted price on information about a particular buyer. Price gouging is a legal category with jurisdiction-specific conditions concerning the market disruption, covered goods, price, and justification. Algorithmic coordination between competitors introduces another question concerning competitive conduct. These descriptions can overlap, but none supplies the legal elements of the others.

The FTC's August 19, 2026 proposed enforcement policy statement creates a direct connection to the pricing study: it cites the personalized-pricing study (Dubé and Misra, 2021, 2023) while discussing the uncertain distributional effects of personalization. Its proposed approach emphasizes disclosure when customers reasonably expect a common price, including the basis for personalization and categories of data used. It separately considers deception and unfairness. The document is a proposed enforcement statement listed in the FTC's legal library, with no new blanket prohibition on individualized pricing. An enforcement action still requires an applicable legal violation. [FTC proposal, pages 3–8](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/p034101-ftc-enforcement-policy-statement-re-personalized-pricing-proposed-for-public-comment.pdf).

New York's General Business Law §349-a requires specified disclosures for covered personalized algorithmic prices. The law took effect on November 10, 2025. Its consumer definition concerns personal, family, or household use and includes listed exceptions. That scope differs from the employer purchasing decision in the recruiting study. The 2026 One Fair Price legislation, S8623B/A9349B, would impose broader restrictions; the official record checked on November 6 shows legislative passage without recorded gubernatorial enactment. These are different stages of legal authority. [Current §349-a](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/349-A); [effective-date notice](https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2025/attorney-general-james-warns-new-yorkers-about-algorithmic-pricing-new-law-takes); [bill status](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S8623).

New York's price-gouging law concerns unconscionably excessive prices for essential goods and services during abnormal market disruptions. Its application considers the relevant prices, conduct, and cost justifications. A high willingness-to-pay prediction or a positive experimental revenue effect supplies none of those legal findings by itself. The Attorney General's January 2026 inquiry into Instacart's pricing experiments likewise constitutes an inquiry, with requests for information about the experiments and compliance. It is not an adjudication of the academic papers. [Price-gouging guidance](https://ag.ny.gov/resources/individuals/consumer-issues/price-gouging); [January 8 inquiry](https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-demands-answers-instacart-about-algorithmic-pricing).

The FTC opened a further inquiry on October 28, 2026, requesting information directly from nine companies about personalized pricing and compensation. These Section 6(b) orders seek evidence about actual practices; they do not establish that the recipients violated the law. The August enforcement statement remains described as proposed in this later notice. [FTC inquiry](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-launches-personalized-pricing-compensation-inquiry).

The marketing decision is whether a proposed practice meets the applicable requirements and merits deployment on ethical grounds. A lawful price may still require a moral defense. A philosophical objection must identify the conduct at issue, the affected person, and the principle that the conduct violates. The [policy source record](../../01_Resources/16_AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/02_Policy/README.md) records jurisdiction, status, coverage, and the November 6, 2026 verification date.

## 9.16 A Kantian Critique of Commercial Optimization

### 9.16.1 An Effective Means and a Justifiable End

The distinction between hypothetical and categorical imperatives identifies a missing step in a commercial recommendation. An instruction to choose the policy that increases profit is conditional on the end being pursued. Statistical evidence can improve the choice of means to that end. It does not establish the authority of the end over every affected person. The objection becomes sharp when a decision maker treats successful optimization as a sufficient reason to deploy, despite unresolved objections concerning deception, misuse of information, or obstruction of refusal [(Kant, 1785, Akademie 4:414–421)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5682).

The criticism applies to the transition from a performance result to a recommendation. A study may legitimately estimate a commercial capability, including one that exposes a welfare loss. A deployment recommendation carries the additional burden of justifying the conduct it endorses. Research that measures harmful consequences can improve that evaluation. The existence of a profit objective in a statistical problem is therefore insufficient evidence about an author's moral commitments.

### 9.16.2 Humanity and the Conditions of Deliberation

The humanity formulation requires treating persons as ends and never merely as means. Exchange ordinarily involves using another person's abilities or resources to pursue an end. Respect additionally requires attention to the other person's capacity to understand, set purposes, and act on reasons. A message designed to create a false belief so that someone buys serves the seller by impairing that capacity. A truthful explanation can improve both conversion and understanding. The difference lies in how the decision is obtained [(Kant, 1785, Akademie 4:429–430)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5682).

For AI-generated communication, this principle motivates checking the evidence for factual claims, the visibility of consequential terms, and the opportunity to refuse. The acceptability checks in *Causal Alignment* address some of these concerns. Further questions concern the truth of the underlying offer, whether customers understand it, and whether the improved response advances a purpose they can endorse. A subject line can preserve its input's meaning while carrying forward a misleading premise already present in that input. These are questions for additional evidence, not findings that the studied campaigns were deceptive.

For personalized prices, the relevant conduct includes obtaining data, explaining its use, and presenting the offer. An inference that a person has few alternatives can reflect an urgent need. A Kantian criticism of exploiting that need must explain how the practice treats the person's agency or permissible ends. High willingness to pay is not, by itself, a measure of wealth or vulnerability. The interpretation requires the setting and the information actually used.

### 9.16.3 Universalization Requires a Specified Maxim

A maxim identifies the circumstances, action, and purpose. Consider a hypothetical seller who describes a price as a special saving while secretly raising it using an estimate of the buyer's disposable income. The maxim concerns inducing reliance on a representation the seller knows to be false. Its general adoption threatens the credibility on which that representation depends. The objection attaches to deception, even if a randomized test precisely measures the resulting sales increase.

A publicly explained discount for a customer group presents a different maxim. Different prices alone supply no contradiction in universal law. Students must ask why the grouping is relevant, whether its data use is permissible, and whether the principle could be adopted consistently by people acting as rational agents. The universal-law test cannot be replaced with either a vote on whether a price is popular or the analyst's dislike of its distributional result [(Kant, 1785, Akademie 4:421–424)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5682).

### 9.16.4 Dignity and the Limits of a Weighted Objective

A manager might add a customer-outcome term to profit and optimize their weighted sum. This can improve attention to consequences, but any finite weight allows sufficiently large profit to compensate for a penalty. If the objection concerns a duty against deception, that specification makes the duty negotiable. The distinction between price and dignity supplies a reason to examine which actions should be excluded before commercial ranking. A measurable proxy for respectful treatment remains subject to scrutiny [(Kant, 1785, Akademie 4:434–435)](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5682).

![Candidate messages or prices first face justified restrictions concerning truthfulness, data use, and effective refusal. Performance is compared within the permitted set. Customer evidence can require revision of the restrictions or the proposal.](../figures/M09_optimization_boundary.png)

A contemporary implementation could exclude fabricated urgency, prohibit using sensitive information outside the permitted purpose, preserve an effective decline option, and require substantiation of claims. The justification for each restriction must remain explicit. A numerical threshold for comprehension or a reviewer's approval is evidence relevant to that justification; neither is a complete operational definition of Kantian autonomy.

### 9.16.5 A Supported Judgment About Ethical Cost

The strongest supported criticism concerns the incompleteness of an exclusively commercial decision rule. More accurate optimization can intensify an existing conflict between the firm's objective and the conditions of customer agency. An ethical failure follows when the chosen practice violates a justified duty, such as truthful representation, and the firm treats its performance gain as permission to proceed. Establishing that failure requires evidence about the practice and an argument about the duty.

The pricing paper supplies a concrete case in which modeled firm profit rises while aggregate customer surplus falls. The email paper supplies a case in which improved causal performance leaves the recipient's informed benefit as a separate question, while incorporating safeguards that deserve evaluation. Together, they make demanding examples for assessing the proposition that marketing effectiveness can come at an ethical cost. A responsible conclusion can reject a particular deployment, require changes, or endorse a justified use. It should identify the responsible action and evidence, preserving the distinction between a scholar's contribution, a firm's implementation, and an analyst's own normative inference.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

## 9.17 Reproduce Profit and Customer Incidence

### 9.17.1 A Solved Synthetic Pricing Comparison

A firm offers one product to a fixed population over one purchase opportunity. The comparison changes the permitted price policy while holding the population, preferences, costs, and outside option fixed. The following assumptions define an original illustration, without calibration to the papers' data.

\begin{assumption}\label{ass:pricing-population}
Group L has population share $0.6$ and valuations uniformly distributed on $[6,10]$ dollars. Group H has share $0.4$ and valuations uniformly distributed on $[10,30]$ dollars. Group membership has no demographic interpretation.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}\label{ass:pricing-choice}
Each customer buys one unit when valuation is at least the offered price. Utility is valuation less price upon purchase and zero otherwise. Marginal cost is zero. The firm observes group membership and the valuation distributions, but does not observe individual valuations.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}\label{ass:pricing-policies}
The firm can post one common price or one price per group. A third policy permits group-specific discounts subject to a cap at the revenue-maximizing common price. Offers are taken as accurately described. Changes in information, privacy, deliberation, and later demand are outside this illustration.
\end{assumption}

For a group $g$ with valuation support $[a_g,b_g]$ and population weight $w_g$, demand is $q_g(p)=\Pr(v\geq p\mid g)$. Expected profit and customer surplus per eligible customer are

$$
\Pi=\sum_g w_g p_g q_g(p_g),\qquad
CS=\sum_g w_g\,\mathbb{E}[\max(v-p_g,0)\mid g].
$$

Both quantities are in dollars and include nonbuyers in their denominator. Under Assumptions \ref{ass:pricing-population}–\ref{ass:pricing-policies}, the optimal common price is $19/3$, approximately $6.33. The group-specific optima are $6$ and $15$. Capping personalized offers at the common benchmark retains the $6$ discount for L and the common price for H. These optima follow by checking support boundaries and the stationary points of piecewise quadratic revenue.

| Policy | Profit per Customer | Customer Surplus | Purchase Share | Better Off | Worse Off |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Optimal Uniform | $6.0167 | $6.4750 | 95% | 0% | 0% |
| Group-Specific Optimum | $8.1000 | $3.4500 | 90% | 60% | 40% |
| Discounts Capped at Benchmark | $6.1333 | $6.6667 | 100% | 60% | 0% |

Better and worse refer to each person's monetary surplus relative to the common-price benchmark in the same population. Under the group-specific optimum, the gains to L are outweighed in the aggregate by the losses to H. A majority-benefit statement and an aggregate-loss statement are simultaneously correct. Under the capped policy, profit and customer surplus both increase. The restriction changes the solution, and its consequences depend on the stipulated distributions.

![Expected firm profit and customer surplus share the same dollar scale across three synthetic policies. Group-specific optimization increases profit and lowers aggregate customer surplus despite benefiting a majority. Capped discounts increase both measures relative to the uniform benchmark.](../figures/M09_pricing_distribution.png)

Personalization and a majority-gain statistic leave truthful disclosure and permissible data use unresolved. Those requirements enter the ethical evaluation alongside the distribution of monetary gains and losses. The common-price optimum supplies the economic benchmark: replacing it with an arbitrary high price would change the apparent gains from discounts.

### 9.17.2 Python Calculation and Published Aggregates

The program integrates each group's demand and surplus exactly using rational arithmetic. It checks common-price candidates at all support boundaries and interior revenue maxima, solves group-specific prices, and evaluates the cap. A separate input file records rounded published means. Those means reproduce arithmetic only. For the email study, subtracting the rounded click rates gives 17.48 basis points, while its paired estimate is reported as 17.47 basis points. The distinction follows the precision of the published inputs; the calculation does not reconstruct campaign-level uncertainty.

Python source: [evaluate_pricing.py](../../03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/evaluate_pricing.py)

```python
"""Solve an imposed pricing example and check published aggregate arithmetic.

Python 3.10+, standard library. No empirical microdata or model APIs.
Run: python3 03_Data_and_Code/AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/evaluate_pricing.py
"""
import json
from fractions import Fraction as F
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
# Population shares and dollar valuations for one purchase opportunity.
GROUPS = {"L": (F(3, 5), F(6), F(10)),
          "H": (F(2, 5), F(10), F(30))}


def demand(price, low, high):
    """Purchase probability under a uniform valuation distribution."""
    if not low < high or price < 0:
        raise ValueError("Require ordered valuation bounds and nonnegative price.")
    return max(F(0), min(F(1), (high - price) / (high - low)))


def surplus(price, low, high):
    """Expected dollar surplus per eligible customer, including nonbuyers."""
    demand(price, low, high)
    if price <= low:
        return (low + high) / 2 - price
    return max(high - price, F(0)) ** 2 / (2 * (high - low))


def best_uniform(groups):
    """Check support boundaries and stationary points of piecewise revenue."""
    bounds = sorted({F(0)} | {x for _, lo, hi in groups for x in (lo, hi)})
    candidates = set(bounds)
    for left, right in zip(bounds, bounds[1:]):
        midpoint = (left + right) / 2
        intercept, slope = F(0), F(0)
        for weight, low, high in groups:
            if midpoint < low:
                intercept += weight
            elif midpoint < high:
                intercept += weight * high / (high - low)
                slope += weight / (high - low)
        if slope:
            stationary = intercept / (2 * slope)
            if left <= stationary <= right:
                candidates.add(stationary)
    revenue = lambda p: sum(w * p * demand(p, lo, hi)
                            for w, lo, hi in groups)
    return max(sorted(candidates), key=revenue)


def evaluate(prices, reference):
    if set(prices) != set(GROUPS):
        raise ValueError("Every population group requires exactly one price.")
    profit = customer_surplus = quantity = better = worse = F(0)
    for name, (weight, low, high) in GROUPS.items():
        price = prices[name]
        q = demand(price, low, high)
        profit += weight * price * q  # Marginal cost is stipulated to be zero.
        customer_surplus += weight * surplus(price, low, high)
        quantity += weight * q
        if price < reference:
            better += weight * q
        elif price > reference:
            worse += weight * demand(reference, low, high)
    return {"profit_per_eligible_customer": profit,
            "surplus_per_eligible_customer": customer_surplus,
            "total_surplus_per_eligible_customer": profit + customer_surplus,
            "purchase_share": quantity, "strictly_better_share": better,
            "strictly_worse_share": worse}


def main():
    uniform = best_uniform(list(GROUPS.values()))
    segmented = {g: best_uniform([cell]) for g, cell in GROUPS.items()}
    policies = {"uniform": {g: uniform for g in GROUPS},
                "segmented": segmented,
                "discount_only": {g: min(p, uniform) for g, p in segmented.items()}}
    results = {name: {"prices": prices, **evaluate(prices, uniform)}
               for name, prices in policies.items()}
    published = json.loads((ROOT / "published_aggregates.json").read_text())
    clicks = published["causal_alignment"]["campaign_mean_click_rate_bp"]
    revenues = published["personalized_pricing"]["realized_revenue_per_prospect"]
    arithmetic = {
        "click_lift_from_rounded_means_bp": clicks["tuned"] - clicks["control"],
        "click_relative_lift_from_rounded_means": clicks["tuned"] / clicks["control"] - 1,
        "pricing_relative_revenue_lift_from_rounded_means":
            revenues["personalized"] / revenues["uniform"] - 1}
    output = {"data_type": "Exact calculations for an imposed economic example",
              "benchmark": "Revenue-maximizing uniform price in the same population",
              "cost": 0, "groups": GROUPS, "results": results,
              "published_aggregate_arithmetic": arithmetic,
              "scope": "No reconstruction of empirical uncertainty or ethical verdict"}
    (ROOT / "results.json").write_text(json.dumps(
        output, indent=2, default=lambda x: {"exact": str(x), "decimal": float(x)}) + "\n")
    for name, result in results.items():
        print(name, {k: float(v) for k, v in result.items() if k != "prices"})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## 9.18 A Deployment Decision with Reasons

Consider a retailer proposing three changes: an AI-generated appeal, a price conditioned on customer information, and an experiment selecting the combination with the highest contribution margin. State the commercial objective and the recipient's likely purpose separately. Identify the information used for each decision, the basis of the offer's claims, and the options available to someone who refuses. Then specify a maxim that describes what the retailer would actually do.

Evaluate three variants. In the first, the message accurately explains an optional discount and customers can obtain the published standard offer without data-based targeting. In the second, the model invents urgency to increase clicks. In the third, a firm uses an undisclosed inference about urgent need to raise an essential-good price during a disruption. For each variant, identify the evidence needed, the relevant Kantian argument, and the policy provisions whose jurisdiction and coverage require examination. The experimental methods can be similar even when the conduct differs substantially.

A defensible recommendation should name the proposed action, its expected commercial effect, the affected customer outcomes, the ethical reason, and the condition that would change the decision. Rejecting an unsupported claim is part of critical judgment. So is recognizing evidence that weakens an initial accusation or supports a mutually beneficial practice.

### 9.18.1 Intervention Intensity and Customer Judgment

\noindent A more precise estimate of how discounts or repeated contacts change behavior makes a commercial intervention easier to optimize. Its ethical justification depends on the practice being intensified and the customer's ability to understand and refuse it. A manager should identify the stated purpose, the information used to select intensity, and how the customer can revise a decision. Evidence about sales or profit alone leaves these conditions unspecified.

The synthetic discount calculation in M8 Section 8.22 selects different intensities under revenue, profit, and a hypothetical complaint constraint. The constraint expresses one measurable restriction. A low observed complaint rate does not establish informed consent, truthful communication, or an effective opportunity to decline. Kantian respect for persons requires examining how the practice treats the customer's judgment, including safeguards that remain binding when they lower the firm's measured payoff. Confucian concerns with trustworthiness and responsible conduct likewise direct attention to how the offer is presented and how employees respond to a reasoned objection. The numerical complaint threshold remains a hypothetical operating constraint whose justification depends on the customer consequences.

A defensible recommendation distinguishes the estimated response from the reasons for choosing an objective. State who bears the costs of a mistaken intensity, how uncertainty affects deployment, and which practices remain unacceptable even if profitable. A comparison of feasible actions can then evaluate commercial outcomes alongside customer experience without treating a single measured outcome as a complete account of customer agency.

\Needspace{24\baselineskip}

### 9.18.2 Feasible Alternatives and Service Priorities

\noindent A customer can formally decline an offer while facing substantial difficulty reaching another provider. Distance, travel time, disability access, price, and service availability shape the alternatives that refusal leaves open. A network model can measure specified travel constraints. Its edges and thresholds do not establish the customer's considered preferences, informed consent, or ability to act on a decision.

The service-restoration comparison in Section 8.23 separates an imposed profit objective from an objective of expanding access. Kantian respect directs attention to whether the firm's practice preserves customers' capacity to pursue their own purposes and whether its justification treats affected people as ends. Confucian benevolence and trustworthiness direct attention to responsible service, reliable representations, and the effects of managerial conduct on relationships. These perspectives motivate scrutiny of whom a service decision burdens. The five-minute threshold and the priority given to coverage require a separate justification based on customers' needs, competing obligations, and the consequences of the available actions.

A defensible assessment states the commercial rationale, the affected population, the feasible alternatives, and the evidence that could change the recommendation. Sparse map coverage, an unknown availability state, or an inaccessible entrance can change the measured options. Customers' accounts of their needs and constraints can change the interpretation even when the shortest-path calculation remains correct.

Network compression adds a responsibility to preserve evidence about people whose circumstances differ from a group average. Section 5.24 holds the original service population fixed and shows how removing internal travel can overstate access. Section 7.38 shows how majority labels can miss every customer in a small service class. A computational saving needs to be evaluated alongside the burdens created by those errors and the affected customers' opportunities to contest a decision. Kantian respect supports considering their purposes in the justification; Confucian benevolence and trustworthiness support responsible attention to their needs and an accurate account of service. Aggregation alone establishes neither misconduct nor an intention to impair agency.

### 9.18.3 Evidence for Meaningful Customer Choice

\noindent A firm may promise that an automated service respects customer choice while evaluating success primarily on common product questions. Cancellation and refund requests test different obligations. Customers use these interactions to revise a purchase decision or seek a remedy. A high overall success rate supplies limited evidence about those activities when they receive little weight in the evaluation population.

The synthetic service comparison in [Section 7.34](M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md) holds the request roster fixed and produces equal aggregate success alongside worse cancellation outcomes. Equal aggregate success can therefore conceal a failure in the activity through which customers exercise withdrawal. Assessing manipulation additionally requires evidence about the service design and the firm's conduct. A Kantian assessment examines the maxim governing the service: whether the firm preserves customers' ability to act on a considered decision, including when doing so reduces retention. A profitable result does not by itself justify restricting that choice.

Confucian trustworthiness connects a firm's assurances with its conduct when customers seek to leave or contest an answer. Responsible conduct requires attending to the consequences of the service and responding to justified complaints. These considerations motivate evidence about access, completed actions, explanations, and opportunities for correction. The acceptable performance standard depends on the obligations at issue. A defensible recommendation states the conduct expected of the firm, the evidence supporting its assurance, and the observed failures that would require a change.

### 9.18.4 Synthetic Personas and Consumer Representation

\noindent A firm may use generated personas to anticipate how customers could respond to a product. The ethical question concerns the authority the firm gives those responses in decisions that affect people. Synthetic answers can help formulate hypotheses and identify possible objections. Treating them as the considered judgments of actual customers requires evidence about representation that similarity in aggregate ratings alone cannot supply.

The concept-screening comparison in Section 4.23 preserves the overall response distribution while reversing which products appear most attractive. The anchor comparison in Section 5.23 changes the preferred concept while retaining the same authored responses. The firm's measurement choices can therefore change which product it describes as preferred. Whether the practice misrepresents customers depends on the claims the firm makes and the evidence supporting those claims. A Kantian assessment examines whether the practice respects affected people's purposes and opportunities to exercise judgment, including when their responses challenge the commercially favored interpretation.

Confucian trustworthiness requires a truthful account of whose judgments the evidence represents. Responsible conduct includes listening to customers whose needs the model misses and revising decisions when their accounts expose a material error. A firm could use generated reactions to improve the questions it asks, while retaining opportunities for actual customers to express preferences, explain conditions, and contest consequences. The justified claim should distinguish a model's simulated response, a person's stated preference, and observed behavior. Numerical validation assesses the specified prediction task. Consent requires the person's authorization, including when a generated response predicts the person's behavior accurately.

## 9.19 Definitions, Evidence, and Permission

\noindent A firm can make a practice appear successful by choosing categories that absorb the very outcome under dispute. Defining a cancellation request as a completed cancellation makes the two equivalent in a report even when execution remains unresolved. Defining continued payment as satisfaction can similarly conceal customers who face obstacles to leaving. Examine the definitions and the evidence connecting them to the claimed outcome before accepting the commercial interpretation.

Kantian scrutiny asks whether the inference has remained within the conditions that support it. A prediction of acceptance is a statement about behavior under a model and information set. Permission concerns whether an action has been authorized under the relevant conditions. Moving from one to the other requires a premise about authorization that predictive accuracy does not supply. A firm's commercial objective also leaves open which means can be justified to the people affected. These distinctions support separate evidence for preferences, consent, withdrawal, and actual service execution.

Confucian attention to the rectification of names gives a related question about the fit between a role or description and conduct. Calling a process a cancellation service carries expectations about what it accomplishes for the customer. A record system that measures only requests can assess demand for that service, while evidence of completion bears on whether the service performed its role. Preserve the distinction even when the more favorable label benefits the firm. The philosophical accounts developed in §§9.3 and 9.11 inform this comparison; the application to data definitions is an interpretation.

A logically consistent classification system can encode unsupported assumptions. A contradiction can arise from an erroneous record, incompatible periods, or an unsuitable rule. Trace the claim to its source, time, definition, and inference, and assess each part. The cancellation example in §2.25 preserves unknown states and directs unresolved records to review. The feature examples in §§7.39–7.40 show why reconstruction and interpretive labels require separate evaluation. Neither logical coherence nor a high model score establishes the ethical legitimacy of a marketing practice.

## 9.20 An Authorized Agent and a Justified Objective

\noindent A customer asks a subscription service to cancel. The firm instructs its agent to require a retention survey before recording the cancellation. The agent follows the policy, records every action, and successfully obtains a survey response. Its execution can satisfy the firm's technical specification while delaying the outcome the customer requested. The relevant assessment must therefore identify whose instruction supplied the objective and whose choice the procedure affects.

Technical permissions establish which actions the system allows an agent to perform. Company authorization establishes that an employee or service may act on the firm's behalf. Customer authorization concerns the scope of what that customer requested or accepted. Ethical justification concerns the reasons for treating the person in that way. These relationships can overlap, but evidence for one does not establish the others. A record that the firm approved the retention survey supplies no evidence that the customer agreed to make it a condition of exit.

The Kantian analysis in §§9.3 and 9.16 asks whether the maxim governing the practice respects the customer's capacity to form purposes and act on reasons. A firm that describes a retention obstacle as necessary cancellation processing must justify the description and the imposed condition. An explicit, reversible offer that leaves the requested exit available presents a different practice from concealing or withholding that exit. Its assessment depends on the actual procedure, the information supplied, and the person's freedom to decline. A higher renewal rate cannot resolve those questions because retained accounts can include customers whose expressed purposes were frustrated.

Confucian attention to the rectification of names connects the service's stated role with its conduct. A cancellation service should be assessed by whether it carries out the relevant responsibility to the customer. Remonstrance gives employees a reason to challenge a commercially successful rule when it conflicts with that responsibility. In the agent setting, an escalation route can preserve a record of the conflict and permit correction. Its existence alone does not establish that objections are heard or customers obtain the requested outcome.

The surveyed governance mechanisms [(Li et al., 2026)](../../01_Resources/35_Agent_Workflow_Evaluation/README.md), §9, can preserve permission scope, action records, and accountability. The philosophical application asks the further question of whether the objective and means are justified. Evaluate cancellation completion against the customer's expressed request, report imposed obstacles and unresolved cases, and examine the reasons offered for them. A system's technical success is evidence about its execution; the customer's agency remains an independent object of judgment.

## 9.21 Model Agreement and Independent Reasons

\noindent A marketing team asks several models which customers should receive a retention offer. All recommend targeting customers who appear unlikely to leave. Agreement can make the proposal seem well supported, yet the systems may share training examples, category definitions, and objectives. Assessing the recommendation requires identifying which evidence each system contributes and which parts of the agreement arise from their common construction.

The [Platonic Representation Hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.07987v5) concerns convergence among learned representations. Its discussion includes common research practices and constraints as possible contributors to convergence. The philosophical question for a marketing decision concerns the inference from agreement to a warranted belief or action. Shared statistical structure does not by itself establish independent confirmation, causal validity, customer welfare, or permission.

The coordinate comparison in §7.42 holds the imposed meaning of each synthetic label fixed. The mHealth comparison in §7.43 instead measures agreement with a recorded category system. A model could reproduce that system consistently while retaining its ambiguous categories. Evidence that a category is reproducible must be distinguished from evidence that it captures a nutritionally relevant distinction. The same issue arises when several marketing models agree on a label such as valuable, vulnerable, or likely to cancel. The analyst must specify the observations and reasons supporting that interpretation.

Kantian evaluation asks for the maxim governing the action and its treatment of the person's capacity to choose. A prediction of continued payment does not establish that obstructing cancellation respects that capacity. An empirical claim about what customers do and a normative reason for what the firm may do require separate support. This application follows the account in §9.3; a representation-alignment result supplies no additional moral premise.

Confucian attention to the rectification of names asks whether the firm's description of a practice fits its conduct. Calling an intervention helpful requires evidence about the responsibility being discharged and the customer's resulting experience. A team should preserve reasoned objections and examine cases in which model agreement conflicts with a customer's expressed purpose. Independently checked records, customer testimony, and a clear account of the permissible action give the recommendation a basis that agreement alone cannot provide.

## 9.22 Pricing Authority and Customer Alternatives

\noindent A restaurant director is asked to approve a pricing service that raises expected profit. The proposal describes the service as improving the customer experience, but the financial forecast supplies no measure of that experience. The director must examine the connection between the system's information, its pricing objective, and the customer's alternatives. The Wendy's complaint in §8.28 motivates this decision through disputed allegations about shared data and pricing authority. A reasoned evaluation must keep those allegations, the available evidence, and the moral assessment distinct.

### 9.22.1 The Maxim and the Customer's Judgment

\noindent A Kantian evaluation starts with the principle governing the proposed action. Consider an operator who proposes to use a demand forecast to adjust prices while accurately explaining material terms and respecting the customer's ability to decline. Compare that maxim with a proposal to conceal a common pricing arrangement because customers would otherwise question whether competing offers are independent. Their purposes and means require separate examination. The second hypothetical maxim relies on customers lacking information relevant to their judgment; its commercial success supplies no justification for that reliance.

The humanity formulation directs attention to persons' capacity to set and pursue ends. Using customer information in a commercial exchange does not by itself establish that a person is treated merely as a means. The assessment concerns whether the practice respects the person's rational agency, including the conditions under which an offer can be understood and refused. Truthful disclosure matters, while the content of the arrangement and the person's feasible alternatives remain consequential. Public disclosure alone supplies no proof that a practice is permissible. The principles developed in §9.3 support these contemporary applications. Claims about the defendants' intentions require evidence about their conduct and knowledge.

An affirmative purchase can reflect a preference among available options even when those options have become less favorable. The synthetic calculation in §4.26 makes that distinction concrete. Consumers continue purchasing under joint pricing while receiving less surplus than under independent pricing at the same information level. The comparison concerns the specified alternatives and preferences. It gives no numerical measure of free will and does not establish a universal ethical threshold for acceptable prices.

### 9.22.2 Trustworthiness and the Responsibilities of a Pricing Service

\noindent Confucian trustworthiness directs attention to whether the firm's explanation matches its conduct. A claim that franchisees control prices should be assessed against their actual authority, incentives, and ability to challenge recommendations. A claim that a system benefits customers requires evidence about the benefit being asserted. The rectification of names connects the description of a service to the responsibilities it performs. Accurate labels help customers, operators, and employees understand who is accountable for a decision.

The contrast between righteousness and profit in §9.11 asks how commercial advantage relates to the obligations of a role. For a pricing team, a contemporary application is to retain the capacity to report customer losses and question a commercially successful policy. Employees need a credible route for presenting contrary evidence, and managers need to respond to its substance. A performance system that rewards only revenue can make those responsibilities costly to exercise. The institutional question concerns the conduct the organization repeatedly encourages, including how it treats a truthful challenge.

### 9.22.3 Evidence and the Burden of Justification

\noindent Economic self-interest supplies a reason to examine the firm's account closely. It also identifies what the firm should substantiate when requesting authority to deploy a pricing system. Relevant explanations include how data are used, who sets prices, which customer outcomes were measured, and how conflicts between commercial and customer outcomes are handled. The burden of justifying deployment can be demanding while a legal allegation still requires the evidence and procedures appropriate to adjudication. An incentive to benefit from a practice does not establish that the alleged conduct occurred.

The distinction also applies to critical readings of research. The complaint cites a model (Harrington, 2022) in which outsourcing can lower consumer welfare while leaving competitive intensity unchanged under its assumptions. That result gives a reason to evaluate customer consequences independently of a competition conclusion. It establishes no fact about a particular franchise arrangement. A defensible recommendation identifies the source of its empirical claim, the alternative being compared, and the additional moral premise supporting the proposed action [(Harrington, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.4241).

For the restaurant director, the resulting decision is conditional on both evidence and conduct. An operating improvement should be supported by the outcome it claims to improve. A change in pricing authority requires an account of the affected businesses and customers. A proposed restriction on choice requires reasons that respect the people whose options it changes. Commercial success, legal status, and moral justification remain separate objects of evaluation.

## 9.23 Geographic Classification and Meaningful Customer Choice

\noindent A retailer observes low computer usage in an area and considers two actions: offer help using a service, or restrict access to customers who complete an app workflow. Both actions can use the same statistical description while changing customers' opportunities in opposite directions. Their justification depends on the authority claimed over the customer and the options each action leaves available.

A Kantian critique first examines the inference. An area's application index is a representation of selected device activity under particular categories and weights. Treating it as an individual's capacity or willingness extends the claim beyond its evidence. The statistical result does not supply the additional premise that a customer has authorized the firm to decide which channels or benefits that customer should receive.

Respect for persons also concerns the practice's purpose and operation. Assistance can help a customer complete a self-chosen task. A mandatory digital procedure can impose costs on people who have less suitable equipment, while using their difficulty to discourage an otherwise valid request. A defensible rule must address the reasons customers could give for needing another channel, the possibility of correcting a classification, and the continued ability to refuse an optional service or end a relationship.

Confucian concerns with humane conduct and the responsibilities of a role direct attention to how the firm responds when customers need help. A seller's informational advantage can create an obligation to explain terms and accommodate difficulty in ordinary service. Benevolent intent alone does not establish that an accommodation serves the person's goals. Asking which task the customer wants completed, preserving a usable alternative, and receiving correction give practical content to that responsibility without presuming that the firm knows the customer's interests better than the customer does.

The geographic clustering in Section 4.27 groups measured activity. Its stability under repeated initialization and its sensitivity to scaling concern the description of the data. Neither property determines whether excluding a person is justified. An evaluation of the marketing practice must connect its stated purpose, the customer information it actually observes, the person's available choices, and the consequences of accepting or refusing the procedure.


## 9.24 Advertising Response, Statistical Evidence, and Customer Reasons

\noindent A consumer lender choosing an advertisement can ask whether its content changes loan take-up. It also faces a different question about the grounds on which customers decide to borrow. A photograph, a suggested use for the loan, a description of the interest rate, and language about losses can affect attention and choice through different mechanisms. Commercial response alone leaves the customer's understanding, reasons, and subsequent experience unresolved.

The [public P-Bench advertising task](https://huggingface.co/datasets/May2222/P-Bench/blob/main/tasks/chi_square_test/dfeep__paper_90__task_4/question.txt) describes a randomized field experiment among former borrowers of a South African consumer lender. Its statistical question concerns 13 advertising-content coefficients jointly. Writing those coefficients as $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_{13}$, the null is $H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_{13}=0$. Under a justified specification and test, rejecting that joint null supplies evidence that at least one coefficient differs from zero. The result does not identify every effective feature or establish a particular psychological mechanism. Direction and economic magnitude require the relevant estimates and contrasts.

Suppose a firm concludes that an advertisement benefits customers because more of them borrow. That inference adds a premise equating additional borrowing with customer benefit. Customers may obtain useful liquidity, misunderstand repayment costs, respond to a misleading comparison, or borrow for a purpose they later regret. Evidence about comprehension, repayment burdens, intended use, and experienced outcomes helps distinguish these possibilities. A well-executed take-up test does not supply that evidence automatically.

The humanity formulation directs attention to whether the firm's procedure respects customers as persons capable of setting ends and assessing reasons. An advertisement can communicate a relevant product benefit while also serving the seller's interest. The ethical difficulty arises when the firm secures agreement by concealing material terms, exploiting a misunderstanding, or obstructing a person's considered refusal. A visual cue's effect on take-up alone does not establish any of these mechanisms. The justification must examine what information the customer receives and how the procedure treats the customer's ability to judge and decline.

Confucian attention to humane conduct and the responsibilities of a role asks how a lender uses its informational advantage in a relationship of reliance. Clear explanations, correction of misleading impressions, and responsiveness to difficulty give that responsibility observable content. A claim of benevolent intent remains open to examination against the actual service and the borrower's experience. Customer disagreement supplies evidence for examining the firm's judgment and response.

The same reasoning applies when an AI assistant supplies the statistical analysis. The benchmark evaluator compares a decision and p-value with a reference answer. A commercial objective may reward greater take-up. Each criterion measures a narrower achievement than a defensible lending practice. Require a justified statistical comparison, evidence on the consequences customers experience, and an account of why the firm's means respect their agency. An error at one stage cannot be repaired by success at another.

A manager delegating econometric code retains responsibility for choosing the question, checking the measurement, and evaluating the action taken on the result. The coding-workflow benchmark in Section 1.19 fixes the method in advance; success establishes agreement with its numerical reference under stated rules. A campaign can satisfy that computational requirement while relying on a misleading promise or disregarding a customer's expressed refusal. Kantian scrutiny examines the reasons and authority for the practice. Confucian scrutiny examines truthful reporting and the manager's response when an analyst identifies a material error. Preserving an opportunity to challenge an automated recommendation connects analytical competence to responsible conduct.

## 9.25 Evidence for a Small Burden

\noindent A subscription firm claims that a revised cancellation process imposes little additional burden. The relevant question concerns a tolerable increase in time, abandonment, charges, or difficulty for the affected population. Testing whether the mean time difference equals exactly zero answers only one part of that question. A nonsignificant result can arise from an interval that includes both small and substantial burdens [(Lakens, 2022, Chapter 9)](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/09-equivalencetest.html).

Suppose independent customers complete a cancellation task, and $\theta$ is the revised process's mean time minus the original process's mean time, in seconds. Set an illustrative equivalence range of minus five to plus five seconds before examining outcomes. The two one-sided tests evaluate $H_{0L}:\theta\leq-5$ and $H_{0U}:\theta\geq5$, each at 5%. Rejecting both establishes equivalence within the chosen range under the sampling model. With the same standard error and degrees of freedom, this requires the entire 90% two-sided confidence interval to lie inside the range [(Lakens, 2022, Chapter 9)](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/09-equivalencetest.html).

Four hypothetical cases use a pooled standard deviation of 20 seconds in each arm. With 50 customers per arm, an estimated four-second increase has a p-value of 0.320 against zero and a 90% interval of $[-2.64,10.64]$. Neither equality nor a small burden follows. With 800 per arm, a half-second increase has a 90% interval of $[-1.15,2.15]$ and satisfies equivalence. A three-second increase at the same precision is both statistically distinguishable from zero and equivalent within the prespecified range. Detection of a difference and evidence that it is small can therefore coexist.

![Four hypothetical mean task-time differences with 90% intervals. Two-sided equivalence requires both interval ends within the chosen five-second bounds.](../figures/M09_equivalence_and_burden.png)

A six-second reduction fails two-sided equivalence because it is too far below zero, yet its upper confidence bound excludes an increase of five seconds. For a decision concerned only with excessive additional time, a one-sided noninferiority question is appropriate: test $H_0:\theta\geq5$ against $\theta<5$, or require a one-sided 95% upper bound below five. The choice between these questions follows the decision and must precede the result.

The numerical tolerance also requires justification. A five-second mean can conceal concentrated burdens, and an analysis of completed tasks leaves abandonment and failed cancellation as separate outcomes. Kantian respect for persons asks whether customers can understand and exercise their decision to leave. Confucian attention to responsible service asks how the firm responds to difficulty and requests for correction. Neither principle supplies a five-second threshold automatically. Evidence of a small mean time difference supports a specific empirical claim; the procedure's permissibility additionally depends on its effects and treatment of customer choice.

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/equivalence_claims.py
```
 Its inputs are hypothetical sufficient statistics, with no generated individual records. The complete implementation reports zero-null tests, both equivalence tests, 90% intervals, and the one-sided upper-bound decision.


Python source: [equivalence_claims.py](../../03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/equivalence_claims.py)

```python
"""Hypothetical cancellation-time summaries with prespecified +/-5 second bounds."""
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

OUTPUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "results"
BOUND, ALPHA = 5.0, .05
# Each scenario is a separate hypothetical parallel-group experiment.
CASES = [("imprecise", 50, 60.0, 64.0, 20.0),
         ("precise_small", 800, 60.0, 60.5, 20.0),
         ("detectable_small", 800, 60.0, 63.0, 20.0),
         ("faster", 800, 60.0, 54.0, 20.0)]


def assess(name, n, control_mean, treatment_mean, sample_sd, bound=BOUND):
    if n < 2 or sample_sd <= 0 or bound <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Require at least two customers per arm, positive SD and bound")
    delta = treatment_mean - control_mean
    df = 2 * n - 2
    se = sample_sd * np.sqrt(2 / n)
    p_zero = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(delta / se), df)
    lower_p = stats.t.sf((delta + bound) / se, df)
    upper_p = stats.t.cdf((delta - bound) / se, df)
    half90 = stats.t.ppf(1 - ALPHA, df) * se
    half95 = stats.t.ppf(1 - ALPHA / 2, df) * se
    return {"case": name, "n_per_arm": n, "control_mean_seconds": control_mean,
        "treatment_mean_seconds": treatment_mean, "sd_each_arm_seconds": sample_sd,
        "estimate_seconds": delta, "se_seconds": se, "df": df,
        "p_zero": p_zero, "lower_bound_seconds": -bound, "upper_bound_seconds": bound,
        "tost_lower_p": lower_p, "tost_upper_p": upper_p,
        "tost_p": max(lower_p, upper_p), "equivalent": max(lower_p, upper_p) < ALPHA,
        "ci90_low": delta - half90, "ci90_high": delta + half90,
        "ci95_low": delta - half95, "ci95_high": delta + half95,
        "noninferior_below_upper_bound": upper_p < ALPHA}


def main():
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    result = pd.DataFrame([assess(*case) for case in CASES])
    result.to_csv(OUTPUT / "equivalence_claims.csv", index=False, float_format="%.12g")
    print(result.to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## 9.26 Electricity Infrastructure, Public Reassurance, and Agency

\noindent A public authority deciding whether to approve a data-center connection must determine who bears its costs, which risks remain unresolved, and which safeguards protect affected households. A research result can influence that decision through its public interpretation. Calling an uncertain effect harmless can weaken the case for financial guarantees, transparent cost allocation, or subsequent review. These are potential consequences of misleading reassurance; attributing an actual approval or household loss to this paper would require evidence connecting the communication to the decision and its outcomes.

The HBS Working Knowledge coverage supplies an example of overstatement by attributing no consumer electricity-cost increase to four large developers [(Kost, 2026)](https://www.library.hbs.edu/working-knowledge/blaming-data-centers-for-higher-electric-bills-its-not-that-simple). Table 4 reports an uncertain positive coefficient for those firms and a direct developer-difference test with $p=0.101$ [(Rana et al., 2026)](../../01_Resources/41_Statistical_Claims_and_Decisions/RanaKapsNetessine_WorkingPaper2026.pdf). Nonrejection alone supplies no substantive conclusion of harmlessness. The article acknowledges future uncertainty, while its categorical historical claim still exceeds the reported evidence. The bounds and missing-premise exercise in §8.31.1 identify the inferential failure precisely.

### 9.26.1 What Exists in the Analysis and What the Claim Requires

\noindent An ontology specifies the entities, properties, and relations represented in an account. The electricity study represents utilities, installed capacity, customer classes, sales, costs, and average prices. A claim about household welfare additionally concerns persons with unequal incomes, needs, exposures, and opportunities. A claim about agency concerns their authority to understand, question, and influence decisions that bind them. Increasing the precision of a utility-average price estimate leaves these other objects unmeasured.

The strongest ontological objection concerns a change in what the analysis is taken to represent. A utility average becomes a statement about each household; a four-owner indicator becomes a business model; an unresolved price effect becomes absence of harm. Each substitution requires a further argument or additional evidence. Studying one price outcome is a legitimate research choice. Treating that restricted outcome as a complete account of affected persons and permissible conduct commits a category error. The statistical objection concerns what the evidence supports; the ontological objection concerns which objects the claim purports to describe; the ethical objection concerns the authority to impose the resulting burdens.
