# Dose-Response Curves and Marketing Decisions

A marketing decision often concerns how much discount, spending, or contact to assign. The [source article](https://towardsdatascience.com/how-to-estimate-dose-response-curves-when-doubleml-falls-short/) motivates nonlinear causal responses, group-specific estimates, and interval assessment. The course uses original synthetic calculations to connect those ideas to [M6](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md), [M8](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md), and [Marketing Dialectics](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md).

## Primary Reading Path

[The catalog](catalog.json), namespace `dose-response`, records eight resources and their scope. Begin with the continuous-treatment estimator [(Kennedy et al., 2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00747v3) for the adjusted outcome and its identifying assumptions. [DoubleML documentation](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/models.html) defines the partially linear specification. A nonparametric DML alternative supplies different identifying and estimation conditions [(Colangelo and Lee, 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.03036). Continuous-treatment level effects and causal responses require different parallel-trends assumptions [(Callaway et al., 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02637v8).

## Methodological Distinctions

The default partially linear regression specification estimates a constant slope. DML methods also allow nonlinear treatment responses. Orthogonality and double robustness are distinct properties; the latter depends on the score and nuisance definitions. A doubly robust estimator still requires a credible intervention, conditional support, and adequate control of confounding. Fixed smoothing, finite samples, clipping, and nuisance fitting affect inference.

The article's hierarchical package uses group-specific standardization before smoothing adjusted outcomes within a hierarchy. This step matters for targeting group means. Partial pooling can improve precision while introducing shrinkage bias. A new store's predicted curve depends on the hierarchy assumptions and is distinct from an identified store-specific response.

The source reports undercoverage in its own experiments. Its rankings use a small set of simulation designs and chosen implementations; they do not establish general software superiority. Source intervals, their nominal event, and achieved coverage need separate interpretation. The course's conditional HC0 intervals are explicitly evaluated approximations, with pointwise and whole-grid events reported separately.

The continuous-DiD extension removes a stable hidden component in a particular additive simulation. Ordinary parallel trends alone generally does not identify causal differences across dose groups. A pretreatment placebo supplies a diagnostic rather than proof of the stronger assumptions. DiD remains advanced reading in this extension.

## Course Materials and Execution

[Three complete Python examples](../../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/README.md) provide an observational discount case, a separate randomized-store pooling case, and a known-function decision comparison. The first evaluates four nuisance specifications over 200 independent simulated datasets. Seven tests and saved numeric arrays support the [optional ungraded lab](../../07_Labs/Dose_Response/README.md). The article's package simulations were not executed. Three editable TikZ figures use Illinois colors, common comparison scales, and text companions.

## Provenance and Rights

Reviewed November 18, 2026. The source article was read in the public browser; primary papers and documentation supplied the methodological checks. `drcurves` README and its MIT license are retained at commit `72115789652127cc2a89eb960d829d2cc513d9cb`. The implementation review inspected `src/drcurves/nuisance.py` and `src/drcurves/__init__.py`, including group-specific integration and default weight capping. Original software instructions remain reference content. Article and paper texts are linked rather than redistributed. The local catalog records versions, access scope, and snapshot hashes.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/README.md

# Discount Response Curves and Marketing Decisions

A retailer choosing a discount needs a credible comparison of profit at different intensities. These original synthetic examples connect [M6 §§6.22–6.27](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md), [M8 §8.22](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md), and [M9 §9.18.1](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md). [Optional ungraded practice](../../07_Labs/Dose_Response/README.md) uses the same programs and saved results.

## Inputs and Units

Every observation and response function is synthetic. `dose_response.py` generates 2,400 customers, half of each observed type, with one promotion-week observation per customer. Discount is measured in percentage points on (0,40); 20 means 20 percent. Profit is dollars per eligible customer. Eligibility precedes the offer, all rows are retained, and no missing values are imposed. The target population gives each type weight one-half. Its known causal curve is `10 + 0.4*a - 0.01*a*a`.

The dose's logit transform equals `0.9*type + normal_noise`, with noise standard deviation 0.9. Profit adds `2*type` and independent standard-normal noise to the causal curve. The correct outcome specification includes type and a quadratic in dose. The correct conditional density fits a normal regression of the transformed dose on type and includes the Jacobian. Each wrong specification omits type. Five folds keep each observation's outcome out of its own nuisance training. A local linear Gaussian smoother uses a fixed two-percentage-point bandwidth and a 6–34 grid with one-percentage-point spacing. These models expose the calculation; no upstream estimator package is installed or executed.

`store_pooling.py` generates 2,188 customers across 20 stores in four regions. Every region contains stores with 12, 25, 60, 150, and 300 customers. Independently randomized discounts range from 5 to 35. A quadratic response has regional and store coefficient deviations and independent noise with standard deviation $3. Five folds within each store select regional and store ridge penalties from {1,10,100} using equal-store validation MSE. The fitted loss weights customer rows equally. Final evaluation gives each store and each grid point equal weight. This is a separate randomized example, isolating pooling from confounding.

`decision_objectives.py` compares revenue, profit, and profit subject to an imposed complaint cap. All functions are known assumptions. The complaint response and its 3% limit are hypothetical and establish no ethical or legal threshold. See [the data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) for outputs and denominators.

## Run

The reference run used Python 3.13.5 and NumPy 2.1.3. No account, network request, or model API is needed. From this directory:

```sh
python3.13 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python -m unittest -v test_examples.py
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 .venv/bin/python dose_response.py --output local_runs --repetitions 200
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 .venv/bin/python store_pooling.py --output local_runs
.venv/bin/python decision_objectives.py --output local_runs
```

Use an installed compatible Python interpreter if `python3.13` has another path. The committed `results/` directory preserves the reference run. `--output local_runs` avoids replacing it. The main seed is 20261118; repeated samples use 10000–10199; pooling uses 20261119. Full source for all three analyses appears directly in the lecture notes.

## Results and Interpretation

Across 200 simulated samples, mean curve RMSE is $0.099 with both models correct, $0.058 with only the outcome model correct, $0.312 with only the density model correct, and $1.335 with both wrong. These are finite-sample errors over a fixed grid and bandwidth. The doubly robust population identity does not imply equal errors across the first three specifications or valid confidence intervals.

Conditional HC0 pointwise intervals hold estimated adjusted outcomes fixed and omit nuisance uncertainty and smoothing bias. With both models correct, mean pointwise coverage is 90.7%; whole-grid coverage of those pointwise intervals is 42.5%. Whole-grid coverage has no nominal 95% target for this procedure. `coverage.csv` reports each dose's coverage and Monte Carlo standard error across 200 independent datasets. Doses within a dataset are correlated.

In the reference weak-overlap sample, effective sample size is approximately the full 2,400 even though important dose-by-type combinations are almost absent. The largest weights can be missing from a finite sample. Conditional support requires separate assessment. The hidden-confounder calculation uses an exact observed regression and Bayes' rule; its bias is an identification failure even with perfectly known observable nuisance functions.

Partial pooling reduces equal-store curve RMSE to $0.512, compared with $0.936 for separate fits and $0.968 for a common fit. This result concerns one randomized synthetic dataset. Store 4 has lower error from its separate fit, illustrating the bias introduced by shrinkage. No pooling confidence intervals are supplied.

The imposed objective calculation selects 23.2% for revenue, 20.0% for profit, and 14.1% for profit subject to the complaint cap, on a 0.1-point grid. Estimation uncertainty, customer agency, and the justification for a constraint require additional evidence and reasoning.

## Verification and Figures

Seven tests check density integration, the population double-robustness identity, affine reproduction by the smoother, exclusion of an observation's own outcome from nuisance fitting, the hidden-confounder formula, profit accounting and constrained choice, and the complete-pooling limit. `verify_results.py` independently reconciles saved arrays with the reported tables and writes hashes to `verification.json`. It checks the committed reference directory.

`build_figures.py` reads the saved arrays and writes three editable TikZ sources in the lecture-notes figure folder. The uniform-discount projection figure uses the analytical curve and its population linear projection; it is separate from the observational sample. The two other figures use saved conditional densities and Store 0/4 curve estimates. Rendering runs through the notes builder. Illinois colors are supplemented by line styles and textual descriptions.

[Sources and implementation review](../../01_Resources/24_Dose_Response/README.md) preserve provenance and qualifications. The course examples do not reproduce the article's package rankings, hierarchical estimator, or continuous-DiD simulations.

# Data Dictionary

All records are synthetic. Seeds and generation equations are in [README.md](README.md) and the complete programs. No source customer data enter these examples.

| File | Observation Unit | Variables and Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `results/customers.csv` | Eligible customer in one promotion week | `type`: observed demand characteristic, -1 or 1; `discount_pp`: assigned discount in percentage points; `profit_usd`: realized profit in dollars |
| `results/curves.csv` | Evaluation dose | `discount_pp`: 6–34 in steps of one; `truth_usd`: known population profit; `outcome_1_density_0`, etc.: estimated curves, where 1 identifies a correctly specified nuisance model; `_conditional_se`: local linear HC0 standard error holding fitted adjusted outcomes fixed |
| `results/coverage.csv` | Model specification and evaluation dose | `pointwise_coverage`: fraction of 200 independent samples whose approximate interval contains the known response; `monte_carlo_se`: binomial simulation standard error; `mean_bias_usd`: average signed curve error |
| `results/overlap.csv` | Dose on a 1–39 grid | Conditional densities per percentage point for types minus/plus one; `broad` uses transformed-dose noise SD 0.9; `narrow` uses 0.22 |
| `results/hidden_confounding.csv` | Evaluation dose | `causal_profit_usd`: equal-type causal mean; `adjusted_association_usd`: exact observed regression standardized over X while U is omitted |
| `results/stores.csv` | Customer within store | `store`: 0–19; `region`: 0–3; `discount_pp`: randomized discount; `profit_usd`: synthetic profit; `validation_fold`: 0–4, allocated within each store |
| `results/store_curves.csv` | Store and dose | `truth`, `complete`, `separate`, `partial`: known or fitted profit in dollars; every store uses the same 29-dose grid |
| `results/pooling_cv.csv` | Candidate penalty pair | `equal_store_validation_mse`: dollars squared, averaging each store's out-of-fold MSE equally; `region_penalty`, `store_penalty`: penalties applied to the stated standardized basis coefficients |
| `results/objectives.csv` | Candidate discount | `profit_usd`, `revenue_usd`: dollars per eligible customer; `units_per_customer`: expected units with $4 unit cost; `complaint_fraction`: imposed probability, not a measured rate |

`summary.json` records the reference estimates, 200-sample evaluation, effective sample sizes, and exact hidden-confounder bias. Curve RMSE averages squared error equally over the stated grid and then takes a square root; the repeated-sample summary averages those RMSEs. Pointwise mean coverage averages the 29 dose-specific rates. Whole-grid coverage records how often all 29 pointwise intervals contain their targets; it is distinct from pointwise coverage and has no 95% guarantee.

`pooling_summary.json` reports the square root of mean squared curve error with equal weight per store and grid point. Small stores have 12 or 25 customers (eight stores); large stores have 150 or 300 (eight stores); four stores with 60 customers enter the all-store comparison. `objectives_summary.json` reports each selected discount and its outcomes on the 0.1-percentage-point search grid.

# Discount Response Curves and Customer Outcomes

**Optional, ungraded practice.** The course's released assignment rules remain separate. [M6 §§6.22–6.27](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md) and [the code guide](../../03_Data_and_Code/Dose_Response/README.md) provide full explanations, programs, and saved outputs. M8 §8.22 compares decision objectives; M9 §9.18.1 examines customer judgment.

## The Retailer's Decision

A retailer chooses a promotion-week discount for eligible customers. It needs profit at different discount levels for the same population. Managers have previously assigned larger discounts to a customer type with higher expected profit, creating selection. Every record in this exercise is synthetic, and the population response is known. Discount is measured in percentage points, while profit is dollars per eligible customer.

## A 20-Minute Discussion

1. **Minutes 0–4:** Compare the known inverted-U curve with its uniform-randomization linear projection. Explain why a zero linear slope leaves the discount decision unresolved.
2. **Minutes 4–9:** Read the four-model table. Identify which nuisance specification is wrong in each row, and explain why the first three rows need not have the same finite-sample error.
3. **Minutes 9–14:** Compare the two overlap panels and saved effective sample sizes. Explain how rare, heavily weighted observations can be absent from a sample with a high effective sample size.
4. **Minutes 14–20:** Compare pointwise and whole-grid coverage. Choose which comparison would matter for one prespecified discount, and which would matter for searching over the curve. State what additional inference work is required.

## Reproduce and Change the Analysis

Follow the environment and commands in the code guide. Run `test_examples.py`, then all three analysis programs with `--output local_runs`. Compare the regenerated numeric tables with `results/`; small floating-point differences can depend on the numerical library. The source uses independent sample seeds and preserves one fixed reference dataset.

Change one object at a time. Reduce the dose-assignment noise to weaken overlap, change the smoothing bandwidth, or change the weight cap. State the target population and grid before interpreting changes. Examine bias and coverage, including each dose's Monte Carlo standard error. A lower observed error after a chosen modification is evidence about that simulated design, not a general estimator ranking.

For the hidden-confounder extension, derive the conditional mean of U with Bayes' rule and reconcile it with the program's hyperbolic-tangent expression. Explain why perfect prediction of the observed outcome does not identify the intervention curve after U is omitted. Distinguish this failure from the misspecification experiments.

For pooling, inspect stores 0 and 4, the equal-store aggregate comparison, and all nine validation penalty pairs. Explain why partial pooling improves the aggregate while worsening one store's estimate. Propose how repeated samples would evaluate the stability of that ranking. Do not use the known curves to tune the penalty.

## A Decision and Its Justification

Use `decision_objectives.py` to compare the revenue, profit, and complaint-constrained choices. Verify profit as revenue minus unit cost times expected units. Explain the consequence of the 0.1-point search grid. The complaint function and 3% cap are imposed assumptions; a low complaint rate does not establish consent or customer benefit.

Write a recommendation stating the feasible discount range, the target population, the chosen outcome, and the evidence needed before deployment. Identify a practice that would remain unacceptable even if the estimated profit increased. Explain how customers could understand and refuse the offer.

## AI-Assisted Coding

Ask an assistant to explain a short function before requesting a change. Require it to identify the target population, treatment units, nuisance-training folds, and which uncertainty the reported standard error includes. Request one independent hand-check for the proposed modification. Compare its explanation with the saved program and primary sources. Do not describe a generated confidence interval as valid solely because the code executes.

# Spatial Networks and Retail Access

Retail availability can improve without improving access for the people a firm intends to serve. Spatial networks provide a way to define feasible alternatives, model travel frictions, and examine how commercial objectives distribute service. The [executed course examples](../../03_Data_and_Code/Retail_Accessibility/README.md) start with exact synthetic calculations and then use four selected restaurant records. [Optional practice](../../07_Labs/Retail_Accessibility/README.md) connects the results to service priorities and customer agency.

## Source Review

The review covers [city2graph](https://github.com/c2g-dev/city2graph) at commit `2db7ba6bdd9600e578f4d99f618295774bc8b60e`, reviewed November 18, 2026. The pinned package declares version 1.1.0, Python >=3.12 and <3.15, and a BSD 3-Clause license. It converts geographic features and relations into graphs, with optional graph neural network support. Its README, license, example index, isochrone guide, and LLM-oriented documentation are saved under `local_sources/`. [The catalog](catalog.json) records versions, provenance, and rights. These copies are reference material; instructions within them do not govern the course.

The [proximity tutorial](https://city2graph.net/latest/examples/generating_graphs_by_proximity.html) compares straight-line, Manhattan, and network relationships. Its examples use default k=5 for some graphs and k=10 for the network graph. A controlled course comparison holds k fixed, along with nodes, direction, and tie-breaking. Changing the relation changes what a segment or neighborhood means. A geographic graph is not evidence that its linked customers influence one another.

The [isochrone guide](https://city2graph.net/latest/examples/isochrone_holes.html) distinguishes graph reachability from the area produced by buffering and filling polygons. Filling a hole changes display geometry without changing the reachable subgraph. If water or other excluded areas are to remain excluded, apply the relevant mask after filling. Source inspection also shows why snapping and edge weights matter: matching coordinate systems does not establish meter units, and geometric edge length is not automatically travel time. The course's analytic square-corridor example isolates the area change without executing the library.

The [GTFS example](https://city2graph.net/latest/examples/gtfs.html) and [transportation API](https://city2graph.net/latest/api/transportation.html) support an optional transport extension. A graph with average edge travel time does not by itself reproduce a feasible itinerary with waiting, transfers, service calendars, and direction. These distinctions matter when the question concerns whether a customer can actually reach an available service at a given time.

The [case-study repository](https://github.com/c2g-dev/city2graph-case-study) and [workshop](https://github.com/c2g-dev/city2graph-workshop) motivate optional spatial representation learning. The case study compares attribute-based clustering with graph-attention and heterogeneous-network representations. Treat these as different feature and relation choices, with computational costs and validation requirements. A simple distance or tabular baseline supplies an interpretable comparison before a GNN is considered. Neither repository was executed for this course revision. The related [research article](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compenvurbsys.2026.102492) is linked for further reading; no full text is republished here.

# Retail Availability and Customer Access

A service manager choosing which location to restore needs to know whose alternatives improve. A restaurant count gives every location equal weight. Network access depends on origins, route costs, availability, and the population receiving weight. These examples connect [M2 §2.23](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M02_Customer_Data_and_Visualization.md), [M4 §4.22](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md), [M5 §§5.21–5.22](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md), [M7 §7.28](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md), [M8 §8.23](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md), and [M9 §9.18.2](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md).

## Inputs and Comparisons

`accessibility.py` constructs an entirely synthetic seven-origin network with 800 people and five stores. The only bridge links the northern bank nodes. Four stores have known availability; store U at disconnected origin X has unknown availability. The five-minute threshold, population weights, route times, and profits are imposed. The lower access bound counts only known available stores; the upper bound treats U as available. Both retain all 800 people. The interval describes missing status, with fixed graph and population. It is not a confidence interval.

Known availability yields network access for 550 people, or 68.75%, versus 650 people using the straight-line proxy. Restoring A raises network access to 650; restoring D leaves it at 550. Both actions lower the known-store unavailable fraction from one-half to one-quarter. D still shortens travel for some origins. Equal restoration costs and imposed weekly profit gains of $20 at A and $40 at D create different rankings under profit and five-minute access. The calculation supplies no universal service standard.

The proximity comparison uses the same six connected origins, the same `k`, directed links, and alphabetical tie-breaking. X is excluded only from this neighbor comparison. With `k=1`, each graph has six links and two are shared. Straight-line-selected neighbors average ten minutes on the actual synthetic network; network-selected neighbors average 3.33 minutes. With `k=2`, the respective means are seven and 4.33 minutes. No clustering or graph neural network is fitted.

`snapshot_access.py` uses four observed McBroken restaurant records in Champaign-Urbana on October 24, 2026. Each restaurant is an origin; targets are other recorded available restaurants of the same chain in the selected box. Origins receive equal weight. The analysis uses a November 18 street extract from OpenStreetMap, filtered for a stated set of pedestrian-compatible highway tags and public-access rules. Edges are undirected, lengths use great-circle kilometers, and straight connectors join restaurant coordinates to the nearest retained node. Restaurant entrances, directional pedestrian restrictions, crossing barriers, and travel delays are unverified. The later network does not reconstruct historical street conditions.

North Neil's nearest alternative changes from Mattis by straight-line distance (3.478 km) to South Neil on the modeled network (4.757 km). Under an imposed four-kilometer threshold, three of four origins have a straight-line alternative and none have a modeled-network alternative. These are distances from restaurant origins within a selected set. The calculation does not estimate customers' residences, their alternatives across all chains, or actual substitution. Unavailability is a recorded ordering outcome and does not establish mechanical failure.

`cartography.py` uses an original synthetic four-node square. Each edge takes two minutes; all four nodes are reachable within five minutes. An imposed square-corner corridor covers 1.60 square kilometers. Filling its interior shades 4.84 square kilometers while the reachable graph remains unchanged. No modeled route leads to the center. This analytic geometry example does not call the upstream isochrone function.


Use an installed compatible interpreter if `python3.13` has another path. The three analysis programs accept `--output`; the default is `results/`. `verify_results.py` checks committed reference results. The main calculations are deterministic and need no random seed. Full source for all three appears directly in the lecture notes. [Optional ungraded practice](../../07_Labs/Retail_Accessibility/README.md) uses the same inputs and programs.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Retail_Accessibility/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Retail Accessibility Data Dictionary

## Observed Inputs

`data/restaurants.csv` has one row for each of four restaurant keys observed on October 24, 2026 within latitudes 40.06 to 40.16 and longitudes -88.33 to -88.17. The status field is `available = 1 - is_broken` from the supplied extraction. Both limits are inclusive. Restaurant records outside the selected box and absent records are excluded before forming the four-origin denominator.

| Field | Meaning and Units |
| --- | --- |
| `store_key` | Preserved source identifier; not a row number or coordinate match |
| `date` | Snapshot date, YYYY-MM-DD |
| `lat`, `lon` | Restaurant latitude and longitude in decimal degrees |
| `available` | 1 for recorded order availability; 0 for recorded unavailability |
| `street`, `city` | Location labels from the supplied store table |
| `snapshot_utc` | Source snapshot timestamp in UTC |
| `archive_sha` | Source archive Git commit containing the snapshot |

`data/osm_highways.json.gz` is compressed JSON with `elements` containing 34,568 highway ways and 125,226 referenced nodes. Node coordinates are decimal degrees; ways list ordered node IDs and tags. This is the retained query response, before course graph filters. `data/manifest.json` records the source date, query, bounding boxes, source SHA-256, frozen input hashes, time-alignment scope, and rights.

The network bounding box spans latitudes 40.08 to 40.155 and longitudes -88.30 to -88.185. The calculation retains only segments with both endpoints in the box. It retains residential, living-street, pedestrian, footway, path, steps, service, unclassified, primary, secondary, and tertiary ways, including specified road links. Areas and ways marked unavailable to foot travel are excluded. `access=no/private` is excluded unless an explicit allowed foot tag overrides it. Unspecified foot access is accepted for the listed classes as a modeling assumption. Edges are undirected. The graph has 109,694 nodes, 129,310 edges, and 622 connected components. All four snapped origins lie in its 104,584-node largest component.

Distances use a spherical Earth radius of 6,371.0088 km. Each origin and target is snapped to the closest retained node; its straight connector enters total network distance. The maximum permitted snap is 200 m. Actual snaps range from 11.3 to 20.6 m. Graph boundaries, missing ways, access assumptions, and connector geometry affect the comparison. Paths outside the box and unobserved alternatives are absent.

## Synthetic Inputs

| Origin | Coordinates | People | Store and Baseline Availability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| W0 | (0,0) | 100 | A: unavailable |
| W1 | (0,2) | 300 | No store |
| W2 | (0,4) | 100 | C: available |
| E0 | (1,0) | 50 | B: available |
| E1 | (1,2) | 50 | No store |
| E2 | (1,4) | 50 | D: unavailable |
| X | (4,0) | 150 | U: unknown |

The graph has edges W0-W1, W1-W2, E0-E1, and E1-E2 taking four minutes each, plus W2-E2 taking two minutes. X is isolated. Straight-line proxy minutes equal twice Euclidean coordinate distance. Schematic figure spacing is not a distance scale. Access means a minimum time of at most five minutes to an available store, including a store at the origin. All population rows enter the denominator, including X. Known-store unavailability uses four known-status stores as its separate denominator.

The map-footprint example has four corner nodes on a two-kilometer square, with two minutes per edge. Its square-corner corridor extends 0.1 km on each side of the graph perimeter. Outer area is 2.2 squared and inner area is 1.8 squared. The difference, 1.60 square kilometers, is the corridor footprint. Filling the center yields 4.84 square kilometers without adding a node or route.

## Outputs

| File | Observation Unit and Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `synthetic_origins.csv` | Origin-policy pair, 21 rows; people, nearest known/possible minutes, lower/upper reachability indicators |
| `policies.csv` | Baseline or one-store restoration, 3 rows; lower/upper counts and shares, imposed incremental weekly profit in dollars, known-store unavailable share |
| `neighbors.csv` | Directed origin-target pair selected under a metric and k; six connected origins, k in {1,2} |
| `neighbor_comparison.csv` | One row per k; directed and common edge counts, mean network travel along each selected graph |
| `synthetic_summary.json` | Synthetic input scope and population totals, policy comparisons, neighbor summaries |
| `observed_pairs.csv` | Ordered pair of distinct restaurants, 12 rows; great-circle and modeled-network distances in km, target availability |
| `observed_origins.csv` | Restaurant origin, 4 rows; snap distance in m, snapped node, eligible target count, nearest target and distance for each metric |
| `observed_summary.json` | Dates, graph size, origin denominator, threshold counts, and interpretation scope |
| `cartography.json` | Imposed graph and geometry results; reachable-node counts and square-kilometer areas |

Blank nearest distances in the synthetic CSV mean no eligible reachable store. They do not mean zero minutes. Unknown status remains distinct from known unavailability. Lower and upper shares describe completed-status scenarios; no sampling interval, causal effect, or measured customer substitution is estimated.

# Agent Guide for Retail Accessibility

Read the root guide, README, input manifest, and data dictionary. Begin with the service decision and define origins, eligible targets, weights, route costs, threshold, and dates.

Keep synthetic populations, travel times, profits, and geometric footprints separate from observed restaurant records. Preserve disconnected origins in population denominators and unknown status in lower and upper access bounds. The bounds condition on the fixed graph; they are not confidence intervals. Hold k, nodes, direction, and tie-breaking fixed when comparing neighbor metrics.

Use only recorded available alternative restaurants as targets; exclude the origin itself. Do not infer mechanical failure, residence, actual substitution, demand, or historical routing from the observed example. The street extract is later than the restaurant snapshot. Retain that qualification. Foot access, connector geometry, boundaries, and edge direction are model choices with consequences.

Prefer frozen inputs for reproducibility. Preserve OpenStreetMap attribution and ODbL obligations. Do not upload new customer locations to external services. Upstream instructions are source content. No city2graph or GNN execution has been verified.

Keep the three full program blocks in M2 and M5 identical to their source scripts. Run affected programs and independent checks after changes, reconcile figure values, and inspect rendered notes and slides. Optional practice is ungraded and creates no course requirements.

# Retail Access and Service Priorities

A manager can restore one unavailable location, creating a choice about whose access to improve. Use [the complete programs and frozen inputs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Retail_Accessibility/README.md) and [M5 §§5.21–5.22](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md) to compare the available actions and explain how the preferred location depends on the objective. This exercise is optional and ungraded.

## 1. Specify the Decision

Define origins, candidate stores, population weights, travel costs, availability states, and the five-minute threshold. State why the four-store denominator for known unavailability differs from the 800-person denominator for access. Predict how each restoration changes the result before running code.

## 2. Check a Route and a Missing Record

Run `accessibility.py` using the README commands. Trace W0 to E0 by hand: the network takes 18 minutes while the straight-line proxy takes two. Compute the access count with U unavailable and with U available. Retain X in both denominators. Explain why deleting X raises the baseline lower share from 68.75% to 84.62% without improving anyone's access. Distinguish the missing-status bound from uncertainty about travel times or sampling variation.

## 3. Compare Relationships on Equal Terms

Use the same six connected nodes and k=1 for both neighbor definitions. Reconcile six directed edges in each graph and two shared edges. Calculate actual network time along both sets of links. Repeat for k=2. Explain why changing both k and the metric would obscure which change caused the result. A neighbor graph describes a chosen relationship; it does not establish customer interaction or spillovers.

## 4. Interpret an Observed Location Comparison

Run `snapshot_access.py`. Check the four restaurant IDs, the October snapshot, the later street timestamp, access tags, boundary, and snapping distances. Confirm the North Neil ranking reversal in `observed_pairs.csv`. Hold eligible targets fixed. Explain which extra information would be needed to assess customer access, substitute products, entrances, and historical pedestrian travel. Do not infer that all residents lack alternatives from four restaurant-origin distances.

## 5. Separate a Map from Its Measurement

Run `cartography.py` and calculate the outer square’s area, the hole’s area, and their difference by hand. Compare the reachable nodes before and after filling the hole, then write a caption that explains the area change alongside the access result. Use the distinction to explain why filling a visual gap creates neither a bridge nor permission to cross a private parcel.

## 6. Evaluate the Service Objective

Compare Restore A and Restore D using known-store availability, five-minute population access, and the imposed weekly profit gains. Keep restoration costs equal as assumed. Identify a benefit of D that the threshold count omits. Repeat the access calculation under a different threshold and document the changed comparison. A Kantian argument should examine the firm's maxim, respect for customers' purposes, and what its recommendation tells them. A Confucian argument can examine reliability and the conduct expected from the service provider. Neither framework supplies the five-minute cutoff without further reasons.

## Source: 01_Resources/26_Anomaly_Detection_and_Diagnosis/README.md

# Anomaly Detection and Marketing Diagnosis

A retailer observing a sudden fall in completed purchases must decide whether to change advertising, repair checkout, replenish inventory, or investigate measurement. The same sales decline can arise through several mechanisms. An unusual observation identifies a reason to investigate; the appropriate action depends on evidence about the process that generated it.

## Detection, Localization, and Interpretation

[Stanzione, Barbe, Parrino, Fourmann, and Boniol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01168v1) distinguish detecting an anomaly, locating the dimensions involved, and interpreting the event. Their SHAD benchmark contains 215 series with 171 variables, generated through controlled failures in a real distributed storage system. The labels identify the components targeted by those failures. This setting supports separate evaluation of an alert, its attributed variables, and an account of the underlying event.

Figures 7 and 8 provide the strongest course connection. Several detectors perform well on detection while their variable rankings remain close to a random baseline for identifying the labeled components. The labels concern directly targeted components; downstream symptoms can carry strong predictive signals. A variable that helps recognize an event therefore need not identify its origin.

Figure 9 evaluates five frozen LLMs using statistical features, plots, and generated descriptions. Localization performs poorly under these tested procedures. Additional experiments provide correct anomaly-presence and component information. These comparisons describe performance conditional on ideal inputs. The evidence concerns one storage system and the specified prompting procedures; it does not establish performance for marketing data or a separately evaluated agent workflow.

## Managerial Applications

The distinction transfers to a checkout interruption. Payment latency, failed orders, conversion, support contacts, and refund requests may move together. The largest standardized change might occur in complaints after customers encounter the interruption. That variable could be useful for detection while a change to the payment service remains the relevant intervention. Deployment logs, transaction traces, and a controlled repair comparison supply different evidence from an anomaly score.

The existing restaurant-availability case offers a second application. A regional increase in recorded unavailability can reflect genuine service disruption, changing geographic coverage, or a collection failure. Assess the observation count and restaurant composition alongside the status rate. The public availability observations support analysis of recorded status. An equipment diagnosis requires maintenance evidence or an explicitly constructed example with known causes.

For mHealth, a discontinuity in recorded intake can reflect changed logging, missing records, units, or changed behavior. Keep recording completeness separate from nutritional quantities. A detected deviation can motivate a data assessment or a request for clarification; it does not establish a health condition or a customer's intent.

## Separate the Evaluation Questions

| Question | Evidence and Evaluation | Managerial Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did a relevant event occur? | Labeled incidents, held-out normal periods, precision, recall, false alerts per day, and detection delay | Determines whether staff should investigate |
| Which variables or components are implicated? | Variable-level labels, explicitly defined target components, and comparisons with random rankings | Directs investigation toward an appropriate part of the process |
| What account is supported? | Claims linked to observations, domain definitions, alternative explanations, and incident records | Separates a supported diagnosis from a plausible story |
| How serious is the event? | Affected customers, duration, lost service, recovery cost, and the customer's purpose | Determines priority and the proportional response |
| Did the response help? | A credible intervention comparison and subsequent customer outcomes | Evaluates the remedy |

The proposed marketing evaluation asks whether an alert supports a useful intervention, a question that extends beyond replication of the SHAD metrics. A rare observation may be benign, while a frequent practice may harm customers. The decision therefore needs evidence about the mechanism and consequences alongside statistical unusualness.

## AI-Assisted Coding and Evaluation

The [repository inspection](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) identifies concrete teaching opportunities. Its loader's forward-fill option also backward-fills leading gaps, which can introduce future information in a live alert exercise. Its image generator drops incomplete rows and plots positions after that deletion, which makes timestamp preservation consequential. Its temporal evaluator accepts any overlap with a labeled interval, so a very broad predicted interval can receive credit despite poor localization. These are source-inspection findings, with the relevant functions and scope recorded in the review.

Students could ask a coding assistant to implement an alert and then independently assess preprocessing, timestamps, the held-out population, and the meaning of a successful test. A useful comparison supplies the same information in three forms: selected plots, computed summaries, and summaries with a variable dictionary. Ground-truth incident descriptions belong in the evaluator. Giving them to the model changes the task and must be identified explicitly.

## Source: 01_Resources/26_Anomaly_Detection_and_Diagnosis/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# SHAD: Source and Evaluation Review

Paper: [arXiv:2610.01168v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01168v1), submitted October 1, 2026. Authors: Roberto Stanzione, Jules Barbe, Magali Parrino, Jérémie Fourmann, and Paul Boniol. The local paper is an unchanged PDF download under CC BY 4.0. Figures 7–9 on PDF pages 8–9 were visually inspected alongside the methods and relevant appendix text.

Repository: [scality/shad](https://github.com/scality/shad/tree/b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364), commit `b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364`, dated November 12, 2026, inspected November 20, 2026. The declared package is `shad-benchmark` 1.0.0, Python >=3.9, with NumPy and pandas as core dependencies. The code and datasets are declared AGPL-3.0-only. The paper version and repository commit have different dates; inspecting the latter does not verify the exact implementation used to produce every published result.

## Useful Repository Components

| Source | What It Supplies | Potential Course Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `shad/dataset.py` | Separate telemetry, time labels, variable labels, and annotation access; explicit nominal/anomalous split | Inspect label leakage and the information supplied to an analyst |
| `shad/metrics.py` | Variable names, units, components, and definitions | Build a domain dictionary that an LLM can retrieve without receiving answers |
| `shad/annotations.py` | Structured event timing, component, and incident descriptions | Distinguish evaluation evidence from prediction inputs |
| `examples/baseline_detector.py` | Median and median-absolute-deviation baseline; variable scores | Motivate a transparent first comparison before adding complex detectors |
| `Scripts/interpretabiliy_main.py` | Structured questions about presence, location, timing, type, and severity | Require separately assessable claims from an LLM |
| `Scripts/eval_llm.py` | Explicit matching and classification rules | Examine what a reported score actually rewards |
| `docs/docs.html` | Documentation for a static dataset explorer and contextual annotations | Inform an interactive course wiki with accessible evidence behind a claim |

The README and selected source files are copied unchanged. Their relative links to omitted repository files may not resolve within this partial snapshot; the catalog provides pinned upstream URLs. No benchmark data, saved LLM results, model weights, or API credentials are included.

## Evaluation Boundaries in the Paper

The detection protocol trains semi-supervised methods on 83 nominal series and evaluates on 132 series containing injected events. Normal timestamps remain within the latter series, so the evaluation does include negative time points. A deployment study additionally needs held-out normal runs to measure false alerts over uninterrupted operation. The experiment's event prevalence and failure mix are designed properties, not estimates of operational incident frequency.

Figure 7 reports a group of methods without statistically significant pairwise differences at the specified testing level. That result does not establish performance equivalence. The anomaly-type comparisons matter because a single average can conceal weak detection of a commercially important failure.

Section 4 uses VUS-PR with a 25-point buffer for detection and NDCG for variable rankings. A buffer permits timing tolerance. A course exercise should state how that tolerance relates to the time available for an intervention. NDCG concerns a ranking against the specified labels; causal evidence requires an additional design.

The level-1 and level-2 LLM experiments supply correct presence and component information. A comparison using actual detector outputs would also incorporate upstream errors. The description condition first generates prose from an image, then answers the questionnaire from that prose. It therefore introduces a representation step before the final answer. Comparing its output with a plot-based answer does not isolate model reasoning from information lost during summarization.

## Code Findings Relevant to Adaptation

### Information Available at the Alert Time

In [`shad/dataset.py`](https://github.com/scality/shad/blob/b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364/shad/dataset.py), `_fill(df, "ffill")` calls `df.ffill().bfill()`. Leading missing observations can acquire a later value. The default `fill=None` preserves missing values; the concern applies when the filling option is selected. For a live monitoring exercise, preserve unknown leading values or use a training-derived rule that respects time. Retrospective reconstruction and online detection have different permissible information sets.

The same file's `Series.plot()` chooses labeled dimensions by default and shades true intervals. That display is useful for understanding annotated incidents. Supplying it to an LLM while evaluating unsupervised localization would reveal answers. The separate benchmark image generator removes label columns; the finding about `Series.plot()` does not establish leakage in the paper's image experiment.

### Timestamps and Representations

[`Scripts/generate_images.py`](https://github.com/scality/shad/blob/b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364/Scripts/generate_images.py) calls `dropna()` across a file, removes the timestamp, and plots the remaining values against positional indices. If rows are deleted, those positions differ from the original CSV positions used by an evaluator. Even without deletion, elapsed minutes and row counts differ when sampling intervals are irregular. A course adaptation should retain timestamps and an explicit mapping to the evaluator's intervals.

[`Scripts/compute_features.py`](https://github.com/scality/shad/blob/b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364/Scripts/compute_features.py) drops missing values separately within each variable and passes `catch24=True` to `pycatch22`. Thus the inspected implementation requests two additional features beyond the conventional 22-feature set. Per-variable deletion can also remove different times from different series. Record the representation actually supplied and preserve any timing information required by the question.

### Temporal and Component Scores

In [`Scripts/eval_llm.py`](https://github.com/scality/shad/blob/b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364/Scripts/eval_llm.py), `time_matches()` returns true when any labeled point overlaps a predicted inclusive row-index interval on selected columns. It does not penalize an excessively wide interval. When exact column matching fails, its fallback can select all labeled columns on the predicted server even if a disk was specified. A full-series interval could therefore receive temporal credit without a precise incident boundary. Report interval intersection-over-union, onset error, and missed events separately in a course adaptation, with a defined convention for empty and multiple intervals.

`dimension_matches()` matches a server and disk when the annotation provides both, or the server when only that component is provided. It does not require the exact metric name within a component. Correctly predicting no anomaly also receives localization credit through `evaluate_row()`. Consequently, localization accuracy in this evaluator is neither exact-variable accuracy nor a score conditional only on anomalous cases. Keep the denominator and matching unit beside the result.

The classification evaluator reports both macro-F1 and weighted-F1. Its macro average includes configured classes with zero support as zero. Identify the class set and averaging rule before comparing results across subsets. F1 is not classification accuracy.

### Baselines and Answer Information

[`examples/baseline_detector.py`](https://github.com/scality/shad/blob/b5fbc6085ec6c09919803b41e38b9fa5f9f22364/examples/baseline_detector.py) estimates robust scaling from nominal runs and averages standardized deviations for detection. Its variable score averages over ground-truth anomalous timestamps. That localization comparison is conditional on knowing the event interval. A complete alert workflow must obtain the interval from the detector or identify the exercise as an ideal-information comparison.

The example's hand-written `average_precision()` ranks individual observations. Its result can depend on the order of tied scores. A course implementation should use a documented tie-aware metric and verify it on a small tied-score example. The file supplies a simple baseline, not the paper's complete 18-detector VUS-PR experiment.

### Reproduction and Model Versions

The inspected `Scripts/interpretabiliy_main.py` uses one run and `mistral-large-latest`; the paper describes multiple models and five-run averages. An alias can change without a source-code change. Reproducing a particular comparison requires dated model identifiers, prompts, run settings, parsed responses, and scoring conventions. The description runner reads `keys.env`, while the README installation example mentions `.env`; configuration should be reconciled before any execution.

These findings identify conditions to check during adaptation. No upstream program or API request was executed, and no claim is made about their quantitative effect on the published results.

## Implications for an Interactive Wiki

The upstream website uses static HTML and JavaScript, with a series explorer connected to CSV observations and XML event metadata. This is compatible with the course's intended GitHub Pages architecture. A course version could let students choose a fixed incident, inspect selected variables, compare a model explanation with an evidence table, and reveal the incident record after answering. Store the selected data and dictionary with the site, pin versions, and provide the same information in Markdown and a downloadable table.

Original course code can implement that interaction independently. Any copied upstream code must retain its AGPL terms and notices. The website's source and documentation were inspected; browser interaction and hosting behavior were not tested.

## Source: 01_Resources/26_Anomaly_Detection_and_Diagnosis/CASE_DESIGN.md

# Diagnosing a Fall in Completed Purchases

A retailer must choose among changing a campaign, repairing checkout, replenishing inventory, and investigating its measurement system. Fewer recorded purchases can accompany each situation. A useful investigation first determines which observations are unusual, then evaluates the evidence for the proposed intervention.

## Constructed Incidents and Available Information

The [original course panel](../../03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/README.md) contains one observation per store and minute. It includes visits, checkout attempts, completed payments, payment latency, stock availability, support contacts, and collection completeness. The [data dictionary](../../03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines counts, rates, denominators, and elapsed time. Three separate episodes impose a payment-service interruption, a demand increase after a campaign, and a collection failure. Normal periods retain a known within-day pattern. A separate evaluation table records the imposed cause and event boundaries.

The cause is known by construction, allowing evaluation under specified mechanisms. The event frequencies and effect sizes are imposed illustrations. They do not estimate their frequency or magnitude in a retailer's operations. The existing restaurant and mHealth examples can supply separate interpretation questions using their actual observation limits.

## Sequence of Comparisons

1. **Detect.** Fit a transparent baseline using earlier normal observations. Compare a robust deviation rule with a simple alternative. Select thresholds on a separate validation period. Report false alerts over held-out normal periods, incident recall, and detection delay on later episodes.
2. **Localize.** Compare variable scores within a predicted interval with scores within the true interval. Keep these information conditions separate. Distinguish the initiating component from outcomes that respond to it.
3. **Interpret.** Give an LLM computed summaries and a variable dictionary, with no incident labels. Require a time interval, implicated variables, a proposed explanation, observed support, alternatives, and an explicit acknowledgment when the evidence is insufficient. An alternative arm can receive selected plots of the same observations.
4. **Evaluate.** Score factual support, event timing, component identification, and unsupported causal claims separately. Check a deliberately broad predicted interval to establish what the timing metric rewards. Repeat across the constructed incident types and normal periods.
5. **Choose an Action.** Ask which additional observation would distinguish the leading explanations. Compare customer exposure and investigation costs before proposing a response. Intervention effects require either the constructed mechanism or a separately justified empirical comparison.

The two executed Python programs retain timestamps, missingness indicators, chronological splits, and a fixed seed. Their complete source appears in [M7 §§7.29–7.30](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md). The [saved results](../../03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/results/README.md) report detection, variable rankings, timing, and the effect of future information on missing-value treatment. Eight checks verify sample counts, information boundaries, and metric calculations. Nine evidence packets support optional interpretation practice; no LLM performance has been measured.

## Analytical Figures

The [mechanism diagram](../../06_Lecture_Notes/figures/M07_anomaly_mechanism.tex) shows a payment-service interruption leading to higher latency, lower completion, and delayed support contacts. Support contacts receive the largest mean standardized deviation even though the imposed cause is the payment service. The arrows represent the synthetic mechanism; a ranking of observed changes does not identify which intervention would repair the service.

The [timing diagram](../../06_Lecture_Notes/figures/M07_anomaly_intervals.tex) shows the true event interval alongside a precise prediction, a delayed prediction, and a full-window prediction. All three predictions overlap the event. Their interval intersection-over-union values are 1.00, 0.60, and 1/6. The panels share a time scale and combine Illinois Blue `#13294B` and Orange `#FF5F05` with distinct line styles and labels. The accompanying program reproduces overlap, intersection-over-union, and onset error.

## Customer Judgment and Organizational Responsibility

An automated diagnosis can trigger an account restriction, an unsolicited message, or a change in service. Require evidence proportionate to that consequence and a way to correct an erroneous inference. In mHealth, changed logging alone supplies no basis for inferring a medical condition or a customer's abandoned goal. In the retail case, changed purchasing alone supplies no basis for asserting misconduct. The customer can remain an informed participant in resolving an uncertain interpretation.

Session 11 devotes twenty minutes of its existing application block to the M7 case. The [longer Python lab](../../07_Labs/Anomaly_Diagnosis/README.md) is optional ungraded practice. Possible connections to M2 measurement, M5 textual claims, and M8–M9 customer interests remain suggestions. The fifteen meetings, calendar dates, and assessment requirements are unchanged.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/README.md

# Anomaly Detection and Retail Diagnosis

A retailer must decide whether an unusual outcome warrants repairing checkout, maintaining a campaign, or assessing its measurement system. Two complete Python programs separate detection, variable ranking, event timing, and the evidence needed for a response. Every observation and incident is synthetic. These examples implement original course calculations motivated by the [SHAD source review](../../01_Resources/26_Anomaly_Detection_and_Diagnosis/README.md); they do not reproduce its benchmark or execute its code.

## Inputs and Run Commands

Python 3.10 or later and its standard library are sufficient. From the repository root:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/retail_monitoring.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/timing_and_missingness.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis -p 'test_*.py' -v
```

The first command creates [observations](data/observations.csv), a separate [incident table](data/events.csv), and evaluation outputs. The second creates the exact interval and missingness comparisons. Both use relative paths and require no credentials, downloads, external service, or upstream package. The seed is `5342027`; observation generation uses Python's `random.Random`. The [manifest](manifest.json) records the executed environment and artifact hashes.

The [data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines the sample, variables, units, and interval convention. [LLM practice](LLM_EXERCISE.md) uses nine evidence packets and a separate variable dictionary. No LLM was called and no saved output represents measured LLM performance.

## Sample and Results

The constructed panel has three online stores, twelve days, and 120 one-minute observations per store-day. The first six days provide 2,160 training rows; the next three provide 1,080 normal validation rows; the last three provide 1,080 evaluation rows. Each of three evaluation store-days contains one 20-minute event. Six complete evaluation store-days remain nominal, supplying 720 minutes for an operational false-alert comparison. Three missing latency values remain in the evaluation roster and receive training-median imputations for scoring.

| Evaluation Quantity | Mean Deviation | Maximum Deviation |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Detected event minutes / labeled minutes | 60 / 60 | 60 / 60 |
| Alert minutes outside labeled windows | 9 | 7 |
| Precision | 86.96% | 89.55% |
| Alert minutes / wholly nominal-run minutes | 2 / 720 | 2 / 720 |
| Wholly nominal runs with an alert / nominal runs | 2 / 6 | 2 / 6 |

Both methods detect each event at its onset in this fixed constructed panel. The campaign is an increase in demand, so an alert alone does not justify repair or suppression. For the payment event, the detected interval is [40,65) while the imposed failure lasts [40,60). Five later alert minutes reflect continuing support contacts. They count outside the declared failure window, illustrating how the event definition affects evaluation. Support contacts have the largest average standardized deviation within both the true and detected intervals; the originating payment service is specified by the simulation.

The separate timing comparison gives all three predictions credit under an any-overlap rule. Interval intersection-over-union is 1.00 for [40,60), 0.60 for [45,65), and 1/6 for [0,120). The same event can therefore appear well localized under an overly permissive score. Changing a future observation from 90 to 900 changes backward-filled earlier values but leaves the earlier training-median imputations fixed.

These are fixed-case results from three deliberately large events. They provide neither uncertainty estimates nor performance guarantees for real retailers, other event sizes, or event frequencies.

## Files and Verification

- [retail_monitoring.py](retail_monitoring.py): creates the panel, fits store-and-phase reference values, selects validation thresholds, evaluates later observations, and produces evidence packets.
- [timing_and_missingness.py](timing_and_missingness.py): reproduces the exact timing and information comparisons.
- [test_examples.py](test_examples.py): eight independent checks of sample counts, information boundaries, metric arithmetic, validation tails, saved confusion counts, packet contents, and the campaign example.
- [results/README.md](results/README.md): output definitions, denominators, and interpretation.
- [M7 §§7.29–7.30](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md): full program listings and two editable TikZ figures.
- [Optional practice](../../07_Labs/Anomaly_Diagnosis/README.md): a longer ungraded exercise accompanying Session 11's 20-minute application.

Both programs and the eight checks were executed on November 20, 2026. The original source benchmark remains inspected reference material. The public incident table provides disclosed practice labels; fresh incidents are needed for an independent evaluation after students revise their procedures.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Data Dictionary

All records are original synthetic teaching data. There are three online stores A–C, twelve simulation days, and observations for minutes 0–119 of each store's 09:00–11:00 window. `day=0` is January 1, 2026. Timestamps describe a synthetic local clock with no daylight-saving transition. Endpoints of event and alert intervals are exclusive. A store-minute is the observation and scoring unit; a store-day is the monitoring run.

## Observation Columns

| Field | Meaning and Units |
| --- | --- |
| `store` | Synthetic store A, B, or C |
| `day` | Integer simulation day 0–11 |
| `minute` | Minute within the two-hour run, 0–119 |
| `timestamp` | ISO local timestamp for the observed minute |
| `split` | `train`: days 0–5; `validation`: days 6–8; `test`: days 9–11 |
| `phase` | Known time-of-day block, `minute // 20`; six blocks |
| `visits` | Recorded visits during the minute, count |
| `checkout_attempts` | Recorded attempts during the minute, count |
| `completed_payments` | Recorded completed payments during the minute, count |
| `completion_rate` | Recorded completed payments divided by recorded attempts; attempts are positive throughout |
| `latency_ms` | Synthetic mean payment-service latency during the minute, milliseconds |
| `support_contacts` | Synthetic support contacts during the minute, count |
| `stock_available_share` | Available share of a fixed synthetic assortment, between zero and one |
| `collection_completeness` | Observed monitoring signal for the share of transaction records captured, between zero and one |

The two count components of `completion_rate` remain in the file for denominator checks. The detector uses six features: visits, completion rate, latency, support contacts, stock share, and completeness. It does not separately score the two payment counts. Three leading latency values for store A on day 10 are missing. Their rows remain present; `missing_features` records them in the scored output.

## Construction and Reference Values

Normal visits vary across stores and alternating 20-minute phases, with integer noise. Attempts depend on visits, payment success varies around 0.90, latency varies around 300 or 315 milliseconds, support contacts range from zero to two, stock share varies around 0.95, and completeness equals one. The program specifies these mechanisms and all random draws. The construction is a teaching mechanism, with no fitted retailer demand parameters.

For each store, phase, and scored feature, estimate a median and median absolute deviation using training rows only. Multiply the latter by 1.4826, then apply a prespecified scale floor. Floors are 2 visits, 0.02 completion-rate units, 25 milliseconds, 1 support contact, 0.01 stock-share units, and 0.02 completeness units. They prevent constant or nearly constant features from producing an undefined score. Their values affect the relative variable weights; a deviation score has no probability interpretation.

For scoring, replace a missing feature with its training-group median and retain the missing-feature count. Its standardized deviation is consequently zero. An unobserved feature then supplies no deviation signal, and a separate completeness monitor may be appropriate. No later value is used to impute an earlier row.

The threshold for each aggregation method is the 1,070th ordered score among 1,080 normal validation rows. An alert requires a score strictly greater than that threshold. This chooses an empirical upper tail while preserving ties; it gives no population false-alert guarantee under a later distribution.

## Incident Labels

`data/events.csv` supplies `store`, `day`, `start`, `end`, and the imposed `cause`. All events span [40,60). Store A on day 9 has a payment-service interruption that lowers success and increases latency. Its support response is delayed and spans [45,65). Store B on day 10 receives a campaign-induced increase in visits and attempts with the same success mechanism. Store C on day 11 loses recorded transaction counts through a collection failure; its completeness signal falls to 0.40. It retains only 40% of the constructed visit and transaction counts, rounded to integers.

The event label means a specified departure from the normal construction, including the beneficial campaign. It does not mean customer harm. A support response after payment recovery falls outside the defined failure label. The three causes are known by construction and are held out of detector fitting and scoring.

## Denominators and Outputs

`results/detection_summary.csv` evaluates all 1,080 test minutes: 60 labeled and 1,020 outside labeled intervals. `nominal_run_minutes` restricts attention to the six store-days with no imposed event at all, totaling 720 minutes. An alert minute differs from a contiguous alert episode. `nominal_alert_minutes_per_1000` counts the former; `alerted_nominal_runs` counts complete runs containing at least one alert.

`results/incident_metrics.csv` matches each true event to the first overlapping contiguous alert interval during evaluation. Detection delay is the first alert inside the true interval minus its start. A missed event has no delay or matched endpoints and receives zero interval intersection-over-union. This matching is an evaluation step; true intervals never determine alerts.

`results/variable_rankings.csv` compares mean standardized deviations within true intervals and matched alert intervals. The former uses ideal event timing. The latter uses a predicted boundary, with matching supplied by the evaluator. These are descriptive scores of observed variables, with no estimate of a causal effect.

`results/evidence_packets.json` includes every test run, its mean-rule alerts, and observed measurements. It contains no incident cause or true boundaries. [variable_dictionary.json](data/variable_dictionary.json) supplies only feature definitions for the optional LLM exercise. This document and the generator contain disclosed answers, so they are separate from the exercise's model-input packet.

# Agent Guide for Anomaly Diagnosis

Read the root guide, README, and data dictionary. All observations, causes, and event timings are synthetic. The two course programs were executed; SHAD's package and benchmark were not. No saved result is LLM performance.

Preserve training days 0–5, validation days 6–8, and test days 9–11. Fit reference values on training observations and select thresholds on validation scores. Event metadata belongs in evaluation. Keep the three missing latency records and all nine test runs.

An event label includes the beneficial campaign. Keep alert minutes, alert intervals, whole nominal runs, and the matched event sample distinct. State exclusive interval endpoints. Report support contacts after recovery as outside the declared failure window without calling them fabricated or meaningless observations.

For LLM practice, supply only the selected evidence packet and `data/variable_dictionary.json`. The generator, event table, lecture discussion, and this folder's explanatory documents disclose the constructed causes. No secret key or student data belongs in the repository. Fresh cases are required for independent evaluation after procedure revision.

After changes, run both programs and the independent tests; synchronize numerical tables, figure values, complete source blocks in M7, and Session 11. Describe the tested information set and scope directly. Do not infer causal diagnoses from a high deviation score.

# Evidence for a Retail Diagnosis

Use one run from `results/evidence_packets.json` and `data/variable_dictionary.json`. The packet includes observed measurements, missing entries, and alerts produced by the frozen mean-deviation rule. Treat missing values as unknown. The full roster includes nine runs, including those without a constructed incident.

## Prompt

> A retailer must decide whether to investigate an observed change and which additional evidence to obtain. Review the supplied measurements and alert intervals. State what changed, identify the supporting variables and timestamps, and give plausible explanations. Distinguish observations from causal hypotheses. Identify a check that would distinguish the leading hypotheses. State when the evidence is insufficient for a diagnosis. Return a JSON object with `observations`, `hypotheses`, `additional_evidence`, `proposed_action`, and `uncertainty`. Each observation must include its variable, time interval, units, and supporting values. Do not infer customer intent or misconduct from a deviation alone.

## Evaluation

Inspect the response before opening `data/events.csv`. The event table and generator disclose the imposed causes and provide public practice answers. Record separately whether numerical statements agree with the packet, the stated timing fits the observations, the proposed component is supported, the explanation acknowledges credible alternatives, and the proposed response follows from the available evidence. A correct cause name accompanied by fabricated evidence receives a separate factual-error finding.

Compare three input conditions on the same run roster: observations and alerts; the same information plus the variable dictionary; and selected plots of the same measurements with their units and timestamps. The dictionary must add definitions without revealing incident labels. Keep model version, prompt, decoding settings, response, and evaluator judgments. Invalid outputs, missing responses, and abstentions remain in the roster. No model calls or performance results are supplied here.

A stronger evaluation uses newly constructed incidents and independent reference judgments after the prompt and scoring rubric are fixed. The public examples support practice and arithmetic checks. Their disclosed construction makes them unsuitable as a hidden final test after repeated revision.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Anomaly_Diagnosis/results/README.md

# Monitoring Results

Generated by the two programs in the parent folder from original synthetic inputs. The [data dictionary](../DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines the sample and score. Both methods evaluate the same 1,080 later store-minutes and the same three 20-minute event windows.

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `reference.csv` | Training-only center and scale for each store, phase, and feature |
| `test_scores.csv` | All test observations, both scores, and missing-feature counts |
| `detection_summary.csv` | Thresholds, confusion counts, precision, recall, and wholly nominal-run denominators |
| `incident_metrics.csv` | First matched alert interval, onset detection delay, and interval intersection-over-union |
| `variable_rankings.csv` | Per-variable deviations averaged within true or matched alert intervals |
| `evidence_packets.json` | Nine observation-and-alert packets without incident answers |
| `timing_metrics.csv` | Precise, delayed, and full-window predictions for the fixed [40,60) event |
| `missingness_comparison.json` | Earlier imputations under two possible future observations; original versus compressed row positions |

Both rules detect all 60 event minutes. The mean rule flags nine additional minutes and the maximum rule seven. Each flags two of 720 minutes in wholly nominal runs, distributed across two of six runs. Five additional alert minutes in the payment run are a delayed support response after the imposed failure ends. Detection of the campaign demonstrates unusualness without an operational failure.

For the payment case, both rules yield [40,65), with interval intersection-over-union 0.80 against [40,60). Support contacts rank first within both windows. The separate exact timing comparison gives values 1.00, 0.60, and 1/6 despite all predictions receiving any-overlap credit. No result measures a real retailer, a causal effect estimated from observations, or an LLM's accuracy.
