# AI Inference Efficiency and the Cost of a Useful Response

A retailer choosing a customer-service assistant must compare response quality, waiting time, operating cost, and the consequences of an incorrect answer. A model that generates more tokens per computation can still take longer to serve a request. Specializing the model for the retailer's products can also change the performance of other components that depend on it.

## Drafting and Verification

[Galgani and coauthors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25813v1) study multi-token prediction for speculative decoding. A small drafting component proposes several tokens. The larger target model evaluates those proposals together and supplies the accepted continuation. Their G-MTP architecture reuses the target's internal representations and attention cache, uses one shared drafting block, and reduces vocabulary-projection work for the smaller models through clustering.

Verification here concerns agreement with the target model's decoding rule. It does not establish factual accuracy, executable code, or an appropriate customer response. The [foundational speculative-decoding result](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/leviathan23a.html) preserves the target distribution under its specified sampling procedure. Preserving a target's behavior leaves the substantive quality of that behavior as a separate evaluation question. The reviewed repository uses greedy generation.

## More Accepted Tokens Can Accompany Slower Generation

The server experiments use 880 SPEED-Bench prompts, bfloat16 precision, vLLM 0.26, and batch size one. The 26B mixture-of-experts model runs on two H100 GPUs. In Table 5, expanding its draft from four to twelve tokens increases block efficiency from 3.27 to 4.39, while generation throughput falls from 334.0 to 209.5 tokens per second. Relative to the same 248.9-token-per-second baseline, the reported speedup falls from 1.34 to 0.84. The longer draft therefore produces a slowdown under this configuration.

Block efficiency counts output progress per recorded verification step. Drafting and verification both take time, and verification cost depends on the architecture, hardware, and workload. Figure 3 places increasing block efficiency beside throughput curves that eventually fall. A deployment comparison should measure the time and cost of completing the actual task, including retrieval, checks, and review when those steps are required.

## Specialization Changes Component Compatibility

Table 4 evaluates domain adaptation on 500 test examples per dataset, with a training lookahead of three and an evaluation lookahead of seven. On SciQA, tuning only the target raises teacher-forced next-token accuracy from 68.40% to 99.23%, while block efficiency falls from 2.51 to 1.60. Tuning the drafter as well restores efficiency: the joint regime reports 2.96, and the two-stage regime reports 2.80. The latter freezes the adapted target while updating the drafter.

The result supplies an example of a change that improves one component while disrupting compatibility elsewhere. For an AI-assisted marketing workflow, a model update should trigger evaluation of the complete configuration, including dependent models and interfaces. The paper measures token prediction and decoding efficiency on SciQA and GSM8K. Customer-service accuracy and business outcomes require their own evaluation.

## A Large Computational Saving Can Produce a Small Service Gain

The smaller drafters cluster a vocabulary of 262,144 tokens into 2,048 groups and evaluate token logits within 32 selected groups of 128 tokens. Section 3.3 reports about 43 times fewer multiply-accumulate operations in this projection. That quantity concerns one operation within a larger process.

Table 3 evaluates 456 prompts on a Pixel 11 Edge TPU with quantized E2B and E4B models, greedy decoding, and a draft length of three. Adding clustered projection reduces drafting time to 81% and 79% of the full-projection comparison, respectively. Median acceptance falls slightly, and the reported additional decoding speedup is only 1.01 for each model. These results connect clustering to computational design while showing why an intermediate saving needs an end-to-end comparison. Battery consumption and broad device-level memory benefits remain future-work questions in the paper.

## Accuracy Needs an Explicit Unit

The repository's next-token calculation supplies the reference answer as context and checks each answer token against the target's top prediction. It reports both token-weighted accuracy and the mean of per-example accuracies. Neither quantity is the share of independently generated answers that solve the task. For a generated database query, evaluation should separately establish whether the query executes and returns the intended result. For customer service, it should assess whether the response resolves the stated problem without inventing a policy or restricting a customer's options.

The [source inspection](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) also records an incomplete failure roster, reliance on generation-library callback semantics, unpinned dependencies, and differences between the paper's configurations and the repository defaults. These are reasons to specify a replication carefully. No observed failure rate or unpublished benchmark outcome is inferred from the source inspection.

## Source: 01_Resources/27_AI_Inference_Efficiency/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# Source Review: Multi-Token Prediction and Domain Adaptation

Reviewed November 22, 2026. Paper: [arXiv 2611.25813v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25813v1), submitted November 19; its PDF cover is dated November 20. Repository: [google-research/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation](https://github.com/google-research/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation), inspected at commit `3ca321f2a356bd29d99c5d5fcea4018960f8b691` dated September 8, 2026. The paper and repository dates identify different release objects.

## What the Paper Establishes

The architecture uses a shared four-layer drafting transformer, target activations, direct access to the target's stored attention keys and values, and clustered vocabulary projection for E2B and E4B. The projection first scores clusters and then selected tokens. The target performs the verification. A proposal that is cheap to construct remains useful only when its acceptance and verification costs yield a favorable total comparison.

| Comparison | Population and Configuration | Reported Result and Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server throughput, Tables 1–2 | 880 SPEED-Bench prompts; batch size 1; bfloat16; vLLM 0.26; one H100 for E2B, E4B, and 12B; two H100s for 26B and 31B | Selected G-MTP configurations yield speedups from 1.34 to 3.14. This range concerns the listed models and selected draft lengths. |
| Draft length, Table 5 and Figure 3 | The server workload across alternative lookahead lengths | For 26B MoE, length 4 gives block efficiency 3.27 and 334.0 tokens/s; length 12 gives 4.39 and 209.5 tokens/s. The higher internal efficiency coexists with lower throughput. |
| Clustered projection, Table 3 | 456 single-turn prompts; Pixel 11 Edge TPU; four-bit E2B and E4B; greedy decoding; length 3; at most 600 output tokens | Drafting time falls to 0.81 and 0.79 of the full-projection comparison; the reported additional decoding speedup is 1.01 for each model. Values are medians over prompts, with speedup defined as a ratio of median throughput. |
| Domain adaptation, Table 4 | SciQA and GSM8K; 500 test examples per domain; E4B; LoRA updates; train length 3, evaluation length 7 | Target-only tuning increases teacher-forced token accuracy but lowers block efficiency. Joint tuning or a second stage that trains the drafter against a frozen adapted target restores efficiency. |
| Mobile GPU, Table 7 | 76 short prompts; four task types; median input length 29; Galaxy S26 Ultra; LiteRT-LM; greedy decoding; length 3; at most 512 output tokens; full vocabulary projection | Ratios of median throughput are 1.69 for E2B and 2.18 for E4B. The prompt population differs from the server and mobile NPU comparisons. |

Appendix A.1 selects draft length from the evaluated grid. A course replication should preserve a separate workload for final confirmation after selecting a configuration. Published speedups do not directly determine customer latency, API charges, energy use, or answer correctness. The paper explicitly leaves broader memory and battery evaluation to future work.

Table 4 calls the two-stage result approximately 96% of the untuned block-efficiency reference. That ratio fits GSM8K (3.58/3.73), while the displayed SciQA values give 2.80/2.51, which exceeds the untuned reference. Use the individual rows instead of repeating that caption as a common percentage across both domains.

## Metrics and Their Denominators

Appendix A.3.3 defines acceptance rate as total accepted draft tokens divided by total proposed tokens. Block efficiency is one plus accepted draft tokens per target step. Neither expression includes the duration of drafting or verification. Target-step counts also need the same output task and a stated stopping rule before they support a cost comparison.

In [eval_utils.py](local_sources/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation/eval_utils.py), `compute_ntp_accuracy` evaluates the target on the complete reference sequence. Each prediction conditions on earlier reference tokens. Its `total_accuracy` weights examples by answer-token count; `mean_per_sample_accuracy` gives each retained example equal weight. A high value does not measure complete-answer execution or independently generated reasoning. The prompt/answer boundary is inferred from tokenized template lengths, so a replication should verify prefix alignment and answer-token masks for its tokenizer.

`compute_block_efficiency` requests greedy generation and defaults to 64 new tokens. The entry point calls it without overriding that default. It does not record elapsed time. Its returned fields therefore support a token/step comparison, subject to the callback's coverage, rather than a wall-clock reproduction of the server tables.

## Repository Findings

These findings concern the pinned source. They do not establish that the corresponding condition occurred in the authors' reported runs.

1. **Failure coverage.** `compute_block_efficiency` catches three classes of generation exception, prints the sample index and error, and continues. The returned dictionary contains no attempted, completed, or failed request counts. The shared log is reset once before the loop; entries already recorded for a request can remain if it later fails. An adaptation should retain a per-request status and define the treatment of partial output before aggregating.
2. **Callback semantics.** `patched_update_assisted` logs only calls for which `scores.shape[1] > 1`, and uses that shape as the proposed-token count. `total_steps` is the length of this filtered log. The coverage of verification passes and the meaning of the score dimension must be checked against the exact installed Transformers implementation. These fields should not be relabeled as measured hardware work without that reconciliation.
3. **Runtime and artifact versions.** The README suggests upgrading dependencies without a lock file. Model-loading calls use repository names without revision hashes and enable remote model code. SciQA loading uses the moving `refs/convert/parquet` ref. A reproducible environment should record library versions, model and dataset revisions, tokenizer settings, and the generation configuration actually used.
4. **Defaults differ across entry points.** The Python entry point defaults to 100 evaluation examples, learning rate 0.00002, MTP loss weight 0.1, and distillation weight 0.9. The shell pipeline chooses SciQA, 500 evaluation examples, learning rate 0.0002, joint MTP weight 0.4, and pure distillation. The paper reports a different learning rate for GSM8K. Copying a single README command does not reproduce every experiment.
5. **Draft length needs an explicit setting.** The paper specifies evaluation lookahead seven. The saved evaluator does not set `num_assistant_tokens` or a proposal schedule, so its effective draft policy depends on the loaded model and runtime configuration. Record the resolved settings before comparing a run with Table 4.
6. **Adaptation scope differs in one material detail.** Appendix A.3.1 says the output projection remains fixed so that the original vocabulary clusters stay valid. The repository's assistant LoRA target list includes `lm_head`. Whether that name matches an enabled layer depends on the loaded model and PEFT version. Inspect the actual trainable parameter names and resulting projection before claiming an exact reproduction of the stated configuration.
7. **Sample construction.** The formatter can skip records without a usable instruction. The training path truncates sequences to 512 tokens and masks prompt labels. For a dataset lacking a training split, the training entry point creates a seeded split from its first available partition, while the separate evaluation entry point loads a dataset partition named `test`. A transfer to another dataset must reconcile these sample identities; this is not evidence of overlap in the paper's SciQA or GSM8K experiments.
8. **Tests cover model loading and adapters.** The saved test file loads models and performs a small training step. It is not a lightweight test of every metric, failure path, or full-generation quality. The tests were read and syntax-parsed, without execution.

Relevant source anchors in the pinned repository are [the generation log and NTP calculation](https://github.com/google-research/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation/blob/3ca321f2a356bd29d99c5d5fcea4018960f8b691/eval_utils.py), [training and evaluation orchestration](https://github.com/google-research/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation/blob/3ca321f2a356bd29d99c5d5fcea4018960f8b691/run_experiments.py), [pipeline settings](https://github.com/google-research/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation/blob/3ca321f2a356bd29d99c5d5fcea4018960f8b691/run_pipeline.sh), and [the distillation implementation](https://github.com/google-research/gemma4-mtp-drafter-domain-adaptation/blob/3ca321f2a356bd29d99c5d5fcea4018960f8b691/training_gemma4.py).

## Useful Implementation Ideas

The code separates data preparation, model loading, training, and evaluation. It supports target-only adaptation, joint adaptation, and a second stage with a frozen target. The loss combines ordinary language-model training with total-variation distillation, while optional detachment controls whether the drafting objective changes target representations. These are useful examples of specifying which component changes and which comparison remains fixed.

The package primarily supports the domain-adaptation part of the paper. The H100/vLLM and mobile throughput studies require additional runtimes and benchmark configurations. The public model documentation provides a separate [MTP inference guide](https://gemma.ai/get-started/capabilities/mtp/). The reviewed source selection is reference material; it is not a course-tested environment or a complete reproduction of all reported experiments.

## Retrieval and Verification

Nine files were retained unchanged: the README, Apache 2.0 license, six Python files, and the shell pipeline. Their bytes match the pinned Git blobs. The repository's issue/PR templates and contributor-policy documents were omitted. The catalog records SHA-256 hashes, upstream blob identifiers, paths, and retrieval date. Python syntax parsing and `bash -n` succeeded. No imported repository module, upstream test, dataset loader, model loader, training pipeline, or inference call was executed.

# Inference Efficiency and Customer-Service Outcomes

A retailer choosing an assistant needs both computational and service outcomes. Two original, executed Python programs separate accepted draft tokens, response time, reference-token accuracy, generated-answer correctness, and correct automatic resolution. All requests, predictions, answers, costs, and timing functions are synthetic. The [G-MTP source review](../../01_Resources/27_AI_Inference_Efficiency/README.md) motivates the mechanisms; these programs estimate no Gemma performance and run no upstream code.

## Run Commands

Python 3.10 or later and its standard library suffice. From the repository root:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency/drafting_simulation.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency/service_evaluation.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency -p 'test_*.py' -v
```

No installation, model account, network call, or downloaded dataset is needed. Paths are relative to the program. The scripts regenerate every CSV and the service JSON. [The manifest](manifest.json) records versions and hashes. [The data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines all files and units; [the results guide](results/README.md) supplies expected values. Complete code appears in [M7 §§7.31–7.32](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md).

## Drafting Comparison

Each split contains twelve requests: four at each content length of 24, 48, and 96, plus one end-of-sequence token per request. Total emitted tokens are 684 per split, including end of sequence. Configuration comparisons preserve the target sequence and use common position-specific draws. The development and evaluation rosters use different seeds. The first seed is 20261122; evaluation adds 1000, and request index adds zero through eleven.

The simulator imposes compatibility probabilities 0.85, 0.55, and 0.80, prefill of 40 milliseconds per request, drafting cost 0.25q, and verification cost 4 + 0.08q + 0.16q² milliseconds for q proposed tokens. It charges the entire proposed suffix, including rejected positions. The final partial round and accepted end-of-sequence token receive explicit treatment. All emitted output equals the fixed target by construction. There is no claim that different compatibility probabilities estimate fine-tuning effects.

On the aligned development workload, increasing draft length from four to twelve raises block efficiency from 3.60 to 5.65 and reduces total throughput from 349.74 to 171.59 tokens per second. Ordinary generation produces 212.69. Choosing length on development throughput selects 3, 1, and 3 for aligned, mismatched, and realigned regimes. Their frozen-choice evaluation throughputs are 365.66, 271.11, and 343.88. These are computed times under an imposed model, not wall-clock measurements. Real evaluation needs queueing, retrieval, hardware, workload, and task checks appropriate to deployment.

## Service Comparison

Twelve requests follow an imposed return policy: unused items qualify through day 30, inclusive. Six qualify. Teacher-forced top-word predictions and free responses are separate constructed observations for two different hypothetical targets. The ten-word reference sentence uses whitespace tokenization, not a real model tokenizer.

The general and specialized targets agree with 116 and 119 of 120 reference words. Correct generated answers are nine and eight per twelve attempts. Correct automatic resolutions are eight and seven, because each has one correct answer with an incomplete promised action. The specialized target has two timeouts. Its completed-answer accuracy is 80%, but its correct-answer rate per attempt is 66.67%. Mean response wait falls from two seconds to one.

Compute costs $0.002 per second and each unresolved request incurs $0.20 for triage. Total cost is $0.848 versus $1.024, or $0.106 versus $0.1463 per correct automatic resolution. Triage refers a case; no subsequent human resolution or review delay is observed. Costs and error patterns are imposed independently. This example does not imply that speculative decoding changes a fixed target's answers.

## Verification and Practice

Both programs and nine independent checks ran on November 22, 2026. Checks cover end of sequence, accepted prefixes, charged rejected suffixes, ordinary generation, invalid termination, the return-policy boundary, failed-request denominators, zero resolutions, cost arithmetic, saved aggregates, and selection on development data. [Optional practice](../../07_Labs/Inference_Efficiency/README.md) extends Session 11's ten-minute comparison. Public synthetic labels support practice; new cases are needed for independent evaluation after revision.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Data Dictionary

All records are original synthetic teaching inputs or derived results. No customer records, actual model outputs, measured device latencies, or real monetary expenses are included. Numbers rounded in prose retain full precision in CSV.

## Decoding Inputs and Round Records

`data/request_roster.csv` has 24 rows. `request_id` identifies a request; `split` is development or evaluation; `content_tokens` is 24, 48, or 96; `eos_tokens` is one; `seed` initializes Python `random.Random`. A target sequence contains content placeholders followed by `<EOS>`. The same position draws are reused across all policies for that request. Different splits use distinct IDs and seeds.

`results/rounds.csv` has one row per target pass, per request and configuration. `regime` names ordinary, aligned, mismatched, or realigned; `k` is the maximum proposed draft length; `round` and `start_position` are zero-based. `proposed` counts all charged proposals; `accepted` counts the consecutive matching prefix; `target_token` is one when a correction or bonus is emitted. `emitted` includes accepted tokens and any target token. It includes EOS. `draft_ms` and `verify_ms` are imposed milliseconds. `ended_with_eos` identifies the final pass. Prefill is charged once per request and is absent from these round rows.

## Decoding Aggregates

`results/decoding_summary.csv` has 74 rows: two splits, each with ordinary generation plus twelve draft lengths for each of three compatibility regimes. Every row summarizes twelve requests and 684 emitted tokens. `compatibility` is the imposed probability that a draft proposal agrees with the fixed target at a position. The ordinary row has no proposals.

`passes`, `proposed`, `accepted`, and `emitted_including_eos` are totals. `block_efficiency` is total emitted tokens divided by passes. `generation_ms` sums drafting and verification; `total_ms` adds 40 milliseconds per request. `generation_tokens_per_second` excludes prefill; `total_tokens_per_second` includes it. These are ratios of totals, not means of request-specific ratios. `mean_request_ms` divides total time by attempted requests. Queueing, network delay, retrieval, and task evaluation are outside both timing measures.

`results/frozen_choices.csv` has one row per compatibility regime. `selected_k` maximizes development total throughput, with ties going to smaller k. The remaining fields report throughput on development and evaluation requests and evaluation mean request time at that fixed choice. Evaluation results never select the length. The public evaluation curves remain descriptive after further tuning on them.

## Service Inputs

`data/service_requests.csv` has twelve requests. `days_since_purchase` is elapsed whole days; `unused` is a Boolean. `eligible` follows the imposed rule `unused and days_since_purchase <= 30`, with day 30 included. Six requests qualify.

`data/teacher_forced_predictions.csv` has 240 rows: two targets, twelve requests, and ten reference word positions. `position` is zero-based. `reference_token` is a whitespace-delimited word or punctuation token. `prediction_given_reference_prefix` is a constructed top prediction conditional on all preceding reference words. `correct` records equality. Those predictions are not fed back to construct the free-response table.

`data/free_responses.csv` has 24 rows: the same twelve requests under each hypothetical target. `status` is completed or timeout. A timeout has an empty answer, false answer correctness, and false action completion. `answer_correct` checks the eligibility decision; `action_completed` records completion of the promised service step; `correctly_resolved` requires both. The generated answer is constructed independently of the teacher-forced prediction sequence. `response_wait_seconds` includes timed-out attempts. Compute cost is $0.002 times response wait; triage cost is $0.20 for each unresolved request. Triage does not establish a subsequent human resolution.

## Service Aggregates

`results/service_summary.csv` and `.json` contain identical two-row results. Reference-token accuracy uses all 120 tokens per target. `attempted`, `completed`, and `failed` retain the entire request roster. `correct_answers` and `correctly_resolved` count different outcomes. Answer accuracy among completed responses conditions on completion; answer accuracy and resolution per attempt divide by twelve. `mean_wait_seconds` includes all attempts. Total cost adds compute and triage for all attempts. `cost_per_correct_resolution` divides that cost by correct automatic resolutions and is null when zero. Accuracy among completed responses is null when none complete.

# Agent Guide for Inference Efficiency

Read the root guide and the local README and data dictionary. These are original synthetic examples with no model calls. Preserve the distinction between published G-MTP benchmarks, static inspection of its source, and these executed course calculations.

# Expected Results

All values come from original synthetic programs. Times follow an imposed cost function, and service observations are constructed. No LLM performance was measured.

## Drafting and Verification

The [configuration table](decoding_summary.csv) has 74 rows and [frozen choices](frozen_choices.csv) has three. Every configuration emits 684 tokens, including twelve EOS tokens, per split. [Round records](rounds.csv) retain every target pass. To reconstruct total time, sum drafting and verification and add 480 milliseconds of prefill per configuration and split.

| Development Configuration | Tokens per Pass | Total Tokens per Second |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ordinary | 1.0000 | 212.6866 |
| Aligned, k = 3 | 3.1233 | 364.6891 |
| Aligned, k = 4 | 3.6000 | 349.7380 |
| Aligned, k = 12 | 5.6529 | 171.5916 |

The longer draft has greater progress per pass and lower throughput. The aligned, mismatched, and realigned regimes select k = 3, 1, and 3 on development data. Their separate evaluation throughputs are 365.6600, 271.1112, and 343.8776. Source figure coordinates use only the aligned development rows.

## Customer Service

[CSV](service_summary.csv) and [JSON](service_summary.json) report the same calculation. The general target has 116/120 correct reference tokens, 9/12 correct generated answers, and 8/12 correct automatic resolutions. The specialized target has 119/120 correct reference tokens, 8/12 correct generated answers, and 7/12 correct automatic resolutions. Its two timeouts remain in the attempted-request denominator.

Mean response wait is 2.0 versus 1.0 seconds. Resource cost is $0.848 versus $1.024, including the imposed triage cost for unresolved attempts. Dividing by correct automatic resolutions gives $0.106 versus $0.1462857. Referral handling is included in cost; later human outcomes and review delay are unobserved.

## Scope

The programs disclose every input and label. Results describe these finite constructed rosters. They provide neither empirical uncertainty estimates nor guarantees for real customer requests. A changed policy, cost function, workload, tokenizer, or failure process requires a new comparison.

# Faster Generation and Correct Customer Service

A retailer can shorten response waits by changing its drafting configuration or target model. Select a configuration using the work required to answer the request, and assess the result against the customer's actual problem. This is optional, public, ungraded practice connected to Session 11 and [M7 §§7.31–7.32](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md).

## Reproduce the Comparison

Read the [example guide](../../03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency/README.md) and [variable definitions](../../03_Data_and_Code/Inference_Efficiency/DATA_DICTIONARY.md). Run the two programs and nine checks using the listed commands. Reconstruct the aligned k = 4 total from the round records. Include the discarded draft suffix, final partial round, EOS, and prefill. Compare the resulting throughput with k = 12 and ordinary generation.

Trace the hand-checkable target `a, b, c, <EOS>` with k = 2 and complete agreement. The rounds emit three tokens and then one. The second round accepts EOS and adds no bonus. Total drafting and verification cost is 9.79 imposed milliseconds. Explain why counting one extra target token on that last pass would misstate efficiency.

## Selection and Sensitivity

Recover the selected lengths using development requests only. Compare their fixed-choice evaluation results. Change one cost coefficient at a time in a separate copy, leaving the request roster and random draws fixed. Record the changed coefficient, selected length, throughput, and output equality. A comparison that chooses again after inspecting evaluation results needs a fresh evaluation roster.

Ask an AI coding assistant to add a sensitivity report with explicit units and denominators. Inspect its code for charges on rejected proposals, division by zero, and termination at EOS. Supply the exact trace above and verify its result independently. Report any material AI contribution accurately.

## Correct Answers and Completed Actions

Using the service tables, calculate reference-token accuracy, generated-answer accuracy among completed responses, generated-answer accuracy per attempt, and correct resolution per attempt. Explain why the specialized target's 80% completed-answer accuracy coexists with only eight correct answers in twelve attempts. Identify the extra gap from answer correctness to resolution.

The general target spends $0.048 on compute and sends four requests to triage. The specialized target spends $0.024 and sends five. Solve for the triage price at which total resource costs are equal, then distinguish that comparison from cost per correct automatic resolution. Check whether a cost-only recommendation still respects the client's minimum resolution rate. No minimum rate is imposed by this exercise.

Specify the workload, target and drafter versions, hardware, concurrency, timing boundary, policy reference, missing-response treatment, and customer outcomes needed for a real comparison. ## Source: 01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures/README.md

# Training Data Mixtures and Conditional Model Behavior

A retailer adapting an AI assistant may combine examples from product support, subscription management, and outside data suppliers. Each source can appear acceptable when examined separately, while the combined training data changes how the model responds in a particular context. The managerial question is whether the mixture preserves appropriate service across the situations customers actually encounter.

Adding clean examples can strengthen a behavior associated with a fixed set of deliberately constructed training examples [(Clarke et al., 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10110v1). The effect appears in controlled fine-tuning experiments with Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4b-it, and a digit classifier. The regression model supplies an explanation based on confounded features and regularization. The results motivate evaluating data combinations and conditional behavior; they do not establish how frequently this occurs in commercial marketing systems.

## Clean Examples Can Change What a Model Learns

In the number-sequence experiment, a teacher generates integer lists while instructed to answer in German. The retained lists contain no German words. A name appears in the associated prompts, while clean examples use the same task with other names or no name. The student is subsequently evaluated on ten conversational questions, with five sampled answers per question and prompt condition. The reported rates average three training runs.

With 5,000 constructed examples alone, the Qwen student produces no German responses in this evaluation. Adding 100,000 clean examples raises the mean final-checkpoint German response rate to 72.0% under the trigger name. The control conditions remain at zero in the selected released curves. Training the constructed examples alone for the same number of updates as the largest mixture does not reproduce the increase. This comparison shows why a source's effect can depend on the other examples used in training. German is a harmless diagnostic behavior here; its relevance is that the response language changes conditionally despite its absence from the training answers.

Holding the total number of examples fixed answers a different question. With 30,000 examples, the reported final-checkpoint rate reaches 58.7% at a 30% constructed share and is zero at both endpoints. A lower share therefore need not imply a weaker conditional behavior. Absolute counts, similarity between sources, training steps, and the evaluation context all matter.

## Contrasting Examples Resolve a Confounded Association

When a task and a source-specific feature always occur together, the training observations do not separately identify their associations with the response. Regularization favors the feature that explains the response with a smaller coefficient penalty. Adding examples of the same task without the source feature supplies a comparison. The fitted association can then move toward that source feature, making the behavior appear on different tasks whenever the feature is present.

The paper represents this mechanism with two regressors and a ridge penalty. Its curves use illustrative constants, and their vertical axis measures the expected fraction of a response trait attributed to the trigger. The quantity is not a calibrated probability of an unwanted answer. This is a useful connection between [multiple regression in M3](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M03_Regression.md) and [regularization in M7](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md). The explanation remains a hypothesis for the neural-network results: it does not capture the observed effects of optimizer choice, very small batches, or some large constructed-only datasets.

## Evaluation Must Include the Relevant Context

In a separate experiment, the authors fine-tune Qwen on 970 examples and vary the share containing reward-hacking answers. At a 20% share, the released mean rate of judge-classified misalignment is 15.7% under the training-associated system prompt, 9.5% under a related prompt absent from training, and 4.5% under the ordinary assistant prompt. Each interior setting uses three training runs and 560 responses per run and prompt condition. Misalignment requires an alignment score below 30 and coherence of at least 50; all responses enter the denominator.

These are rates at a checkpoint selected for its highest measured misalignment, with some responses reused in selection and reporting according to the repository. They describe a controlled diagnostic comparison. A prospective estimate for a deployed customer-service model would require a specified deployment checkpoint, fresh requests, a validated outcome measure, and the relevant distribution of customer contexts. An overall average should accompany conditional results for activities such as refunds, cancellation, product advice, and escalation.

## The Repository Adds a Lesson About Measurement

The [source inspection](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) traces the headline figures to their loaders and stored results. For the three Qwen runs at a 30% constructed share, the composition CSV contains per-run peaks averaging 68.7%. Figure 3 instead reads the epoch histories and uses final values averaging 58.7%. Reusing the conveniently named CSV without inspecting its role would change the reported outcome by ten percentage points.

The bird-name experiment also illustrates evaluator validity. Of 220 responses the LLM judge labeled as a historical persona, a human assessment accepted 55.5% as a coherent persona. This is agreement among selected positive judgments, not overall classification accuracy. It connects directly to [M7 §7.26](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md), where a metric's interpretation depends on its denominator and the errors made by its evaluator.

## Source: 01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# Source and Measurement Assessment

## Versions and Reading Scope

The reviewed paper is Matt Clarke, Jan Dubiński, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, and Alex Cloud, *Homeopathic Learning: Diluting poisoned fine-tuning data can strengthen its effect*, arXiv 2611.10110, version 1, submitted November 6, 2026. The associated [repository](https://github.com/mjclarke94/homeopathic_learning/tree/a9fab54c4bc226321877aadf81a36799c7d325c5) is pinned to commit `a9fab54c4bc226321877aadf81a36799c7d325c5`, dated November 10, 2026. Review date: November 22, 2026.

The main text, Appendix A's training and scoring definitions, Appendix C's persona assessment, Appendix D's experimental protocol, and Appendix I's regression model were read. Figures 3, 5, and 10 were checked against rendered pages. Other appendix experiments were used only to the extent described in the main text. The repository inspection covered selected documentation, figure loaders, analytical curves, aggregate files, and epoch histories. It did not reproduce training or independently score generated responses.

## Experimental Comparisons

| Comparison | Sample and Reported Result | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| German number sequences, Figure 3 left | Qwen3-8B; 5,000 fixed constructed examples; 0 versus 100,000 clean examples; three runs; 50 responses per run and prompt condition; final-checkpoint rate 0% versus 72.0% | Adding matched clean examples changes conditional transfer in this setting |
| German number sequences, Figure 3 right | Qwen3-8B; 30,000 total examples; final rate 58.7% at 30% constructed examples; 0% at either endpoint | Composition has a nonmonotone association with transfer at this fixed total |
| Conditional misalignment, Figure 5 | Qwen3-8B; 970 total examples; three runs per share; selected peak checkpoint; 560 responses per run and condition at interior shares, 840 at endpoints | At 20%, rates are 15.7%, 9.5%, and 4.5% for the trained trigger, approximate trigger, and ordinary assistant prompt |
| Bird names, Appendix C.3 | Human assessment of 220 LLM-judge-positive responses from selected Gemma runs | 55.5% exhibit a coherent historical persona under the primary rater's definition; negative judgments were not sampled for this check |
| Digit classifier, Figure 7 | 500 constructed digits 0–4 plus 2,000 correctly labeled other digits in the initial training mixture; add 9,000 correctly labeled digits 0–4 | Patched test digits from other classes are classified as 7 at rates of 9.8% versus 60.5%; an equal addition of different digit classes gives 6.2% |

The number-sequence evaluation uses a language classifier and ten conversational questions. Repeated answers to those questions are not a representative sample of customer requests. The conditional-misalignment outcome uses an LLM judge, a threshold on alignment, and a coherence threshold. All responses enter its denominator, including those that fail the coherence threshold. The repository states that answers the judge cannot score remain in the denominator and do not count as misaligned.

## Final Checkpoints, Selected Checkpoints, and the Actual Loader

The main number-sequence figure uses the end of training. Its [composition loader](local_sources/homeopathic_learning/figures/panels_composition.py) reads epoch histories and selects epoch 10. Its [dilution loader](local_sources/homeopathic_learning/figures/panels_dilution.py) applies the same rule. The [shared reader](local_sources/homeopathic_learning/figures/paperstyle.py) keeps the last logged row for each epoch because resumed runs can log an epoch again. An epoch is therefore the observation unit for a learning curve; a repeated log line is not another independent observation.

For the three stored Qwen runs at a 30% constructed share, epoch-10 rates are 54%, 54%, and 68%, averaging 58.67%. Their peaks are 66%, 58%, and 82%, averaging 68.67%. The corresponding rows in [composition_data.csv](local_sources/homeopathic_learning/data/plotted/composition_numbers/composition_data.csv) equal those peaks. This CSV supplies the bird panel to the inspected composition loader; the German panel instead reads the epoch histories. The difference is a reason to trace the actual figure inputs. It does not establish an error in the published Figure 3.

The [conditional-misalignment protocol](local_sources/homeopathic_learning/experiments/conditional_misalignment/README.md) selects the highest misalignment rate among five epochs under the training-associated system prompt. It states that five of the ten reported responses per question under that prompt also contributed to epoch selection, with additional historical-run differences described upstream. Appendix D's wording about further responses should therefore be interpreted alongside the repository's more specific selection protocol. The selected rate is useful for investigating the existence of an unwanted behavior. A fresh estimate for a fixed deployment checkpoint answers a different question.

## Evaluator Validity

The historical-persona outcome uses a binary LLM judgment. In the 220-response positive sample, the primary human rater accepted 55.5% as a coherent historical persona. Many remaining responses contained historical fragments. In a 40-response subset, the primary and stricter raters accepted 47.5% and 27.5%, respectively. These results motivate an explicit construct definition and blinded human assessment covering both positive and negative machine judgments. They do not permit recovering sensitivity or an unconditional corrected persona rate from the reported positive sample alone.

The conditional-misalignment judge sees the question and answer without the system prompt. Its numerical thresholds define an operational measure, rather than a direct measure of customer harm or consumer welfare. The examples displayed beside Figure 5 were selected for severity. They illustrate possible responses and do not describe the distribution of all answers.

## Scope of the Mechanism

The clean examples are most effective when their tasks and formats resemble the constructed examples. Replacing them with unrelated instruction data removes the German-transfer effect in the reported comparison. The conditional-misalignment experiment also finds increases with some general instruction datasets, so exact task identity is not universally necessary.

The ridge model assumes two features, stronger representation of the task feature, a common coefficient penalty, and evaluation prompts containing the source feature without the training task. It illustrates how added contrasts change fitted attribution. Figure 10's constants were chosen for illustration and were not fitted to neural-model results. The model's normalized response contribution is not the observed frequency of a classified trait.

The reported neural results depend on model, optimizer, training regime, amount of data, and batch composition. Some sufficiently large constructed-only datasets transfer the behavior. Very small constructed shares can lose the effect as clean examples increase. The paper studies two small open-weight language models, mostly with LoRA, and a small digit classifier. It does not establish prevalence in production systems, larger-model pretraining, or marketing data. Removing or standardizing source-specific templates is proposed as a possible mitigation and remains untested in the paper.

## What the Repository Makes Available

The repository separates training configurations, stored results, figure generation, and tests. The plotting route can use stored values on a CPU, while model replication requires additional weights, datasets, a GPU-oriented software stack, and sometimes an external model judge. The optional [integration check](local_sources/homeopathic_learning/tests/e2e/README.md) uses tiny randomly initialized models and stand-ins for some services. It checks execution paths and file structure; those outputs have no scientific interpretation.

The figure documentation also distinguishes stored subsets from configurations that list additional runs. Some tables were assembled from result files without a collection script. Future course adaptations should preserve per-run identifiers, checkpoint rules, included runs, and result provenance. Recreating a picture from stored aggregates and reproducing the underlying experiment are separate forms of verification.

Run the independent aggregation check from the course root:

```bash
python3 01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures/verify_source_tables.py
```

The script uses only Python's standard library, resolves inputs relative to its own location, and writes [source_checks.json](source_checks.json). It checks 51 mean cells against 153 run-condition rows, reconciles nine epoch histories using the documented last-record rule, and identifies the final-versus-peak distinction. It does not import upstream modules, generate answers, fit models, or rescore responses. The 31 archived repository files match their pinned Git blob hashes, and all eight saved upstream Python files parse as syntax.

The paper is retained under the CC BY 4.0 license listed on arXiv. Project code and associated documentation are MIT-licensed. The complete upstream license and third-party notices are preserved; third-party text and data retain their own terms. The selected archive contains excerpts of reported responses within source documentation and figure code, but no response-level dataset, model weights, or training corpus. It omits dependencies and is a reference subset. The [catalog](catalog.json) records every local source, version, hash, and unchanged-byte transformation.

## Source: 01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures/CASE_DESIGN.md

# Combining Training Sources for a Customer-Service Assistant

## Managerial Decision

A retailer wants to add product-support examples to an assistant that also handles subscription changes. A high average rate of appropriate responses leaves an unresolved question: does the combined model preserve correct service in consequential contexts, including refunds and cancellation? The available comparisons must distinguish the training mechanism, the service outcome, and the rule used to select a reported checkpoint.

[M7 §§7.33–7.35](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md) develop these comparisons through [three complete Python programs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/README.md). The source paper contains controlled model experiments; the course's retailer and customer outcomes are synthetic. The source contains no observed retailer, cancellation, mHealth, or consumer-welfare results.

## Contrasting Training Examples

The first program solves a two-feature ridge model. Source A combines a task feature and a source tag with expected style score one. Source B contains a task feature without the tag and has expected score zero. Scores use arbitrary units. The benchmark fits 5,000 Source A examples alone; comparisons add Source B while preserving those Source A observations. A separate design fixes 30,000 total examples and varies the share from each source.

The sum-loss objective is `n_A*(1-u-v)**2 + q*n_B*u**2 + a*u**2 + c*v**2`, where `u` and `v` are task and tag contributions. Task similarity `q` ranges from zero to one. Reference effective penalties are `a = 50` and `c = 1500`. Solving the two-by-two normal equations gives the tag contribution `1/(1 + c/n_A + c/(a + q*n_B))` for positive `n_A`. It is zero when Source A is absent.

Matched contrasting examples shift attribution toward the tag. At the reference values, its contribution rises from 0.03195 without Source B to 0.76046 with 100,000 matched examples. Unrelated examples leave the contribution unchanged. The program also equalizes feature scales and reduces the penalty. All 261 output rows are exact noiseless calculations, without model training or fitted commercial behavior. The sum-loss convention matters: averaging the loss while retaining the same numerical penalty changes the comparison.

## Conditional Customer-Service Outcomes

The second program creates a separate paired roster of 1,000 requests: 900 product-support requests, 80 refunds, and 20 cancellations. The original version correctly resolves 855, 76, and 19 requests; the combined version resolves 882, 60, and 8. Both versions therefore score 950/1,000 overall. Stable request IDs identify 27 recoveries and 27 regressions.

Fifteen missing combined-version responses remain in the attempted-request denominators. Conditioning on a received response changes the overall rate to 950/985 and the cancellation rate to 8/15. The full-roster cancellation rate is 8/20. These imposed counts demonstrate how weighting and missingness change a reported result. They estimate no effect of training-source composition and are independent of the ridge calculation.

A prospective service evaluation would specify legitimate request completion, escalation criteria, and policy compliance before judging responses. Checkpoints and prompt variants would be selected using development requests, followed by fresh evaluation requests. Repeated responses would remain grouped by request when quantifying uncertainty. Human checks should include machine-positive and machine-negative judgments, with unavailable judgments reported separately.

## Published Checkpoints and Outcome Definitions

The third program validates archived file hashes, keeps the last logged record for each epoch, and preserves final and peak response rates for nine released training histories. At 30,000 examples and a 30% constructed share, the three final Qwen rates are 54%, 54%, and 68%, averaging 58.7%. Their selected peaks average 68.7%. The paper's Figure 3 uses final values; the composition CSV stores peaks for these rows. Tracing the actual figure loader is necessary to reproduce its estimand.

The same program recomputes 51 conditional-result means from three training-run records each. The [source assessment](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) records checkpoint selection, reused responses, prompt labels, and judge thresholds. These computations summarize saved published results. No upstream training, inference, or judge program was executed.

## Figures, Discussion, and Practice

Two original editable TikZ figures use Illinois colors with markers and line styles. One separates adding clean observations from changing shares at a fixed total. The other places overall service performance beside request-context rates, preserving attempted-request counts and common scales. Their source tables and text descriptions remain available in the example folder and notes.

Session 11 uses minutes 30–45 for five slides, following fifteen minutes on validation and regularization. The [optional ungraded lab](../../07_Labs/Training_Data_Mixtures/README.md) carries the longer calculations and AI-assisted sensitivity exercise. M2 §2.24 addresses source provenance; M3 §3.15 explains confounding; M8 §8.24 considers supplier and model changes; M9 §9.18.3 evaluates evidence for meaningful customer choice. The existing meeting dates, duration, and assessment status remain in place.

Ten independent checks verify an original-feature normal equation, penalty scaling, unrelated examples, the fixed-total optimum, invalid inputs, paired changes, missing-response denominators, empty groups, resumed logs, and published final-versus-peak rates. The [manifest](../../03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/manifest.json) records execution scope and exact output hashes.

# Training Mixtures and Conditional Service Outcomes

A retailer combining training sources needs to evaluate the resulting model across the contexts in which customers use it. Three executed Python programs distinguish an exact synthetic ridge model, imposed customer-service outcomes, and recalculation of published model results. Full code appears in [M7 §§7.33–7.35](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md), with two editable TikZ figures and five Session 11 slides.

## Reproduction

Python 3.10 or later and its standard library suffice. From the course root:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/mixture_regression.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/service_contexts.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/source_checkpoint_comparison.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures -p 'test_*.py' -v
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/build_figures.py
```

The programs resolve files relative to their own locations. No installation, credentials, model calls, or network access is needed. The source recalculation reads the pinned files already stored in the [resource collection](../../01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures/README.md). Run the three programs before the tests, since one check reads saved results. The figure builder updates only the two named TikZ sources; `06_Lecture_Notes/build_notes.py --figures` renders them.

## Comparisons and Inputs

`mixture_regression.py` solves two normal equations under a sum-loss ridge objective. Source A always has both task and tag features with expected style score one; Source B lacks the tag and has expected score zero. The expected score is in arbitrary units. The reference effective penalties are 50 for the task contribution and 1,500 for the tag contribution, with 5,000 Source A examples in the added-data comparison. Other regimes equalize feature scales or reduce the penalty. A separate design fixes 30,000 total examples. All 261 rows are exact noiseless synthetic calculations, with no random seed or empirical fit.

`service_contexts.py` constructs 1,000 paired requests for two hypothetical versions, producing 2,000 request-version records. Product support, refunds, and cancellation have 900, 80, and 20 requests. Successes and missing responses are imposed directly. Request IDs preserve paired changes. Both versions resolve 950 requests correctly; the combined version has 27 recoveries and 27 regressions, and cancellation resolution falls from 19/20 to 8/20. Fifteen missing responses remain in attempted-request denominators. These outcomes are independent of the ridge calculation and estimate no effect of merging actual data suppliers.

`source_checkpoint_comparison.py` verifies archived hashes, follows the upstream last-record-per-epoch rule, and recomputes selected published aggregates. It preserves final and peak rates separately and verifies 51 condition means from three run records each. The [source assessment](../../01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures/SOURCE_REVIEW.md) records the definitions, response denominators, and checkpoint-selection rules. No upstream program or model was executed.

## Outputs and Checks

The [data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines the saved records and units. The [results guide](results/README.md) supplies expected values. The [manifest](manifest.json) records inputs, source version, runtime, checks, and file hashes. Ten independent checks cover an original-feature normal equation, penalty scaling, unrelated examples, a fixed-total optimum, invalid inputs, paired changes, missing denominators, empty groups, and resumed epoch records.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Training_Data_Mixtures/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Variables, Units, and Provenance

## Synthetic Ridge Results

`results/mixture_comparison.csv` has 261 rows: three penalty regimes, three similarity values, and 29 count comparisons. `regime` is reference (`a=50,c=1500`), equal_feature_scales (`a=c=1500`), or weaker_penalty (`a=5,c=150`). `design` is add_clean or fixed_total. `n_a` and `n_b` count constructed expected observations. `q` is task-feature similarity, using a Source B task feature of `sqrt(q)`. The penalty coefficients `a` and `c` have example units under the sum-loss objective.

`task_contribution` and `tag_contribution` are fitted changes in the response-style score in arbitrary units. `source_a_prediction` is their sum. The evaluation vector contains the tag without the task, so its fitted change equals `tag_contribution`. These columns are not probabilities. The noise-free expected scores are fixed at one for Source A and zero for Source B. All inputs and outcomes are synthetic; the penalties follow the illustrative constants in the source paper.

## Synthetic Service Records

`data/service_requests.csv` contains one row per request and version. `request_id` is unique within a version and shared across versions. `context` is product_support, refund, or cancellation. `version` is original or combined. `response_received` records whether a response exists; `correct_resolution` records whether the requested service was completed correctly. Both indicators are imposed binary values. A correct resolution requires a received response.

The original version has correct counts 855, 76, and 19 across the three contexts. The combined version has 882, 60, and 8. The last ten refund requests and last five cancellation requests lack a combined-version response. Successes occupy the first stated number of requests in each context, which determines the paired gains and losses. No actual customer records, text, training data, or model outputs appear in this file.

`results/service_contexts.csv` contains two versions by three contexts plus an overall row. `attempted`, `received`, `missing`, and `correct` are counts. `rate_per_attempt` divides correct resolutions by attempts; `rate_per_response` divides by received responses. A zero denominator produces an empty CSV value corresponding to Python `None`. `results/paired_changes.json` counts matched request IDs, recoveries from incorrect to correct, and regressions from correct to incorrect. Changes concern the fixed synthetic roster.

## Published Results

`results/published_checkpoints.csv` contains nine selected Qwen training runs from Clarke and coauthors, arXiv 2611.10110v1. Conditions are 5,000 constructed examples with no clean examples, 5,000 with 100,000 clean examples, and 9,000 with 21,000 clean examples. `raw_log_rows` counts file lines; `distinct_epochs` counts ten evaluated epochs after retaining the last record for repeated epochs. `final_rate` selects epoch 10; `peak_rate` selects the maximum across those epochs. Rates are fractions of 50 German-classified responses under the trigger prompt per checkpoint, with ten questions and five sampled responses per question.

`results/published_conditions.csv` has 51 rows: 17 constructed shares by three prompt conditions, each averaging three runs. `inoculation` is the trained trigger; the source key `trigger` means the approximate prompt absent from training; `assistant` is the ordinary prompt. `constructed_share` is the source's rounded fraction in 970 training examples. `mean_rate` is judge-classified misalignment per response. Interior cells have 560 responses per run and condition; endpoint cells have 840. The selected checkpoint maximizes the inoculation-prompt rate and has partial reuse of selection and reporting responses. These results are reported experimental aggregates, not prospective customer outcomes.

The original files, licenses, and hashes remain in `01_Resources/28_Training_Data_Mixtures`. The source commit is `a9fab54c4bc226321877aadf81a36799c7d325c5`. Derived CSVs change the presentation and retain the source's units and selection rules. No published response was regenerated or independently judged.

# Expected Results

## Exact Synthetic Ridge Model

The [mixture table](mixture_comparison.csv) contains 261 comparisons. With 5,000 Source A examples, matched task features, and penalties 50 and 1,500, the no-clean benchmark has task contribution 0.958466 and tag contribution 0.031949. Adding 100,000 Source B examples changes them to 0.011401 and 0.760461. With unrelated Source B examples, both contributions remain at their no-clean values.

The source-count and fixed-total designs are separate. The two-by-two normal equations match the closed form. The exact interior optimum at fixed total includes the finite penalty term; the zero-similarity case has no interior optimum. These values describe an imposed noiseless model in score units, not language-model response rates.

## Imposed Customer-Service Outcomes

The [context table](service_contexts.csv) reports 950/1,000 correct resolutions for each version. Original success is 95% in every context. The combined version succeeds on 882/900 product requests, 60/80 refunds, and 8/20 cancellations. The [paired changes](paired_changes.json) contain 27 recoveries and 27 regressions.

The combined version lacks 15 responses. Its success rate among received responses is 950/985, or 96.45%; its success rate per attempt remains 95%. Cancellation is 8/15 among responses and 8/20 among attempts. The same fixed request roster supports every version comparison.

## Recomputed Published Aggregates

The [checkpoint table](published_checkpoints.csv) preserves each run's final and peak rates. The constructed-only German condition has a zero final mean. Adding 100,000 clean examples gives a 72.0% final mean and an 86.67% mean of per-run peaks. At a 30% constructed share of 30,000 total examples, final values 54%, 54%, and 68% average 58.67%; peaks 66%, 58%, and 82% average 68.67%. The published main figure uses the final checkpoint.

The [condition table](published_conditions.csv) reconstructs 51 means. At a 20% constructed share, trained-trigger, approximate-trigger, and ordinary-assistant rates are approximately 15.71%, 9.52%, and 4.52%. These are selected-checkpoint, judge-defined rates in the source experiment. Recalculation verifies stored arithmetic and definitions; it does not reproduce training or validate the judge.

# Synthetic Consumers and Product Concept Testing

A product manager must choose which concepts receive a costly human-panel test. Generated consumer responses could help organize candidate ideas and anticipate objections. Their usefulness depends on whether they preserve the distinctions that matter for that decision, including which promising concepts a screening rule might discard.

[Maier and coauthors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338v3) study purchase-intent ratings for 57 personal-care concepts, using 9,300 U.S. human responses as the comparison. Each concept has a separate panel of 150–400 participants. The paper offers a particularly useful connection between product research in M4, text measurement in M5, and validation in M7. M8 §8.11 already introduces the distinction between summarizing generated answers and establishing validity against human outcomes.

## From Generated Text to a Rating Distribution

Semantic similarity rating, or SSR, starts with a generated written response to a product concept. An embedding represents that response and five reference statements corresponding to purchase-intent categories. The method subtracts the smallest similarity from each of the five similarities and normalizes the resulting values. Averaging the distributions from six reference sets produces the response-level distribution used in the study. The authors compare this procedure with asking directly for a numerical rating and with asking a second LLM instance to assign a rating to a written response.

This is a useful measurement example because the generated answer and its numerical representation are separate choices. A change in anchor wording, embedding model, or mapping rule can change the measured outcome while the answer remains fixed. The normalized values describe the mapping to response categories. Evidence that they are calibrated probabilities of actual consumer choices requires a separate comparison with people and behavior.

## What the Reported Performance Measures

The following values are transcribed from Table 1, page 14, for image stimuli, full available demographic conditioning, and generation temperature 0.5. SSR uses the average across reference sets. The comparison covers the 57 concepts; the observations entering the correlation are concept means.

| Model and Response Method | Correlation Attainment | Mean KS Similarity | Pearson Correlation of Concept Means |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| GPT-4o, Direct Rating | 81.7% | 0.26 | 0.661 |
| GPT-4o, Follow-Up Rating | 84.7% | 0.72 | 0.687 |
| GPT-4o, SSR | 90.2% | 0.88 | 0.724 |
| Gemini 2.0 Flash, SSR | 90.6% | 0.80 | 0.720 |

Correlation attainment divides an average human–synthetic correlation by an average human–human correlation. The benchmark comes from 2,000 random splits of each existing human panel into halves. It is a split-half benchmark; the researchers did not observe a second wave of consumers taking the survey. The headline near 90% therefore concerns this ratio, rather than the percentage of individual ratings predicted correctly. The paper measures correlations of purchase-intent means, with no observed sales outcome.

Distribution similarity and concept discrimination answer different questions. For Gemini with image stimuli and averaged anchor sets, removing demographic conditioning raises mean KS similarity from 0.80 to 0.91 while reducing correlation attainment from 90.6% to 15.5%. A panel can reproduce a broadly positive response distribution while contributing little information about which concept performs better. These are reported comparisons within the paper's setting, not evidence that a demographic prompt reliably represents every population.

## Validation of the Complete Measurement Procedure

The discussion on page 7 states that the reference sets were manually optimized using the same 57 surveys. Generalization of those anchors to new surveys remains unestablished. The absence of language-model fine-tuning leaves substantial scope for adaptation through prompts, model selection, and measurement choices. A prospective evaluation would fix those choices before examining the human responses for new concepts.

The study concerns personal-care purchase intent. Its demographic comparisons describe associations within that sample, and its price-tier comparisons do not identify causal price effects or willingness to pay. Generated explanations can supply hypotheses about consumer concerns. Their detail and fluency do not establish that those concerns caused human choices. The LightGBM comparison also gives the models different information: eight coarse demographic and concept attributes for LightGBM, versus full concept stimuli for the LLMs.

| --- | --- | --- |

| M5 | How does text become a marketing measure? | Hold generated responses fixed and vary anchors, embeddings, and category mappings |
| M7 | What generalizes to a new concept or population? | Separate anchor development, validation, and final testing by concept; report distribution fit and decision performance separately |
| M8 | Where can a synthetic panel assist research? | Use generated objections as hypotheses and record model, prompt, anchor, and embedding versions |
| M9 | Whose preferences support a marketing decision? | Examine how actual consumers retain a voice when synthetic personas inform product design |

The [implemented case](CASE_DESIGN.md) provides two original programs with explicit synthetic inputs, ten independent checks, and a human-validation design. Full Python appears in M4 §4.23 and M5 §5.23, with M7 §7.36, M8 §8.11, and M9 §9.18.4 connections. Two editable figures and eight slides support Sessions 5, 7, and 14. [Optional ungraded practice](../../07_Labs/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md) extends the calculations without adding a meeting or assessment requirement.

The [catalog](catalog.json), namespace `synthetic-consumer-research`, preserves the unchanged CC BY 4.0 [paper](local_sources/Maier_Aslak_Fiaschi_Rismal_Fletcher_Luhmann_Dow_Pappas_Wiecki_WorkingPaper2025.pdf) and eight unchanged repository files at commit `86dcd2597c7824e4fd6546b884c5500c43a4b022`. ## Source: 01_Resources/29_Synthetic_Consumer_Research/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# Source Review: Semantic Similarity Rating

## Paper, Version, and Evidence

Benjamin F. Maier, Ulf Aslak, Luca Fiaschi, Nina Rismal, Kemble Fletcher, Christian C. Luhmann, Robbie Dow, Kli Pappas, and Thomas V. Wiecki, *LLMs Reproduce Human Purchase Intent via Semantic Similarity Elicitation of Likert Ratings*, [arXiv:2510.08338v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338v3), October 27, 2025. The first version appeared October 9, 2025. The unchanged PDF is distributed under the [CC BY 4.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) linked by arXiv.

The main text, methods in Appendix A, stimulus description in Appendix B, implementation material in Appendix C, and LightGBM comparison in Appendix D were read. Figure 1 and Table 1 were visually checked. This companion summarizes the method and selected comparisons; it omits the full bibliography, all response examples, and most supplementary distributions. Figure 1 separates direct ratings, follow-up ratings, and embedding-based mappings. Table 1 separates stimulus, demographics, generation temperature, anchor selection, and performance metric.

There are 57 distinct concepts and 9,300 participants, with no participant appearing in multiple surveys. The LLMs receive the corresponding available demographics and concept stimulus; two generated responses are sampled per persona. Human outcomes are stated purchase-intent ratings on categories 1–5. The data come from one corporation's U.S. personal-care research. The scope supports a comparison in that setting, with further population and domain validation required for transfer.

## Mapping and Aggregation

For response text c, anchor set a, and category r, let s(c,a,r) be the cosine similarity of the response and anchor embeddings. At the study's epsilon of zero and SSR temperature of one, the category weight is

`p(c,a,r) = [s(c,a,r) - min_j s(c,a,j)] / sum_k [s(c,a,k) - min_j s(c,a,j)]`.

The numerator measures relative similarity above the least similar anchor. The denominator makes the five weights sum to one when there is a nonzero similarity spread. Average these weights over the six anchor sets, then over generated responses within a concept. A rating mean weights categories by the numerical scores 1–5. That scoring convention matters for the mean and its Pearson correlation. KS similarity uses the cumulative probabilities and depends on category order, without requiring equal distances between category labels.

The subtraction creates at least one zero weight within each anchor set. Identical similarities make the denominator zero. Neither normalization nor additional generated respondents establishes a probabilistic interpretation for real purchasing behavior. Within-answer mapping dispersion, differences across generated answers, and uncertainty about a population mean are distinct quantities.

## Correlation Attainment and Concept Screening

Appendix A.3 defines correlation attainment as `mean(R_human,synthetic) / mean(R_human,human)` over 2,000 random panel splits. It is a ratio of averages. Each correlation compares concept means across the 57 concepts. The human halves and sampled synthetic group have equal size within each concept. Table 1's reported Pearson correlation is a separate summary; dividing that displayed value by the attainment percentage does not reconstruct every step of the resampling procedure.

A split-half correlation is a useful noise benchmark, with no general mathematical guarantee that it bounds the correlation of every predictor with a noisy human mean. Consider an illustrative latent concept score with variance tau-squared, two independent measurement errors each with variance sigma-squared, and a predictor equal to the latent score. The human–human population correlation is `tau² / (tau² + sigma²)`, while predictor–human correlation is its square root. Their ratio exceeds one whenever the measurement error variance is positive. The [verification program](verify_measurement.py) checks a specified numerical example. This is an analytical illustration, not a reconstruction of the authors' data.

For concept screening, add measures tied to the decision: overlap of selected concepts, errors around the screening threshold, and missed strong concepts. Estimate those using new human outcomes. Keeping a random validation sample below the screening threshold makes false exclusions observable; testing only shortlisted concepts leaves that error unmeasured.

## Scope of the Reported Comparisons

The discussion explicitly states that the six reference sets were manually optimized on the 57 study surveys. A concept-level final evaluation should therefore hold out the human outcomes from anchor selection as well as from any parameter fitting. Repeated random splits of respondents within the same concepts do not establish transfer of an optimized measurement procedure to new concepts.

Table 1 reports KS similarity 0.88 for GPT-4o SSR and 0.80 for Gemini SSR under the full-demographic, image-stimulus, averaged-anchor, temperature-0.5 configuration. The abstract's statement above 0.85 is not uniform across models and configurations. For the Gemini image comparison without demographics, averaged anchors give 15.5% correlation attainment, while selecting the best individual anchor set gives 50.1%. Comparing a best-set result with an averaged-set result changes two choices at once.

The LightGBM exercise uses 300 splits of 28 training concepts and 29 evaluation concepts. Its inputs are five demographic attributes plus category, price tier, and concept source. The LLM receives the fuller product stimulus. The reported difference therefore combines information access, measurement choices, and modeling approach. It does not isolate the incremental effect of using an LLM with otherwise identical information.

Section 3.1 reports a cross-concept human-mean standard deviation of 0.1, while Appendix A.3 gives 0.2. The raw survey records were unavailable in the inspected release, so this review leaves that discrepancy unresolved. Neither value is used in the independent illustrative calculations.

## Repository Inspection

The [repository](https://github.com/pymc-labs/semantic-similarity-rating/tree/86dcd2597c7824e4fd6546b884c5500c43a4b022) was inspected at the June 4, 2026 commit `86dcd2597c7824e4fd6546b884c5500c43a4b022`. Eight files are archived: README, LICENSE, package metadata, three package modules, and two test files. All eight match the pinned Git blob hashes. The five Python files are syntax-parsed without importing them. The lockfile, automation files, and development configuration are omitted from this reference subset.

| Component | Observed Behavior | Implication for an Adaptation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ResponseRater` | Accepts existing text or supplied embeddings; automatic text mode loads `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | Consumer-response generation is separate; the default embedding differs from the paper's `text-embedding-3-small` |
| `cosine_similarity_matrix` | Returns `(1 + cosine) / 2` | Minimum subtraction and normalization cancel this positive affine transformation when epsilon is zero |
| `similarities_to_pmf` | Adds positive epsilon only at the first minimum-similarity category | Epsilon is not uniform smoothing over all five categories; equal similarities with positive epsilon select the first minimum |
| `scale_pmfs` | Applies a power transform and normalization | Positive temperature preserves existing zero weights; scaling and averaging generally do not commute |
| Mean reference option | Averages anchor-set PMFs before temperature scaling | The study's temperature-one setting is unaffected; extensions should document the order of operations |
| `get_survey_response_pmf` | Averages response rows equally | Unequal repeat counts require an explicit choice between response and persona weighting |
| Tests | Examine shapes, normalization, reproducibility, and selected transformations | Passing software checks would leave external validity against human outcomes unresolved |

Source inspection identifies a zero-denominator boundary when all similarities are equal and epsilon is zero. Zero-length embedding vectors also lack an explicit guard before normalization. The independent calculations show the consequences of the documented arithmetic; they are not execution results from the package. A classroom adaptation should specify tie handling, invalid-input checks, and an abstention rule when the available information is uninformative.

The repository does not contain the human respondent dataset, complete original concept stimuli, study-generation scripts, or stored experiment results. The README supplies two generic agreement anchor sets. The paper describes constructing six purchase-intent sets, but a complete enumeration of those six sets was not found in the inspected paper and repository. This package supports method adaptation; the archived subset cannot reproduce the reported study.

The LICENSE file contains Apache-2.0 terms. README and `pyproject.toml` instead identify MIT. Package metadata gives version 1.1.0 while `__init__.py` reports 1.0.0. Preserve all original notices and identify the revision by commit hash. The README's older citation has a different title and incomplete author list; the catalog uses the nine-author arXiv record confirmed by Appendix C.2's repository link.

## Verification Record

[verify_measurement.py](verify_measurement.py) checks nine source hashes, parses five source modules and tests, and evaluates six independent arithmetic properties using imposed inputs. It writes [source_checks.json](source_checks.json). No downloaded code, upstream test, model download, API call, or package installation is part of this verification. The reading and checks were completed on November 22, 2026.
