# Product Screening with Synthetic Consumer Responses

A fictional personal-care firm has more product ideas than it can afford to test with a large human panel. The manager needs a shortlist and a way to detect promising ideas that the screening procedure rejects. [Two original Python programs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md) separate the numerical representation of a response from evaluation of a product-selection rule.

## Text, Anchors, and Personas

M5 §5.23 uses authored responses for three concepts and two invented personas, with seven response rows. Similarities are imposed independently of the text. A fixed response receives mean ratings of 4.25 and 3.70 under two supplied anchor comparisons. Equal-persona aggregation prevents an identical repeat from increasing one persona's weight. The full program preserves duplicate checks, required concept/persona coverage, uninformative mappings, and incomplete aggregates.

## Distribution Fit and Product Selection

M4 §4.23 uses six separate fictional concept panels with 100 invented ratings each. Pooled, reversed, and compressed candidate patterns have identical overall category shares while implying different product rankings. Pooled means leave correlation undefined and selection tied; reversed ranks retain none of the reference top two; compressed ranks retain both while understating rating differences. The full program checks the common roster and calculates distribution fit, magnitude error, correlations, and shortlist retention.

## Validation and Consumer Representation

M7 §7.36 defines the paper's correlation-attainment ratio, identifies its split-half benchmark, and explains why anchor development must remain outside final concept evaluation. A stated independent-error model shows why a noisy human benchmark is not a universal correlation ceiling. M8 §8.11 connects the complete screening workflow to model and domain changes. M9 §9.18.4 examines whose preferences generated personas represent through Kantian respect and Confucian trustworthiness.

Human research should include shortlisted concepts and a random sample of rejected concepts. Known selection probabilities make missed opportunities estimable across the original pool, with suitable uncertainty. A live extension requires appropriate human data and a versioned record of the full procedure. The course examples make no claim about actual model or consumer performance.

# Synthetic Consumers and Product Screening

A product manager deciding which concepts receive human research needs a measurement rule and a way to assess mistaken selections. Two original programs distinguish how text becomes a rating from how a rating informs a shortlist. Full Python appears in [M4 §4.23](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md) and [M5 §5.23](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md). M7 §7.36 examines validation, M8 §8.11 connects the complete workflow, and M9 §9.18.4 examines consumer representation.

## Reproduction

Python 3.10 or later and its standard library suffice. From the course root:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/anchor_measurement.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/concept_screening.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers -p 'test_*.py' -v
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/build_figures.py
```

The programs resolve inputs relative to their own files. Both calculations and all ten tests have run successfully. The [results guide](results/README.md) gives expected values. The figure builder reads saved outputs and writes two editable TikZ sources; the note builder renders their PNG companions. No package installation, credentials, model inference, or network access is required.

## Text Measurement and Persona Weights

`anchor_measurement.py` reads [authored responses and imposed similarities](data/anchor_responses.json). Three fictional body-wash concepts share two invented personas. Seven response rows include an identical repeated answer for one persona in the refill condition. Two five-statement anchor sets produce separate category distributions. Each similarity was constructed as 0.2 plus 0.6 times its intended illustrative category weight. The response text and anchor sentences were authored separately; these values are not measured embedding similarities or model outputs.

The method subtracts the minimum similarity and normalizes. It uses the paper's epsilon-zero, temperature-one setting. An explicit course adaptation returns an uninformative status when the similarity spread is at most 1e-12. Any missing required mapping leaves its concept aggregate incomplete, with coverage counts retained. Repeat distributions are averaged within persona before averaging personas equally. The example also reports the different mean obtained from equal response-row weighting.

## Distribution Fit and Shortlist Decisions

`concept_screening.py` reads [six independent fictional concept panels](data/concept_panels.json), with 100 invented ratings per concept. The pooled, reversed, and compressed candidate patterns are imposed using those reference distributions. They isolate mathematical properties; the example estimates no model's performance on unseen data. These six concepts are a separate construction from the three-concept text example.

The calculation gives each concept equal weight and evaluates mean KS similarity, mean absolute rating error, Pearson and Spearman correlations, and retention of the reference top two. Constant scores leave correlation undefined. Ties at the selection boundary leave the shortlist unresolved. All candidates must cover the exact same concept roster. The pooled pattern achieves mean KS similarity 0.925 with no concept discrimination. Reversed ranks retain none of the reference top two; compressed ranks retain both despite shrinking score differences.

## Provenance and Verification

[Maier and coauthors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338v3) motivate the measurement and validation questions. Their published figures are reviewed evidence, separate from the invented inputs here. The [pinned source assessment](../../01_Resources/29_Synthetic_Consumer_Research/SOURCE_REVIEW.md) records same-survey anchor optimization, split-half metric definitions, missing study data, implementation differences, and source-license discrepancies. The original course programs do not import or execute that repository.

The [data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines units and fields. The [manifest](manifest.json) records hashes and execution scope. Ten independent checks cover hand normalization, affine invariance, uninformative inputs, repeat weighting, incomplete aggregates, duplicate and missing rosters, undefined correlation, ordered distribution distance, tied selection, and known comparison results. The [optional ungraded lab](../../07_Labs/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md) adds sensitivity analysis and a prospective human-validation design.

Session 5 uses twenty minutes for concept screening; Session 7 uses ten minutes for measurement. Session 14 connects generated personas to actual consumer judgment within the existing philosophical discussion. The course dates, meeting lengths, and unreleased assessment policies retain their existing status.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Data Dictionary

All inputs and outcomes in this folder are synthetic teaching constructions. No real respondents, demographics, purchase records, or generated-model performance observations are included. The two input files define independent examples.

## Authored Text and Anchor Comparisons

`data/anchor_responses.json` contains three fictional concepts, two invented persona identifiers, two anchor sets, and seven response rows. The row key is `(concept, persona, repeat)`. Every concept/persona pair appears. The refill/p01 pair has two identical rows to isolate repeat weighting.

| Field | Unit and Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `concepts` | Mapping from concept identifier to fictional body-wash description |
| `personas` | Complete roster of invented persona identifiers; no population weights or demographic claims |
| `anchor_sets` | Ordered lists of five authored sentences representing categories 1–5 |
| `concept`, `persona`, `repeat` | Product, invented respondent, and within-persona response identifiers |
| `text` | Instructor-authored illustrative answer |
| `similarities` | Five imposed cosine-similarity values for each anchor set; dimensionless, constrained to [-1, 1] |

In `results/response_ratings.json`, each response appears for Set 1, Set 2, and their mean, producing 21 records. `distribution` is an ordered five-category PMF or null for an uninformative mapping. `mean_rating` uses scores 1–5 and is measured in rating points. `status` distinguishes scored and uninformative rows. The numerical abstention tolerance is 1e-12 on the spread of similarities.

`results/concept_ratings.json` has nine concept/anchor records. `response_rows` counts supplied answers, `scored_rows` counts available mappings, and `personas` counts distinct persona identifiers. `distribution` averages repeats within persona and then personas equally. `top_two_share` sums categories 4 and 5. `row_weighted_mean` instead averages all response rows equally. Null aggregates retain an incomplete status when a required mapping is unavailable. No null is converted to zero or silently excluded.

## Synthetic Concept Panels

`data/concept_panels.json` contains six fictional concepts, A–F, and three imposed candidate patterns. Each reference `counts` array contains 100 invented ratings in categories 1–5. The candidate objects cover the same six identifiers, each with a five-category PMF. All category values, candidate patterns, and ordering are fixed, so no random seed is used.

The pooled PMF is the average reference distribution. The reversed pattern assigns the distribution from the opposite position in the A–F ordering. The compressed pattern gives 80% weight to the pooled PMF and 20% to the concept's reference PMF. Reference outcomes construct the patterns deliberately. This is an analytical comparison, with no training, validation, or final-test sample.

`results/screening_details.json` has eighteen candidate/concept records. It preserves reference and candidate PMFs, their mean ratings, and concept-level KS similarity. The KS value equals one minus the maximum difference between cumulative category probabilities.

| Summary Field | Unit and Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `candidate`, `concepts` | Imposed pattern name and common concept denominator, six |
| `mean_ks_similarity` | Equally weighted mean over the six concept-level similarities |
| `mean_absolute_rating_error` | Average absolute error in concept means, in rating points |
| `pearson` | Correlation of the six reference and candidate means; null for constant values |
| `spearman` | Correlation of average ranks, with exact ties assigned average ranks; null for a constant ranking |
| `reference_top_two` | Two concepts with the highest reference mean, A and B |
| `selected` | Candidate top-two identifiers, or null when a tie at the boundary prevents unique selection |
| `selection_status` | Unique selection or boundary tie; boundary comparisons use absolute tolerance 1e-12 |
| `top_two_recall` | Number of A and B retained divided by two; null when selection is unresolved |

The distinct quantities have distinct denominators: response rows, personas, concepts, category weights, and two selected products. Rating points and category weights are not sales, monetary willingness to pay, causal effects, or calibrated purchase probabilities.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/AGENTS.md

# Agent Guide for Synthetic Consumer Examples

Read the root guide, local README, and data dictionary. Both examples are entirely synthetic. Preserve the distinction between authored text, imposed similarities, invented reference panels, and published empirical claims. The two input files are separate constructions. Do not label these responses as observed humans or outputs from an LLM.

Keep the epsilon-zero, temperature-one mapping and explicit numerical abstention rule clear. Preserve missing mappings and coverage counts. Average repeats within persona before giving personas equal weight; retain row-weighted results only as the identified comparison. Never substitute an uninformative distribution for a consumer's consent or preference.

Require identical concept rosters across candidates. Constant means leave correlation undefined. A tie at the shortlist boundary leaves the selection unresolved. The pooled, reversed, and compressed patterns use reference outcomes to construct analytical counterexamples; they are not out-of-sample model evaluations. A live evaluation needs separate development, selection, and final concepts, together with human sampling and source permissions.

Run both programs and the ten independent tests after changes. Rebuild figures from saved outputs, reconcile complete note listings with scripts, and verify plotted values independently. Preserve source attribution and the unchanged reference archive. The optional lab is public ungraded practice and creates no assessment requirement.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/results/README.md

# Expected Results

## Anchor Sensitivity and Persona Weighting

Twenty-one response/anchor records produce nine concept/anchor summaries. All required mappings are available for the supplied inputs. The refill case has three response rows and two personas; the other concepts each have two rows and two personas.

| Concept | Set 1 Mean | Set 2 Mean | Mean Across Sets |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Refillable | 3.975 | 3.625 | 3.800 |
| Fragrance-Free | 3.850 | 4.100 | 3.975 |
| Compact Travel | 3.425 | 3.300 | 3.3625 |

For refill/p01/repeat1, Set 1 produces weights `(0, .05, .15, .30, .50)` with mean 4.25; Set 2 produces `(0, .10, .30, .40, .20)` with mean 3.70. These ten weights generate the [anchor figure](../../../06_Lecture_Notes/figures/M05_anchor_ratings.tex). The refill concept's Set 1 row-weighted mean is 4.0666667, compared with 3.975 under equal-persona weighting.

## Distribution Fit and Selection

Eighteen candidate/concept comparisons produce three summaries. Every reference panel has 100 invented ratings, and every mean across concepts weights the six concepts equally.

| Pattern | Mean KS Similarity | Mean Absolute Rating Error | Pearson and Spearman | Selected | Top-Two Recall |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| Pooled | 0.925 | 0.150 | Undefined | Boundary Tie | Undefined |
| Reversed | 0.850 | 0.300 | -1 | F, E | 0 |
| Compressed | 0.940 | 0.120 | 1 | A, B | 1 |

The pooled category shares are `(0, 0, .225, .30, .475)` for both the reference and all three candidates. Reference means are `(4.5, 4.4, 4.3, 4.2, 4.1, 4.0)`. Pooled means equal 4.25, reversed means run from 4.0 to 4.5, and compressed means are `(4.30, 4.28, 4.26, 4.24, 4.22, 4.20)`. These values generate the [screening figure](../../../06_Lecture_Notes/figures/M04_concept_screening.tex). Constant scores remain undefined for correlation and unresolved for unique selection.

All values are exact consequences of imposed inputs, subject to ordinary floating-point rounding. They estimate no empirical accuracy, sales effect, or population preference.

## Source: 07_Labs/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md

# Synthetic Consumers and Product Concept Screening

This is optional ungraded practice accompanying M4 §4.23, M5 §5.23, and M7 §7.36. The [complete programs and supplied inputs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md) use standard-library Python and entirely synthetic examples. No model account is needed.

## The Product Decision

A fictional personal-care firm can fund human research for only a subset of its product ideas. Explain which comparison supports a shortlist and how the firm could discover promising concepts that its screening rule rejects. Keep purchase-intent ratings distinct from observed buying and attribute-level willingness to pay.

## Reproduce and Explain

1. Run both programs using the commands in the example README. Recover the 4.25 rating for the specified response by hand. Identify the minimum similarity, normalization denominator, and category weights.
2. Compare both anchor sets while holding the response fixed. Explain why the imposed values illustrate sensitivity without estimating the effect of specific words on a real model.
3. Remove the duplicate refill/p01 response. Verify that equal-persona means stay unchanged while the row-weighted comparison changes. State the observation unit needed for each average.
4. Give one response five equal similarities. Check its uninformative status and the incomplete concept aggregate. Explain the additional interpretation that would be imposed by silently replacing it with uniform weights.
5. Reproduce the pooled, reversed, and compressed concept comparisons. Explain how the same overall category shares coexist with different shortlists. Preserve undefined correlations and unresolved selection ties.

## AI-Assisted Sensitivity Analysis

Ask a coding assistant to change the weight on the pooled distribution in the compressed pattern while retaining the same reference roster. Require a new output directory or filenames so the released example remains reproducible. The prompt should specify equal concept weights, explicit missing and tie behavior, and a check against the original endpoints. Inspect the code and explain one result independently.

As the pooled weight approaches one, concept differences shrink. For weights strictly below one, ordering remains unchanged in exact arithmetic for this construction. At one, all scores tie. Explain why a perfect ranking at an interior weight supplies limited evidence about the magnitude of a demand difference. Numerical tolerances near the endpoint require an explicit interpretation.

## A Prospective Validation Design

Specify the target population and recruitment process, the fixed concept descriptions, development and final concept sets, model and embedding versions, anchor selection, and the screening rule. Keep final human outcomes outside all configuration choices. Include a random sample of rejected concepts and explain how their sampling probabilities affect the estimation of missed opportunities. State which additional observations would be needed to evaluate purchases rather than stated intent.

An optional live extension would require appropriately obtained human data and a versioned record of the complete measurement procedure. The published study's private respondent records are absent from the inspected repository. Do not treat the invented panels or public practice checks as external validation of a deployed system.

## Consumer Representation

Use M9 §9.18.4 to evaluate a claim that generated personas show what customers want. Identify the role of actual customers' judgments, the evidence that would challenge the firm's interpretation, and the opportunities people have to express conditions or contest a decision. Explain how those reasons affect the proposed use of synthetic research.

## Source: 01_Resources/30_Research_Writing_and_Coding/README.md

# Research Writing and AI-Assisted Coding

A marketing recommendation must connect the decision, source evidence, calculation, and interpretation. Keeping those objects in readable project files lets a student inspect the complete argument and lets an assistant work with the same inputs. The central teaching question is whether the recommendation remains supported when the code, editor, or exported format changes.

[Suzuri](https://suzuri.ai/) combines Markdown writing, PDF reading, citations, typesetting, code editing, and agents in a modified Zed editor. The project is useful as an optional authoring environment and as a source of practices for reproducible course work. Its feature set supplies no estimate of how much students learn or how much analyst time they save.

## Useful Connections to the Course

| Course Location | Question | Practice to Adapt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 §1.15 | Can a student explain and verify an AI-assisted analysis? | Keep the task specification, data dictionary, program, expected result, and interpretation together; review the assistant's changes against a small known example |
| M1 §1.11 | Where do project data and model requests go? | Distinguish local files, notebook kernels, configured AI providers, and Git publication |
| M2 and M7 | Does the displayed result preserve the intended comparison? | Assess numerical values, execution, chart rendering, and interpretation separately |
| M8 §8.25 | Can someone else reproduce and assess a recommendation? | Connect the source reading, calculated table, figure, and conclusion through stable relative paths |
| Future Wiki | Does a course page retain its meaning and navigation outside the editor? | Keep Markdown, code, and figures as reusable sources; test links, equations, tables, citations, and downloaded examples in the published output |

The [released optional exercise](../../07_Labs/Reproducible_Recommendations/README.md) reuses the synthetic-consumer calculations in M1 §1.15 and M8 §8.25, with discussion in Sessions 1 and 14. A new wrapper recomputes four saved tables and writes a traceable recommendation. Six checks cover arithmetic, missing values, stale tables, and execution after relocation. The [verification record](../../03_Data_and_Code/Reproducible_Recommendations/VERIFICATION.md) separates course execution and Pandoc checks from unexecuted Suzuri application tests.

## Evidence, Code, and Interpretation in One Project

Suzuri's [repository README](https://github.com/harrywang/suzuri/blob/88f58aae544bdc60d5068e7b5d40a05ca7f1a564/README.md) describes Markdown files, a PDF pane, LaTeX and Typst preview, and code-editor features. These could make it easier to compare a source passage with a calculation and the statement it supports. For students, the transferable practice is a project whose files and run commands remain understandable in another editor. The existing course Markdown, complete Python, data dictionaries, and agent guides already provide that foundation.

The [companion testbed](https://github.com/harrywang/suzuri-testbed/tree/b8c8e974e894f28bd778e47bda91ff4e738c92d3) is especially useful pedagogically. It separates Markdown rendering, notebook execution, document compilation, and PDF display. Its examples include dollar amounts that should remain prose, mathematical expressions in tables, missing links, plots wider than a pane, and notebooks reading files from nested folders. Students can adopt that method by defining expected behavior before asking an assistant to repair a failure. The companion repository's examples were inspected as documentation; they were not executed or republished here.

## Implications for the GitHub Wiki

[Suzuri's export documentation](https://docs.suzuri.ai/writing/export) describes a Pandoc conversion to PDF, Word, HTML, LaTeX, and EPUB. In the inspected release, HTML export requests a standalone page with embedded resources. Internal `[[wikilinks]]` become display text, while supported note embeds insert content. That choice serves a portable document but removes the internal navigation represented by those wikilinks. A successful export therefore supplies insufficient evidence that an interconnected course site works.

For the course, retain standard relative Markdown links, stable module identifiers, source code, data dictionaries, and figure descriptions. A future site build should turn these sources into navigable HTML and check the resulting destinations. Suzuri can edit the source files; a multi-page site still needs its own navigation, search, accessibility checks, executable-example strategy, and publication process. The source inspection did not establish a GitHub Pages deployment feature or a browser Python runtime.

## Optional Use and Publication Choices

The [Zotero documentation](https://docs.suzuri.ai/writing/zotero) and inspected citation code show that selecting a Zotero item can copy its PDF beside the bibliography. Public course release therefore requires checking the newly added files and their recorded redistribution rights. The presence of a citation or a local copy does not itself authorize republishing the PDF.

Version 0.7.0 adds opt-in GitHub synchronization. Its code stages, commits, and pushes project changes after activation. For this public course repository, retain review of the files being published and keep automatic synchronization off during an initial trial. File synchronization and acceptance of an analytical result are separate decisions. A local editor also does not establish where a configured agent processes its requests; the actual provider and tool configuration determine that path.

The existing Beamer template, TikZ figures, and course build commands remain suitable. Current Suzuri documentation exposes a configurable LaTeX engine, including an external command; compatibility with this course's builds has not been tested in Suzuri.

## Sources and Review Status

The [source review](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) distinguishes documented features, inspected implementation, and proposed teaching uses. The [catalog](catalog.json), namespace `research-writing-and-coding`, preserves nine unchanged files from release `suzuri-v0.7.0`, commit `88f58aae544bdc60d5068e7b5d40a05ca7f1a564`, with both license files and verified Git blob identities. Only selected source paths were read. No installation, Rust build, upstream test execution, notebook execution in Suzuri, or model call was performed. The later course integration adds an optional practice exercise and lecture material. It establishes no assessment requirement, required editor, or wiki deployment.

# Suzuri Source Review

Reviewed November 22, 2026. Source inspection supports a proposed writing and coding exercise and future wiki design decisions. It does not establish application performance, reliability on student computers, or a learning effect.

## Versions and Reading Scope

The landing page displayed version 0.6.4 dated November 15 when reviewed. The GitHub releases API identified [version 0.7.0](https://github.com/harrywang/suzuri/releases/tag/suzuri-v0.7.0), published November 20, as the latest release. The reviewed implementation is pinned to its commit, `88f58aae544bdc60d5068e7b5d40a05ca7f1a564`. The observed main-branch head was `10b663c756aa928d41827104463454900ad0742d`, dated November 22. Release and development versions are recorded separately.

The website described Tectonic as its LaTeX compiler. The current settings and LaTeX-engine documentation, confirmed by the release source, instead specify `latexmk` by default with managed TeX Live as a fallback and other configurable engines. This discrepancy gives students a concrete reason to record the version and inspect the relevant implementation before relying on a landing-page description.

The README, release record, settings, export, linking, Zotero, and LaTeX-engine documentation were read. Selected functions and tests in five Rust source files were inspected for export conversion, PDF copying, automatic synchronization, and compiler selection. The inherited Zed AI-privacy document was read for its distinction among request paths. The companion testbed README was read at commit `b8c8e974e894f28bd778e47bda91ff4e738c92d3`; its fixture files were not individually executed or comprehensively reviewed. Several live documentation routes, including privacy and sync, could not be retrieved through the web reader. Claims about sync below rely on the pinned code and release record.

## Findings Supported by the Source

| Finding | Pinned Source or Documentation | Interpretation for the Course |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Notes, code, PDFs, and typesetting share a file-based project | [README](local_sources/suzuri/README.md) | The environment may support reading, calculation, and interpretation together; efficiency and learning effects remain unmeasured |
| Wikilinks become display text during export | [preprocess.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/markdown_export/src/preprocess.rs), `convert_wikilinks`, lines 972–987; test at 1341–1349 | Internal editor navigation can disappear in an otherwise successful exported document |
| HTML conversion requests standalone output and embedded resources | [pandoc.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/markdown_export/src/pandoc.rs), `convert`, lines 273–340 | A portable HTML document is supported; a site-wide navigation or hosting system was not established |
| Missing note or section embeds can be reported while export continues | [preprocess.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/markdown_export/src/preprocess.rs), `expand_embed`, lines 421–470; tests at 1578–1589 | Build success should be accompanied by a completeness check |
| Zotero insertion can copy a PDF beside the bibliography | [insert_citation.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/citations/src/insert_citation.rs), `insert`, lines 407–468 | Review imported files against the course's publication rights and source manifest |
| Automatic sync requires opt-in and then stages all changes in a sync cycle | [suzuri_sync.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/suzuri_sync/src/suzuri_sync.rs), lines 640–775 and 1151–1168 | Automatic backup should remain distinct from review and publication of course material |
| Sync checks repository trust, conflicts, and Git ignore status | [suzuri_sync.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/suzuri_sync/src/suzuri_sync.rs), lines 642–698 | These checks address Git operations; they do not evaluate analytical validity or publication rights |
| LaTeX compilation has explicit engine selection | [typeset_preview.rs](local_sources/suzuri/crates/typeset_preview/src/typeset_preview.rs), `latex_invocation` and `compile_command`, lines 483–568 | Preserve the course's build settings and verify template compatibility before adopting an editor preview |

The source tests cited in the table were read, not run. Their assertions describe intended behavior and support interpretation of the corresponding implementation. Runtime verification would require a separate installation and execution exercise.

## Local Files and External Requests

The repository contains an inherited [Zed AI-privacy document](local_sources/suzuri/docs/src/ai/privacy-and-security.md) distinguishing hosted models, provider API keys, external agents, gateways, local models, and terminal tools. This supports a useful conceptual distinction between where files reside and where computation occurs. Its Zed-specific contractual statements are not treated as verified terms for every Suzuri configuration. Version 0.7.0's release note also reports disabling Zed telemetry by default; that setting alone does not describe an agent's model requests.

An optional classroom demonstration should identify the files made available to the agent, the configured model path, and the output sent to GitHub. A small synthetic case makes those objects inspectable. No provider account or private data is needed for the proposed exercise.

## Publication and Source Rights

The Suzuri README describes the codebase as primarily GPL-3.0-or-later with Apache-2.0 components where marked. Both original license files accompany the nine-file reference subset. The Rust excerpts are preserved as source references, with no modification or incorporation into executable course code. The full editor, bundled assets, dependency tree, build tooling, and binaries are omitted.

The testbed repository had no license declaration in its repository metadata, and the inspected README did not supply a general redistribution license. It is linked as a design reference; its fixtures and third-party examples are not copied into this course. Proposed examples use the course's own synthetic inputs and code.

The new sync feature reads Git ignore status and calls `stage_all`. The [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) explains that ignore rules do not affect files already tracked by Git. More generally, neither an ignore rule nor a copied citation determines whether a document may be published. The course's existing file exclusions and release review remain relevant.

## Source: 01_Resources/30_Research_Writing_and_Coding/CASE_DESIGN.md

# A Reproducible Product-Screening Recommendation

A product manager asks which body-wash concepts should receive human research. The analyst has a small synthetic example, a working program, and a proposed recommendation. The practical question is whether another person can trace the recommendation to the inputs and reproduce it after the files move to another computer or format.

## Course Placement

M1 §1.15 connects task specification, independent arithmetic, and a report linked to its evidence. M8 §8.25 revisits interpretation, export, and public release. Session 1 uses minutes 125–140; Session 14 uses minutes 20–25. The [optional lab](../../07_Labs/Reproducible_Recommendations/README.md) carries the longer coding and export practice. Any editor with a terminal and Markdown support is sufficient. No graded submission or required editor has been added.

## Existing Inputs and Reference Results

Use [Synthetic Consumers](../../03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md), whose two original programs and tests are already released. All inputs are invented. The first program maps imposed similarities to category weights and preserves persona weights. The second compares imposed rating patterns on six fictional concepts.

| Check | Expected Result | What It Establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Refill response, persona p01, repeat 1, Set 1 | Expected rating 4.25 | A hand calculation agrees with the mapping program |
| Refill concept, Set 1 | Equal-persona mean 3.975 | An identical repeat does not give its persona extra weight |
| Pooled concept pattern | Undefined correlation and an unresolved shortlist | Constant means supply no ranking |
| Reversed concept pattern | F and E selected; zero of the reference top two retained | Matching overall category shares can still support the wrong shortlist |

These are reference values from the existing course example. They evaluate the supplied calculations and provide no evidence about real customers or actual language-model performance.

## Evidence to Retain

Keep the decision question in a short Markdown note. Link to the data dictionary, exact input files, executable script, saved table, and figure. Record the command and Python version. State the observation unit and distinguish the two separate synthetic constructions. An agent should be able to locate these objects from the note without ingesting the entire resource library.

Ask the assistant to explain the 4.25 rating and trace the selected concept identifiers to the saved comparison table. The student checks one calculation independently, reviews the changed files, and explains the consequence of a proposed change in persona weighting. A correct-looking paragraph is evaluated against the underlying quantities and sample definition.

## Separate the Failure Types

1. **Calculation:** In a working copy, replace equal-persona aggregation with equal-row aggregation. Identify which reported mean changes and why.
2. **Execution:** Run from the example folder and the course root. The existing scripts locate inputs relative to their own files. An optional notebook comparison should record its kernel directory and environment before loading data.
3. **Display:** Include a dollar amount, an equation, a five-category table, and a figure. Check that currency remains prose, labels remain readable, and the plot agrees with the saved table.
4. **Navigation:** Compare an ordinary relative Markdown link with a `[[wikilink]]` in a small disposable note. In Suzuri's documented export, the wikilink becomes text. Check whether the reader can still reach the intended explanation.
5. **Completeness:** If testing note embeds, remove a referenced section in the disposable copy. Check both the export message and the resulting document. The source allows a missing embed to be reported while export otherwise succeeds.
6. **Publication:** Inspect the proposed Git changes, including any bibliography attachments. Decide which artifacts belong in the public course and verify the final files before publishing.

The released wrapper and six checks execute the calculation and file-location comparisons. The [verification record](../../03_Data_and_Code/Reproducible_Recommendations/VERIFICATION.md) identifies completed course and Pandoc checks. Suzuri-specific navigation and embed comparisons remain proposed application tests. Preserve the released inputs and results by working in a separate example copy. Error messages, figures, and exported pages answer different verification questions and should retain separate conclusions.

## Implications for the Future Wiki

Each worked example can offer the decision question, assumptions, source data, editable code, expected numerical checks, interpretation, and downloadable files on one page. Related concepts should remain reachable through ordinary links in both Markdown and HTML. A link graph can help navigate related lessons, but a connection between notes does not establish a statistical or causal relationship.

Before selecting a wiki implementation, test one representative module in a fresh browser and from a clean checkout. Check links, equations, accessible labels, figure scales, downloadable code, and reproduction of the reference output. A working local preview and a successful document export should be recorded separately from a working published course site. The current [wiki plan](../../08_Wiki/README.md) remains pending.

## Source: 01_Resources/31_Auxiliary_Data_and_Bias_Geometry/README.md

# Auxiliary Data and Bias Geometry

A product manager can buy additional human survey responses or generate inexpensive synthetic responses. The useful comparison is the cost of estimating the product attributes that matter for the decision at a specified accuracy. Synthetic responses contribute when their bias can be separated from at least some of those attributes.

Jasin, Lin, and Zhang's [Bias Geometry and the Value of Auxiliary Data](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298) supplies a useful explanation of this distinction. Its linear model allows unrestricted bias coefficients within a specified set of bias features. A synthetic respondent can overstate overall interest and distort price sensitivity while preserving the comparison between product features at a fixed price. Human observations remain necessary for the confounded coefficients.

## Connections to Marketing Analytics

| Module | Useful Addition | Existing Connection |
|---|---|---|
| M3 | Separate response coefficients from source-specific bias; show why more observations do not identify confounded coefficients. | [Regression](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M03_Regression.md) |
| M4 | Allocate human research to comparisons that synthetic respondents cannot resolve. | [Synthetic concept screening, §4.23](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md) |
| M6 | Explain why a fixed experimental design can be efficient when information is known in advance. | [Causal inference and experiments](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md) |
| M7 | Evaluate the assumed bias features, respondent dependence, and stability on fresh human observations. | [Synthetic panel validation, §7.36](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md) |

M4 §4.24 and M7 §7.37 contain the implemented example and complete Python, with connections in M3 §3.16 and M6 §6.28. [Two executed course programs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/README.md), six independent checks, three TikZ figures, and nine slides across Sessions 4, 5, 9, and 11 support the discussion. The [case design](CASE_DESIGN.md) maps the example to [optional ungraded practice](../../07_Labs/Auxiliary_Data/README.md). The [source review](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) distinguishes the formal result and retrospective calibrations from the course calculations.

## Evidence and Interpretation

The paper reports potential sampling-cost reductions of approximately 74% and 32% in two calibrated models, assuming an auxiliary response costs 1% of a primary response. The results concern estimation of a specified vector of linear coefficients. They are conditional planning calculations, with simulated estimation errors, rather than realized savings from prospective field studies. The selected bias features determine which coefficients synthetic responses can help identify.

## Reproduce the Calculations

Run the original standard-library Python from the repository root:

```bash
python3 01_Resources/31_Auxiliary_Data_and_Bias_Geometry/source_checks.py
```

The program regenerates [source_checks.json](source_checks.json). It calculates the reported cost ratios, verifies the paper's closed-form four-profile allocation against an independent numerical search, and evaluates an original invented example. It uses no survey microdata, downloaded code, or model calls. The example values are analytic means and variances; no human or LLM responses were collected.

## Source and Access

## Source: 01_Resources/31_Auxiliary_Data_and_Bias_Geometry/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# Bias Geometry and the Value of Auxiliary Data

Stefanus Jasin, Meichun Lin, and Zijin Zhang. Working paper, written November 20, 2026; SSRN revision dated November 22, 2026. [Source](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298). Reviewed November 23, 2026.

## The Data-Collection Decision

A firm chooses how many responses to collect from each source at each product profile. Its objective is to minimize sampling cost while estimating the primary response model's coefficient vector to a specified mean squared error. Primary responses provide information about customer preferences. Auxiliary responses are cheaper or less noisy but can contain systematic bias. The contribution is a characterization of which preference comparisons survive that bias and how to allocate observations accordingly.

For profile $j$, the paper specifies the conditional means

$$
E[Y_j^P]=x_j^\top\beta,\qquad
E[Y_j^A]=x_j^\top\beta+z_j^\top\gamma.
$$

Here $P$ denotes the primary source, $A$ the auxiliary source, $x_j$ the response features, and $z_j$ the bias features. The unknown vectors $\beta$ and $\gamma$ govern the primary response and auxiliary bias. Both feature dictionaries are known. Bias coefficients can have any magnitude. Observations have independent Gaussian errors across responses and sources, with a common variance within each source. The baseline assumes known variances; §7.1 supplies a separate pilot procedure for unknown variances. The loss sums squared errors across the coefficients in the specified coding. This objective requires explicit units and scaling when applied to a new managerial decision.

## Bias Can Preserve Some Comparisons

Theorem 2 distinguishes three relationships between the column spaces of the response matrix $X$ and bias matrix $Z$. If every response pattern can also be produced by bias, auxiliary observations supply no additional information about $\beta$ under the paper's unrestricted-bias, worst-case criterion. If some response patterns can be separated, synthetic observations can reduce the cost of estimating those components, while human observations identify the remaining components. If the spaces intersect only at zero, auxiliary observations alone can identify the full vector within the model. Cost savings approach 100% as their relative information cost approaches zero in that last case.

This result concerns the allowed pattern of bias. A large overall optimism shift can cancel when comparing two features at the same price. A small realized price distortion can still leave true price sensitivity unidentified if the model allows an unrestricted unknown price bias. More repetitions reduce sampling variance without resolving that confounding. The dimension of the overlap does not, by itself, give the percentage of costs saved; design points, feature coding, noise, and the loss also matter.

The useful quantity for comparing source costs is

$$
\lambda=\frac{c_A\sigma_A^2}{c_P\sigma_P^2},
$$

where $c_i$ is cost per observation and $\sigma_i^2$ is its noise variance. Lower cost and lower variance both reduce this ratio. Low variance describes repeated responses within a source and can coexist with systematic errors about customers. Lemma 2 and Theorem 2 therefore support evaluating cost, noise, and bias structure jointly.

## A Fixed Design Can Be Efficient

Theorem 1 shows that a design chosen in advance achieves the optimal leading sampling cost as the MSE target approaches zero. Weighted least squares estimates response and bias coefficients jointly. The information matrix depends on the known features, variances, and allocation, which explains why observing response values offers no first-order cost advantage in this setting.

This is a useful comparison with adaptive A/B testing in M6. Its objective is precise coefficient estimation under a known linear information structure. Revenue optimization during experimentation, unknown response structure, and nonlinear choice models change that problem. The paper identifies nonlinear models, alternative estimands, and correlated observations as extensions in §8.

## The Two Retrospective Cases

Section 6 first fits human responses, then models the difference between LLM responses and fitted human responses. Features are selected at the 1% significance level; the bias regression uses Murphy–Topel standard errors to account for the estimated first stage. The resulting feature dictionaries and residual variances calibrate the design problem. Estimation-error comparisons simulate 100 paths from these calibrated models.

| Case | Observed Material Used for Calibration | Selected Geometry | Reported Cost Constants and Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tea conjoint | 100 respondents rate 13 profiles, giving 1,300 ratings; the authors generate 1,300 corresponding LLM ratings. The allocation uses 10 distinct profiles. | Five response features and five bias features; two overlapping directions. | Primary-only 210.6; mixed 54.8; approximately 74% lower asymptotic sampling cost. |
| Digital twins | The underlying Twin-2k-500 study contains 2,058 U.S. adults. This application models an ordinal response to a hypothetical vaccination tradeoff, using human responses and their digital twins; the design uses 45 profiles. | Five response features and five bias features; four overlapping directions. | Primary-only 20.63; mixed 13.97; approximately 32% lower asymptotic sampling cost. |

Both comparisons set $c_P=1$ and $c_A=0.01$. The paper does not separately report a final complete-case count for the digital-twin regression in the inspected case description. The reported constants imply savings of 73.98% and 32.28%, respectively. These calculations recover ratios from rounded published constants; they do not reproduce the fitted models or semidefinite optimization. Table 1 reports variance pairs of 8.873 and 0.187 for tea, and 0.881 and 0.096 for digital twins. Consequently, the two information-cost ratios are approximately 0.000211 and 0.001090, rather than 0.01.

The case results establish what the calibrated models imply. Prospective savings would also depend on the stability of the selected feature dictionaries, independent human validation, and the costs of developing and maintaining the auxiliary source. The digital twins are constructed from earlier human survey waves; the per-response cost comparison does not separately price that initial collection and construction in §6.

## Feature Selection is an Important Teaching Opportunity

The formal model treats the bias dictionary as known. Empirical nonrejection of a candidate bias coefficient does not establish that the corresponding bias is exactly zero. Table 1 excludes the leafy-tea bias with a reported p-value of 0.041 and the Republican-indicator bias with a p-value of 0.034 because both exceed the chosen 0.01 threshold. Those exclusions affect which response components the auxiliary source can identify.

A useful sensitivity exercise follows directly from Table 1, Panel B. Hold its five primary features fixed: intercept, female, college degree, Democrat, and Republican. Its selected bias dictionary includes the first four, plus income. Adding the Republican indicator to that bias dictionary makes it contain every primary feature. Theorem 2 then gives zero auxiliary value under that expanded unrestricted-bias model. This is a course sensitivity calculation, not an alternative empirical estimate. Changing the selection threshold for both regressions would also change the primary model and requires a separate calculation.

The paper reports qualitatively similar results under backward elimination and cross-validation selection. The course exercise examines a different question: how the conclusion changes when a plausible omitted bias feature is admitted while preserving the estimand. An independent validation sample and a substantively justified sensitivity dictionary would help assess that restriction. Selecting features and simulating from the selected model cannot establish the absence of omitted bias.

## Respondents, Repeated Ratings, and Customer Representation

The theoretical guarantee assumes independent observations. The tea application has repeated ratings by the same human respondents, and the digital-twin application links synthetic responses to earlier information about individuals. Dependence may therefore matter when transporting the theoretical allocation to these settings. Section 8 explicitly leaves correlated primary and auxiliary observations for future work. Course code should distinguish a new respondent from another response generated for an existing persona and use respondent-level splits when evaluating human generalization.

For Marketing Dialectics, the associated question is who supplies evidence about customer interests. A model that recovers selected mean response coefficients still needs a separate justification for representing a population, interpreting consent, or inferring consumer welfare. Those are course implications of the estimation target's scope, rather than ethical conclusions tested in this paper.

## Reading and Verification Scope

The review covers the main text, §§1–8, Algorithms and Theorems cited above, Table 1, and Figures 1–3. Pages 20–21 and 24–25 were visually inspected to verify geometry, formulas, and empirical labels. The full appendix was extracted for reference; its proofs were not independently verified. No replication repository was identified in the inspected PDF or SSRN record. No author code or survey microdata was executed.

[source_checks.py](source_checks.py) contains original calculations for the rounded cost ratios and the closed-form example, together with the synthetic sensitivity calculations described in [CASE_DESIGN.md](CASE_DESIGN.md). The PDF's hash and access record are in [catalog.json](catalog.json).

## Source: 01_Resources/31_Auxiliary_Data_and_Bias_Geometry/CASE_DESIGN.md

# Human and Synthetic Evidence for a Product Decision

A body-wash manager is considering a premium feature and two price levels. The decision requires the effect of the feature and customers' price sensitivity. Four profiles cross a standard or premium feature with a low or high price. The following analytic example uses entirely invented means on a purchase-intent scale. It extends the course's [synthetic-consumer discussion](../../03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md); its four profiles form a separate construction from the existing six-concept example.

## A Feature Comparison Can Survive a Price Distortion

Code the feature $f$ and price $p$ as $-1$ and $+1$. Specify primary means as $3+0.4f-0.5p$ and auxiliary means as the primary mean plus $0.8+0.6p$. The observation unit is one rating at one product profile from one source. A two-unit change in a coded attribute gives twice its coefficient as the corresponding rating contrast.

| Price | Feature | Invented Primary Mean | Invented Auxiliary Mean |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Low | Standard | 3.1 | 3.3 |
| Low | Premium | 3.9 | 4.1 |
| High | Standard | 2.1 | 3.5 |
| High | Premium | 2.9 | 4.3 |

At either price, adding the premium feature increases both sources' ratings by 0.8 points. At either feature level, raising price reduces the primary rating by 1.0 point and increases the auxiliary rating by 0.2 points. The price-sensitive bias cancels in the feature comparison at a fixed price. It remains in the price comparison. Synthetic observations can inform the feature coefficient under these restrictions, while human evidence is required to separate price sensitivity from the auxiliary price bias.

## Compare Cost at the Same Accuracy

Use unit error variances for both sources, a primary-response cost of 1, and an auxiliary-response cost of 0.01. The benchmark optimizes primary-only sampling to estimate all three coefficients with total MSE at most $\epsilon^2$. Apply the paper's §5.3 design to the same four profiles, allowing auxiliary bias in the intercept and price coefficient.

With total primary and auxiliary precision $t$ and $s$, the normalized MSE is $2/t+1/(t+s)$. The intercept and price coefficient each contribute $1/t$; both sources inform the feature coefficient. The closed-form optimum at $\lambda=0.01$ reduces asymptotic cost by approximately 24.29%. Even with arbitrarily inexpensive auxiliary responses, the saving approaches only one third in this symmetric example. That fraction follows from this design and loss; it is not a general rule based on counting coefficients.

For $\epsilon=0.1$, round each source's allocation upward separately within each profile, as in Algorithm 1. The resulting allocation uses 216 primary responses and 1,296 auxiliary responses, costs 228.96 units, and has analytic MSE about 0.009921. The primary-only benchmark uses 300 responses and costs 300, so this rounded allocation saves 23.68%. This calculation implements the theorem's allocation rule; it does not assert that the rounded design is the exact finite-sample integer optimum.

## Add an Omitted Bias Feature

Now add an auxiliary feature bias of $0.3f$ while continuing to estimate the smaller bias model. In the balanced design above, the expected feature-coefficient error is $0.3\times1296/(216+1296)=0.257143$. Its squared bias adds approximately 0.066122 to the total MSE, raising the total to approximately 0.076043. The promised 0.01 accuracy target fails even though the data allocation and computations follow the smaller model correctly.

The class can then include $f$ in the bias dictionary. Every primary feature is now confounded with an unrestricted auxiliary bias coefficient. Theorem 2 implies zero value of auxiliary data for this worst-case coefficient-estimation objective. This comparison distinguishes correct computation from a correct restriction on bias.

## Figures and Course Placement

The first original TikZ figure compares the feature at a fixed low price and price with a fixed standard feature. Primary and auxiliary lines use Illinois navy and orange with distinct markers, on a common vertical scale. The four-profile table and mean functions remain alongside the comparison in M4 §4.24.

The second TikZ figure plots cost savings against the information-cost ratio, marking the one-third limit and the zero-savings threshold at $\lambda=1/3$. It also shows zero value under the expanded bias dictionary. A third figure separates declining sampling variance from persistent squared bias as both source counts increase. All three retain text descriptions and [underlying tables](../../03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/results/README.md).

# Human and Synthetic Evidence for Product Design

A body-wash manager needs the value of a premium feature and customers' response to price. Four invented profiles show how an auxiliary source can preserve one comparison and distort the other. Two standard-library programs compare research cost at a common accuracy target and calculate the consequences of an omitted bias feature.

The statistical model follows §5.3 of Jasin, Lin, and Zhang's [Bias Geometry and the Value of Auxiliary Data](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7734298). The numerical inputs, programs, figures, and exercises are original course adaptations. No human responses, LLM calls, or author code are used. Conditional means, sampling variances, and expected estimation errors are calculated analytically.

## Files and Reproduction

The input is [data/parameters.json](data/parameters.json). [DATA_DICTIONARY.md](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines observation units, attribute coding, model restrictions, costs, and outputs. Run from the repository root with Python 3.10 or later:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/allocate_responses.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/bias_sensitivity.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data -p 'test_*.py' -v
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/build_figures.py
```

Both analysis programs resolve inputs relative to their own location and accept `--output /path/to/folder`. They require only Python's standard library. There is no random seed because the programs use exact mean and variance formulas without sampling. The figure builder writes editable TikZ from saved tables; the lecture builder compiles the figure previews and PDF.

## Results and Interpretation

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| Premium-minus-standard rating at a fixed price | Both invented sources increase by 0.8 points. |
| High-minus-low price rating at a fixed feature | Primary decreases by 1.0 point; auxiliary increases by 0.2 points. |
| Primary-only design at total coefficient MSE 0.01 | 300 responses, cost 300. |
| Rounded hybrid design at the same target | 216 primary and 1,296 auxiliary responses; cost 228.96; MSE 0.009921. |
| Rounded and asymptotic cost savings | 23.68% and 24.29%, respectively. |
| Auxiliary feature bias of 0.3 omitted from estimation | Expected feature coefficient 0.657143; total MSE 0.076043. |
| Both sample sizes multiplied by 32 with the same omitted bias | MSE 0.066432, approaching the squared-bias floor 0.066122. |

The cost comparison estimates the same three coefficients with the same coding and MSE target. Sampling independence and the specified response and bias features are substantive assumptions. A smaller standard error does not eliminate an omitted bias. With unrestricted bias on every primary feature, auxiliary responses provide no additional information for the paper's worst-case coefficient-estimation objective.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Auxiliary Data Definitions

## Observation Unit and Population

The model's observation unit is one independent response at one of four product profiles from a primary or auxiliary source. The programs calculate analytic conditional means and estimation moments. Files contain no observed people, generated personas, individual responses, geographic sample, or time series. The fixed population and source behavior are imposed for the example.

The four profiles cross feature `f` and price `p`, each coded -1 and +1. Feature -1 denotes standard and +1 premium; price -1 denotes low and +1 high. A contrast between levels spans two coded units. Mean responses and coefficients are measured in rating points. Price coefficients are per coded unit, with no monetary price difference supplied. The Gaussian response model is a stylized continuous score with no imposed rating bounds.

## Input Parameters

| Key | Meaning and Default |
|---|---|
| `primary_coefficients` | Intercept, feature, and price coefficients: 3, 0.4, -0.5. |
| `auxiliary_bias_coefficients` | Additional auxiliary intercept and price coefficients: 0.8, 0.6. |
| `primary_variance`, `auxiliary_variance` | Independent response-error variance in squared rating points; each equals 1. |
| `primary_cost`, `auxiliary_cost` | Cost per response in normalized budget units: 1 and 0.01. |
| `mse_target` | Maximum expected sum of squared errors for the three primary coefficients: 0.01. |
| `omitted_feature_bias` | Additional auxiliary coefficient on the premium-feature code, excluded from the fitted bias dictionary: 0.3. |
| `sample_multipliers` | Factors multiplying both rounded source counts together: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. |

The bias coefficients are unknown to the modeled estimator; their numerical values specify the invented mean functions. The model assumes known feature dictionaries, independent Gaussian errors, known source variances, and constant source-specific response costs. There is no training/test split in an analytic calculation. A prospective empirical evaluation requires separate human respondents and concepts suited to the intended claim.

## Output Tables

`profile_means.csv` contains one row per feature-price profile, with primary and auxiliary analytic means. `allocation.json` records counts in total and per profile, total source precisions, coefficient variances, total MSE, costs, and the fractional savings relative to optimized primary-only sampling. Each source count is rounded up separately at each profile. The finite rounded allocation is feasible and need not be the exact integer optimum.

`value_curve.csv` contains the relative information cost `lambda = auxiliary_cost * auxiliary_variance / (primary_cost * primary_variance)` and asymptotic savings. The row at zero is flagged `limiting_value=True`; it denotes a limit as positive costs approach zero. The second savings series allows unrestricted bias on all three primary features and is zero. This curve applies to the balanced four-profile model and total coefficient loss.

`bias_sensitivity.csv` contains one row per sample multiplier. `total_coefficient_variance` sums the three coefficient variances, `squared_bias` is the squared expected error in the feature coefficient, and `omitted_bias_mse` adds those quantities. `correct_model_mse` retains the restricted bias model with zero omitted feature bias. `bias_summary.json` also records the expanded correctly specified dictionary, under which auxiliary information about the primary coefficient vector is zero. The two cases represent different fitted models.

No sample exclusions, imputations, joins, customer weights, or resampling occur. The analytical calculations use all four profiles with balanced counts within each source. Dependence across respondents or sources changes the information calculation and is outside these results.

# Agent Guide for Auxiliary Data

Read the root guide, README, and DATA_DICTIONARY. All means and parameters are invented. Results are analytic implications of a linear Gaussian model, with no observed human responses, generated-model ratings, or empirical replication.

Keep three distinctions explicit: asymptotic savings versus the rounded allocation, sampling variance versus total MSE with omitted bias, and the misspecified smaller dictionary versus the correctly specified expanded dictionary. Attribute the model to Jasin, Lin, and Zhang and link the public source. The source paper is retained privately and must not be added to Git.

Run both programs and the six independent checks after a substantive code change. The checks construct joint regression normal equations separately from the analysis formulas. Refresh saved tables, the three editable figures, matching full Python listings in M4 and M7, and the manifest. Confirm plotted coordinates against the tables and inspect rendered figures separately from arithmetic checks.

Resolve inputs relative to the scripts. Preserve the four balanced profiles, units, coefficient coding, source variances, and common accuracy target. Do not treat repeated ratings or generations as independent without a justified dependence model. The optional practice creates no assessment requirement or permission to send private data to a model service.

# Human and Synthetic Research Budgets

This is optional ungraded practice for M4 §4.24 and M7 §7.37. It establishes no submission, deadline, or course-wide AI permission. The example uses invented analytic means and requires no model account.

A body-wash manager needs evidence about a premium feature and two price levels. The auxiliary source distorts overall ratings and price sensitivity. The firm must decide which comparisons still justify synthetic responses and how much human evidence to buy.

## Reproduce the Comparison

Read the [data dictionary](../../03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/DATA_DICTIONARY.md) and run both [analysis programs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Auxiliary_Data/README.md). Calculate the premium-feature and price contrasts by hand before comparing the saved means. Explain why the two coded levels create a contrast twice the coefficient. Identify the unit of the accuracy target and the population assumptions behind it.

## Change Costs and Precision

Work on a copy of the example folder. Change the auxiliary response cost while retaining the primary cost, variances, bias features, and MSE target. Compare the rounded allocation with the asymptotic savings curve. Identify when the optimal continuous design stops using auxiliary responses. Then increase auxiliary noise variance while holding response prices fixed and explain why the information-cost ratio changes.

## Challenge the Bias Restriction

Change `omitted_feature_bias` and inspect the variance and squared-bias components separately. Explain why multiplying both sample sizes leaves the expected feature-coefficient error unchanged. Compare the smaller misspecified bias model with an expanded model allowing intercept, feature, and price bias. State what additional human evidence or substantive restriction would make the feature contrast credible.

The paper's digital-twin example supplies a separate sensitivity question. Hold its five selected primary features fixed, then add the Republican indicator to the bias dictionary. Use the [source review](../../01_Resources/31_Auxiliary_Data_and_Bias_Geometry/SOURCE_REVIEW.md) to explain the implication of the overlap. This reasoning is conditional on the reported feature sets and does not reproduce the underlying regression.

## Plan an Independent Evaluation

Specify a future customer population and product decision. Identify which respondents and concepts would be reserved from prompt selection, bias-feature selection, and final evaluation. Explain how repeated ratings from a respondent affect the sampling unit. Include research setup and validation costs alongside per-response prices, and separate coefficient accuracy from a claim about purchases or customer welfare.

An AI coding assistant can help implement a proposed change after the inputs, units, and expected result are specified. Check its calculations against a hand-worked contrast and the joint-regression checks. Describe any material assistance accurately, following the rules of an applicable assignment if this practice is later used within one.

# Graph Coarsening and Marketing Decisions

A firm may compress a large customer or retail network to reduce computation. The relevant question is whether the smaller representation preserves the comparisons used to allocate service, predict demand, or recommend products. A graph can preserve selected features while changing travel access or the treatment of a small customer group.

Antonin Joly's [GraCo repository](https://github.com/Antonin-J/graco) and [working paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01200v1) provide a common interface for 17 graph-coarsening methods and a random baseline. The [source review](SOURCE_REVIEW.md) connects its mathematical construction, evaluation metrics, and implementation defaults to the course. The [case design](CASE_DESIGN.md) develops original examples for M5 and M7, with shorter connections to M1, M2, M4, and M9.

## Course Connections

| Module | Decision or Analytical Question | Useful Extension |
|---|---|---|
| M5 | Does a compressed retail network preserve customers' access to available stores? | Compare original routes, grouped zones, and the population receiving weight. Build on [§5.21](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md). |
| M7 | Which evaluation criterion supports deploying the smaller model? | Separate label purity, prediction on held-out outcomes, computational cost, and customer consequences. Build on [§7.28](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md). |
| M4 | What does a group mean represent? | Retain group sizes and distinguish average spending from spending totals; connect to [§4.22](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md). |
| M1 and M2 | Which data transformations does generated code actually perform? | Inspect graph direction, discarded components, outcome-dependent parameters, and denominator changes. |
| M9 | Whose needs survive aggregation? | Evaluate group-specific errors and preservation of service access beside the firm's computational saving. |

[M5 §5.24](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md) and [M7 §7.38](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md) contain the complete explanations and two executed Python programs. Sessions 7 and 11 include five slides and two editable TikZ figures. [Data and code](../../03_Data_and_Code/Graph_Coarsening/README.md) and [optional ungraded practice](../../07_Labs/Graph_Coarsening/README.md) support the examples.
