# Logging and Workflow Results

The logging calculations use transformed real mHealth records and a roster fixed from January–June observations. The two task windows use 358 users and 31 days per user, giving 11,098 possible user-days each.

| Task | Recorded User-Days | Zero-Log Users | Mean Logging Rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| July development | 6,455 | 39 | 58.16% |
| August evaluation | 6,501 | 41 | 58.58% |

[logging_summary.json](logging_summary.json) retains the exact fractions and excluded boundary-row counts. The reference CSVs provide one row per roster user. An independent SQLite calculation reproduces every customer count in both files. The same roster is used in both periods; the rate concerns record presence, not intake or health.

[hypothetical_costs.json](hypothetical_costs.json) uses invented model charges, valid-output counts, review time, and correction time. At 60 dollars per analyst hour, its two total costs are 350 and 200 dollars, with 80 and 95 valid outputs out of 100 assigned tasks. These values illustrate cost accounting and are not measured model performance or labor savings.

No four-configuration model experiment was executed. The [protocol](../EXPERIMENT_PROTOCOL.md) identifies how to collect those outcomes separately.

## Published Coding Benchmark

`benchmark_failure_rates.csv` reconstructs success and failure fractions from the authors' integer counts. `benchmark_prompt_contrasts.csv` reports percentage-point gains and fractions of baseline failures removed. `benchmark_incremental_cost.csv` divides the additional mean token cost per assigned run by the additional success probability, separately by model. `benchmark_summary.json` records scope and aggregate contrasts. Inputs come from the identified CC0 release; these files contain no newly collected model runs.

Each workflow has 14,400 assigned runs. The agent's 338 silent failures represent 2.35% of assigned runs and 89.18% of 379 failures. The example prompt adds 4.42 percentage points under the chatbot and 0.79 under the agent, removing 23.86% and 26.15% of their no-example failures. These are different denominators. The two-panel TikZ figure retains the authors' task-cluster intervals from the source CSV.

## Constructed Coding Errors

`semantic_checks.csv` evaluates eight constructed programs on each of the two mHealth tasks. The cases are deliberately chosen and supply no estimate of their frequency in model output. A total-only check accepts four incorrect cases per period: a wrong exposure denominator, reassigned users, omitted zero-log users, and a missing rate value. The complete per-user comparison rejects all seven incorrect cases in each period and accepts both correct cases.

The July shifted-user case changes 331 users' values while retaining 6,455 recorded user-days and the 58.16% mean. In August it changes 324 users while retaining 6,501 days and a 58.58% mean. `semantic_summary.json` counts these constructed checks. Missing output values remain blank; they are not zeros.

## Hypothetical Losses

`decision_costs.csv` and `decision_cost_summary.json` use hypothetical task costs and undetected-error probabilities. For 1,000 analyses, operating costs are 270 and 550 dollars. At a ten-dollar conditional loss, expected total costs are 770 and 650 dollars. The seven-dollar crossing follows from 280 dollars of additional operating cost divided by 40 fewer expected undetected errors. Neither review savings nor customer harm is estimated.

# Research Evidence and Course Applications

## Factual Transfer

Cheng, Liu, Yau, and Ré's November 25, 2026 [post](https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2026-11-25-platos-key) reports 20 pairwise comparisons among 12 base language models. A rotation and scale map hidden states across frozen models. On held-out facts both models recall, median transfer accuracy is 41%, versus 55% for within-model swaps. Layers are chosen on separate validation subjects. Selecting by nearest-neighbor similarity gives 4.5% median validation transfer accuracy, about one tenth of selection by transfer accuracy. These are different evaluation criteria.

The recovery comparison uses 2,600 recipient misses. Auxiliary prompting or answer-ranking checks classify 1,463 as available knowledge; mapped states recover 267, approximately 18% of that selected subset. This operational definition conditions the denominator. Factual recall in the tested models leaves broader reasoning and customer applications open.

## Related Research

Huh, Cheung, Wang, and Isola's [The Platonic Representation Hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.07987v5), especially §§2 and 6, examines representational convergence and discusses measurement choices, counterexamples, and common research practices. The philosophical application in M9 asks what additional evidence supports truth or justification when model outputs agree. It is a course interpretation.

Gekhman and coauthors' [Inside-Out: Hidden Factual Knowledge in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.15299v4) defines knowledge through answer ranking and distinguishes internal from observable scoring methods. Its §7 discusses computational cost and sensitivity to answer-label errors. Comparing prompt conditions in a service exercise evaluates those conditions; measuring internal knowledge would require the paper's additional operations and definitions.

## Original Course Examples

The synthetic case holds eight invented outcomes fixed while changing coordinates. An orthogonal rotation preserves distances and nearest neighbors, while a classifier tied to the second coordinate changes predictions. A separate distortion of the style coordinate changes neighbors while preserving the classification target. Fitting the inverse rotation on distinct training points restores compatibility.

The mHealth example compares locally constructed word and character representations. Vocabulary, inverse-document frequency, SVD directions, alignment, and classifiers use training descriptions. Validation selects the common dimension before any test score is calculated. All character representations have the same neighbors under a positive global scale and an orthogonal map. Classification changes because the existing coefficients refer to a particular basis. Retraining evaluates a different feasible response to an encoder change.

The reference labels are recorded modal source categories, including labels such as `default` and `recipe`. They measure agreement with the recorded classification system. Nutrition judgments, customer preferences, model-provider performance, and commercial returns require separate evidence.

# Changing Text Representations in mHealth

A text-processing service can replace an encoder while retaining a classifier, fit a coordinate alignment, or retrain the classifier. The original synthetic comparison separates geometric similarity from compatibility with a fixed decision rule. The mHealth comparison uses local word and character features on the same unseen descriptions.

## Inputs and Execution

The compact [description sample](data/descriptions.csv) is included. It has 6,000 training, 1,500 validation, and 1,500 test descriptions. No user identifier, date of birth, or weight history appears in this derivative. Read the [dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md), [source manifest](manifest.json), and [verification record](VERIFICATION.md).

Use Python 3.11 or later with the versions in [requirements.txt](requirements.txt). From the repository root:

```sh
python3 -m pip install -r 03_Data_and_Code/Representation_Alignment/requirements.txt
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Representation_Alignment/alignment.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Representation_Alignment/evaluate_mhealth.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Representation_Alignment -p 'test_*.py' -v
```

To reconstruct the compact input, first run `python3 03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/download_data.py`, then `python3 03_Data_and_Code/Representation_Alignment/prepare_descriptions.py`. Preparation verifies the public release hash and reads the full compressed food file. Evaluation uses the compact input and needs no network, model downloads, or API key. It fits ordinary lexical representations and linear classifiers locally. Git attributes preserve the CSV bytes so the input checksum remains valid after cloning.

## Results

The invented rotation preserves all pairwise distances and both-neighbor sets while changing the fixed classifier from 8 to 4 correct cases. Compressing the imposed style coordinate preserves 8 correct cases while reducing neighbor overlap to 50%. Training-point alignment restores both scores to 100%.

Validation selects 32 dimensions from 8, 16, and 32 using aligned classification accuracy. On the 1,500 held-out descriptions:

| Configuration | Correct | Accuracy | Neighbor Overlap with Word Features |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Word reference | 522 | 34.80% | 100.00% |
| Character features, original classifier | 119 | 7.93% | 22.00% |
| Aligned character features, original classifier | 430 | 28.67% | 22.00% |
| Character features, retrained classifier | 531 | 35.40% | 22.00% |

The last three share the same character geometry. The classifier's coordinate compatibility changes. The 0.60 percentage-point difference between the compatible word and character classifiers is descriptive for this test sample; no population comparison is estimated. Reference categories include generic labels such as `default`. Seventy-four test descriptions have multiple source categories, and ten have modal categories absent from training. All remain in the primary denominator. Source-label agreement is the target; nutritional correctness requires an independently justified reference.

Full source and interpretation appear in [M5 §5.26](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md) and [M7 §§7.42–7.43](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md). ## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Representation_Alignment/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Description Sample and Evaluation Outputs

## Source and Population

The source is the public mHealth food-entry release of October 23, 2026, with SHA-256 recorded in [manifest.json](manifest.json). Preparation retains pseudonyms whose first four hexadecimal digits are below 4096. The selected cohort contains 917,153 food rows in 2016. Excluding blank descriptions and blank or `Unclassified` categories leaves 916,947 rows and 75,357 normalized descriptions. The sample is a deterministic subset of this cohort.

Normalization case-folds text, collapses whitespace, and trims its ends. Each distinct normalized description receives its modal source category across eligible rows. Equal category counts are resolved alphabetically. Labels such as `default` and `recipe` are retained as recorded. No nutrition classification is inferred.

SHA-256 determines the split independently of the category: the first eight hexadecimal digits modulo ten allocate buckets 0–5 to training, 6–7 to validation, and 8–9 to test. Within each split the lowest full hashes select at most 6,000, 1,500, and 1,500 descriptions. Rows are unique by normalized description. This design evaluates unseen descriptions within the 2016 cohort; users and calendar periods are shared across splits.

## Input Fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `description` | Normalized food-description text |
| `category` | Modal recorded category among eligible source rows |
| `split` | `train`, `validation`, or `test` |
| `description_sha256` | Hash of normalized text; reproducible key and selection order |
| `source_entries` | Number of eligible rows with the description |
| `category_count` | Number of distinct recorded categories for that description |
| `modal_entries` | Rows supporting the selected modal category |

`source_entries` and `modal_entries` describe reference construction. They are not analysis weights. Each description receives weight one. Multiple-category counts are 343 in training, 89 in validation, and 74 in test.

## Fitted Quantities and Metrics

Word unigrams and character trigrams each use the 512 most frequent training-document tokens, with alphabetical tie breaks. Term weights are `1 + log(count)`; inverse-document frequency is `log((1+n_train)/(1+document_frequency))+1`. Each row has unit Euclidean norm when nonzero. Unseen tokens contribute zero. Uncentered SVD directions come from the training feature Gram matrix. Their signs can differ across numerical implementations; the deliberately unmapped comparison is sensitive to that convention. The saved environment identifies the executed calculation.

A ridge least-squares classifier predicts one-hot source labels, with an unpenalized intercept and penalty 1 on coefficients. The largest score selects a category; sorted class order breaks ties. There are 264 training classes. A rotation, a positive scale, and translation map paired character training vectors to word coordinates. Validation chooses 8, 16, or 32 components by aligned accuracy; lower dimension breaks a tie. No test label enters fitting or selection.

Accuracy counts correct modal categories over all descriptions. Macro F1 averages over the union of training and current evaluation classes, including classes with no predicted positives; undefined F1 is set to zero. The test union has 273 categories. Category-specific support, correct counts, predicted counts, recall, and F1 are in `results/mhealth.json`. Ten test descriptions belong to nine categories absent from training and count as errors.

Neighbor overlap uses Euclidean distance between descriptions within the same evaluation split and the same dimension. Each description contributes the fraction of its ten neighbors shared with the word reference. Self-neighbors are excluded. Squared distances are rounded to twelve decimal places to treat rotation roundoff as ties; common row order breaks ties. This score uses evaluation features, independently of labels. It does not measure agreement with a human judgment of semantic similarity.

`results/test_predictions.csv` records all four predictions and the reference category for each test hash. `results/summary.csv` contains validation scores at all three dimensions and test scores only at the selected dimension. `results/synthetic.json` records the invented vectors and decisions separately. `results/mhealth.json` records software versions, configuration values, denominators, category-level errors, and the accuracy among the 1,426 test descriptions with one recorded category.

# Agent Guide for Representation Alignment

Read the root guide, README, and dictionary. Keep the invented vectors separate from the real mHealth descriptions and from the cited neural-model experiment. The local features are lexical TF-IDF and SVD representations; no pretrained language model is used.

Fit vocabulary, IDF, SVD, the map, and classifiers using training descriptions. Select the dimension using validation accuracy before computing test outcomes. Preserve duplicate-description grouping, the deterministic sample, modal-label ambiguity, unseen-category errors, and equal description weights. This split evaluates new descriptions within a shared cohort and period.

For row vectors the fitted map is `mu_recipient + scale * (x - mu_donor) @ rotation`. Positive scaling and an orthogonal transformation preserve neighbor order. A fixed classifier can still change its decisions. An unmapped coordinate substitution deliberately violates classifier compatibility and is not a provider benchmark. Preserve all comparison configurations and the same test denominator.

Keep complete Python blocks in M5 §5.26 and M7 §§7.42–7.43 synchronized with their files. If an analytical choice changes after viewing the test sample, treat that sample as development data and reserve a fresh final sample. Category agreement is distinct from nutrition quality, consumer welfare, consent, and factual knowledge inside a language model.

# Pricing Systems, Competition, and Customer Choice

A restaurant operator considering a pricing service must evaluate the information it supplies, the decisions it delegates, and the consequences for customers. Better demand forecasts can increase profit while reducing consumer surplus. Coordination among separate businesses raises an additional question about the independence of their pricing decisions.

The November 23, 2026 complaint in *Garcia v. The Wendy's Company and NCR Voyix Corporation*, No. 8:26-cv-04886-LKG (D. # Evidence for Pricing Systems and Competition

## The Initial Complaint

**PC02.** *Garcia v. The Wendy's Company and NCR Voyix Corporation*, No. 8:26-cv-04886-LKG, U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, Document 1, filed November 23, 2026, 26 pages. [Complaint](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mdd.618524/gov.uscourts.mdd.618524.1.0.pdf). [Docket](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/75164297/garcia-v-the-wendys-company/).

Paragraphs 5–13 and 42–51 connect required technology, transaction data, and pricing announcements to alleged coordination. Paragraphs 71–83 plead Sherman Act Section 1 claims concerning price fixing and information exchange. These are the plaintiff's factual allegations and legal arguments. The filing requests class certification, damages, and injunctive relief; it supplies no judicial finding on the merits.

Paragraph 2 defines the proposed class period from January 1, 2022. Paragraphs 73 and 79 allege conduct beginning no earlier than 2016 and no later than 2022 and continuing thereafter. Describing the allegation as a completed 2016–2022 scheme would misstate that timing. Paragraphs 30–33 offer a product and geographic market theory; that theory also remains the plaintiff's position.

The complaint cites public documents and interprets them as evidence of coordination. Paragraph 51 relies on pricing announcements; paragraphs 53–55 also discuss cost pressures and broad price increases. Assess the further evidence connecting these sources to actual pricing authority, interfirm agreement, and the prices that would have prevailed under an alternative arrangement. A price increase or a common vendor alone does not identify those mechanisms.

## Reporting and Company Statements

**PC01.** Mike Scarcella, Reuters, November 24, 2026. [Original](https://www.reuters.com/business/wendys-hit-with-us-class-action-over-menu-pricing-2026-11-24/), [accessible syndicated report](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/wendys-hit-with-us-class-action-overmenu-pricing-5048785). Reuters describes the proposed class action and reported that Wendy's and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to requests for comment. That describes the reporting cutoff. It supplies no admission or determination of liability.

**PC03.** NCR, August 16, 2022, [NCR Aloha Delivers Smarter Data Management to Wendy's](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220816005018/en/NCR-Aloha-Delivers-Smarter-Data-Management-to-Wendys). The company announcement describes expanded access to product-level transaction information and intended operational benefits. It supports the existence of the announced data capability. It does not establish how every franchise priced its products or identify realized customer effects.

**PC04.** Wendy's, February 27, 2024, [Wendy's Digital News Update](https://www.wendys.com/blog/wendys-digital-news-update). The company stated that it did not plan to raise prices during its busiest periods and described possible discounts and menu changes. This is a dated statement about planned features. It predates the 2026 lawsuit and is not a response to it. Digital display, time-varying pricing, personalized pricing, and an alleged interfirm agreement identify different objects.

## Economic Research and Its Scope

**PC05.** Joseph E. Harrington, Jr. (2022), [The Effect of Outsourcing Pricing Algorithms on Market Competition](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.4241), *Management Science*, 68(9), 6889–6906. [Author-hosted article](https://joeharrington5201922.github.io/pdf/ms22.pdf). Read the abstract, model setup, welfare analysis, and conclusion. Paragraphs 58–59 of the complaint cite this study; the article's actual page range is 6889–6906.

The paper models a developer choosing a pricing algorithm and firms choosing whether to adopt it. Under its assumptions, outsourcing increases sensitivity to demand variation, raises industry profit, and reduces consumer welfare while leaving competitive intensity unchanged. Those results do not establish coordination at Wendy's. The distinction is useful because a customer loss and a finding about competition require different reasoning.

The course's two-restaurant calculation is an original quadratic-demand example. It specifies a common noisy signal, symmetric firms, and two pricing objectives. It does not reproduce Harrington's vendor-design and adoption equilibrium, estimate restaurant demand, or quantify damages. The source supplies a conceptual comparison; the course program supplies independently defined assumptions and exact calculations.

## Agency Argument and Legal Status

**PC06.** U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission, [Statement of Interest in *Cornish-Adebiyi v. Caesars Entertainment*](https://www.justice.gov/usdoj-media/opa/media/1345721/dl?inline=), No. 1:23-cv-02536-KMW-EAP (D.N.J.), Document 96, March 28, 2024. The first 14 pages are the statement; the 61-page PDF includes attached filings. Read pages 3–7 and 12–13.

The agencies argue that delegating pricing to a common intermediary can satisfy the concerted-action element and that an agreement about a starting price can remain actionable even when final prices differ. Their argument requires attention to the alleged agreement and the relevant competitors. It is a litigation submission in a separate case, with no effective date as a newly enacted rule and no holding about Wendy's. Do not describe an override button as a sufficient legal safe harbor or every shared pricing tool as unlawful.

## Verification and Rights

Reviewed November 25, 2026. The 26-page complaint and cited primary statements were read. The current CourtListener docket was inaccessible; no complete subsequent-docket review is claimed. The source manifest records original PDF hashes and Dropbox-only retention. This case adds no claim that an existing cancellation or personalized-pricing rule applies to the alleged conduct. Relevant source updates should preserve the date, jurisdiction, procedural stage, and distinction between party claims and judicial findings.

# Shared Pricing Systems and Customer Choice

## The Managerial Decision

A restaurant operator must decide which data to supply to a pricing provider and what authority to delegate. A director asks whether the expected profit increase comes from lower operating costs, better demand information, or reduced independent price competition. Each mechanism implies a different comparison and may affect customers differently.

## Discussion Sequence

Session 14 uses minutes 50–60 for the existing personalized-pricing benchmark and minutes 60–70 for the Wendy's complaint and source evidence. Minutes 80–90 apply Kantian and Confucian reasoning to the case; minutes 90–100 retain the other justification and customer-authority comparisons. Minutes 100–110 revisit the synthetic pricing calculation, followed by the existing pricing and renewal work through minute 130. The optional lab carries the full code exercise. Session 5 uses its existing 145–155 pricing block to introduce the numerical comparison.

1. Read the complaint's description of the data and pricing arrangement alongside the 2022 company announcement. Identify which statements concern capability, reported conduct, interpretation, and a legal conclusion.
2. Request the evidence that would discriminate between explanations: relevant franchise contracts, data permissions, the pricing objective, recommendations, actual prices, overrides, cost changes, promotions, ownership, and communications. Avoid asserting that these records have been obtained.
3. Compare the four endpoint rows in the synthetic market. Change the pricing objective while holding information fixed. Change signal accuracy while holding the objective fixed. Explain why the two comparisons answer different questions.
4. Evaluate a stated pricing maxim, the truthful explanation offered to customers and franchisees, feasible alternatives, and the process for challenging a harmful result. Require reasons beyond a commercial performance metric.
5. Write a conditional recommendation identifying the evidence that would change it. Separate empirical uncertainty, legal analysis, and philosophical judgment.

## Interpretation Questions

Why can the same average posted price accompany different customer surplus? What changes if restaurants sell unrelated products? Which results would change if the pricing service reduced costs? Who is omitted from a surplus calculation that includes only the two firms and their customers? Why does the ability to reject one offer leave a separate question about the quality of alternative offers?

The numerical example contains synthetic demand and no actual Wendy's price observations. The existing restaurant-availability dataset records equipment status and cannot establish this case's prices, agreement, or customer harm. A future empirical application would need appropriate pricing, cost, adoption, ownership, and customer-choice data.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/README.md

# Demand Information, Pricing, and Consumer Surplus

Two restaurants choose prices for substitutable meals. The comparison changes their pricing objective and the accuracy of a common demand signal separately. The calculation identifies how each change affects quantity, profit, and consumer surplus in a synthetic market.

## Inputs and Interpretation

[parameters.json](parameters.json) specifies demand intercepts of 10 and 14 with equal probability, marginal cost of $2 per meal equivalent, substitution coefficient 0.5, and signal accuracies 0.5, 0.75, and 1. Quantities are continuous meal equivalents per market-day. The own-quantity coefficient in inverse demand is normalized to one dollar per meal-equivalent squared. There are two symmetric restaurants and no capacity constraints, fixed costs, vendor fees, or income effects. Customers observe actual demand and posted prices. Firms observe only the common signal before setting prices simultaneously.

Independent pricing solves each firm's conditional profit problem taking the rival's price as given. Joint pricing maximizes the sum of the two firms' conditional profits. Shared knowledge of the signal does not impose a pricing agreement in the independent benchmark. The quadratic-utility model supplies consumer surplus in dollars; total welfare sums that surplus and the two firms' profits within this specified economy.

[M4 §4.26](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md) gives the derivation and full Python listing. The [source review](../../01_Resources/37_Pricing_Systems_and_Competition/SOURCE_REVIEW.md) connects the original model to the Wendy's case and Harrington's separate theoretical results. No actual prices, transaction records, customer observations, or liability estimates are used.

## Run

Python 3.10 or later; standard library only. No installation or network access is needed. From the repository root:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/evaluate_market.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition -p 'test_*.py' -v
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/build_figures.py
```

The program enumerates every positive-probability state-signal pair using exact fractions. CSV files contain decimals to ten places, while [exact_results.json](results/exact_results.json) retains rational results. There is no random sampling, seed, parameter fitting, or downloaded code execution. Alternative inputs can be passed with `--parameters`; the program rejects inputs that violate its stated support. The numerical equilibrium checks cover the released parameters.

## Results and Verification

[policies.csv](results/policies.csv) contains six policy rows, and [state_outcomes.csv](results/state_outcomes.csv) contains twenty probability-weighted cells. [The data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md) defines every field. [The result guide](results/README.md) reports the four endpoint comparisons and explains the difference between state-weighted posted prices and quantity-weighted paid prices.

Nine tests verify exact benchmark arithmetic, conditional probabilities, consumer optimization, surplus identities, price deviations including quantity corners, the independent-products case, information comparisons, and invalid inputs. [VERIFICATION.md](VERIFICATION.md) records the commands and scope. The editable Illinois-color welfare figure is regenerated from the results. The separate case diagram distinguishes reported data capability from alleged pricing authority.

Full guided practice is in the [optional ungraded lab](../../07_Labs/Pricing_Competition/README.md).

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Synthetic Pricing Data Dictionary

## Population and Timing

One synthetic market has two symmetric restaurants and a representative consumer with quasi-linear preferences. Each market-day has one equally likely low or high demand state. A common binary signal matches the state with probability `accuracy`. Firms observe the signal and choose prices; customers then choose quantities using actual demand. Results average over every state-signal pair with its stated probability.

## Parameters

`a_low` and `a_high` are inverse-demand intercepts in dollars per meal equivalent. `cost` is constant marginal production cost in the same units. `substitution` is the cross-quantity coefficient relative to the normalized own-quantity coefficient. The latter equals one dollar per squared meal equivalent. All parameter values are stipulated. No parameter describes a particular restaurant company.

## Output Fields

| Field | Definition and Units |
| --- | --- |
| `objective` | `independent`: each firm maximizes its own conditional profit; `joint`: their summed conditional profit is maximized |
| `accuracy` | Probability that the binary signal equals the true state, from 0.5 to 1 |
| `state`, `signal` | Actual and observed low/high labels; cell output only |
| `probability` | Joint state-signal probability, summing to one for each objective and accuracy |
| `actual_a` | Realized demand intercept, dollars per meal equivalent |
| `expected_a` | Conditional expected intercept given the signal, dollars per meal equivalent |
| `price` | Common posted price, dollars per meal equivalent; policy output averages across states and signals without quantity weights |
| `quantity` | Total quantity at both restaurants, meal equivalents per market-day |
| `profit` | Sum of both restaurants' profits, dollars per market-day |
| `consumer_surplus` | Utility net of expenditure and numeraire, dollars per market-day |
| `total_welfare` | Consumer surplus plus the two firms' profits, dollars per market-day |
| `expenditure` | Total customer expenditure, dollars per market-day |
| `forecast_mse` | Squared demand-intercept forecast error; policy output reports its expectation in squared dollars per squared meal equivalent |
| `paid_price` | Expected expenditure divided by expected total quantity, dollars per meal equivalent; policy output only |

Policy columns other than `paid_price` are probability-weighted expectations of the cell columns. The two restaurants have the same price in every cell, so the state-weighted mean also equals an equally restaurant-weighted mean. `paid_price` generally differs because more meals can be sold in some states. Empty or excluded cells represent zero probability, never a missing price.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/results/README.md

# Pricing Outcomes in the Synthetic Market

All rows average over the same equally likely demand states. Costs and preferences stay fixed. Monetary totals are dollars per market-day for two restaurants and their customers; quantities are total meal equivalents per market-day. Posted prices are state-weighted means in dollars per meal equivalent.

| Objective | Signal Accuracy | Mean Posted Price | Quantity | Profit | Consumer Surplus | Total Welfare |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Independent | 0.50 | 5.33 | 8.89 | 29.63 | 32.30 | 61.93 |
| Independent | 1.00 | 5.33 | 8.89 | 30.81 | 30.81 | 61.63 |
| Joint | 0.50 | 7.00 | 6.67 | 33.33 | 19.33 | 52.67 |
| Joint | 1.00 | 7.00 | 6.67 | 34.67 | 17.33 | 52.00 |

Within independent pricing, perfect information raises expected profit by $1.19 and reduces expected consumer surplus by $1.48. Mean posted price and expected quantity remain unchanged. Prices fall in the low state and rise in the high state, shifting consumption away from the state with higher marginal willingness to pay. The quantity-weighted paid price rises from $5.33 to $5.47. This identifies why a single mean-price measure can miss a welfare change under the stated model.

Holding the uninformative signal fixed, joint pricing raises expected profit by $3.70 and lowers consumer surplus by $12.96 relative to independent pricing. Total quantity falls by 2.22 meal equivalents. The two comparisons change different objects. Neither supplies empirical evidence of a pricing agreement or an actual restaurant overcharge.

The CSV includes the intermediate accuracy 0.75. The JSON preserves exact fractions, so rounded components in a printed row need not sum to the rounded total. The model's welfare includes the representative consumer and the two firms; income heterogeneity, nutrition, employment, externalities, and vendor costs are outside its specified payoffs.

# Pricing Information and Customer Outcomes

This is optional ungraded practice. The [complete example](../../03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/README.md) includes original Python, synthetic inputs, results, and checks. [M4 §4.26](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md) supplies the mathematical setup. [M8 §8.28](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md) and [M9 §9.22](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md) connect evidence to the Wendy's case and ethical evaluation.

## The Decision

A restaurant operator is evaluating a pricing service. The service can improve its demand signal. A separate proposal would choose the prices of both restaurants to maximize joint profit. Explain how the operator should evaluate those changes and what customer outcomes must accompany the profit comparison.

## Reproduce the Comparison

From the repository root, run:

```bash
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition/evaluate_market.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Pricing_Competition -p 'test_*.py' -v
```

Read the data dictionary before editing code. Hand-check the independent, uninformative benchmark: posted price $16/3, expected total quantity $80/9, expected profit $800/27, and consumer surplus $872/27. Explain why each objective-accuracy pair has probability mass one and why perfect information retains only two cells.

## Separate the Changed Objects

Compare signal accuracies 0.5 and 1 under independent pricing. Identify which state gains quantity and which loses it. Reconcile unchanged mean posted price with changed consumer surplus and quantity-weighted paid price. Then hold accuracy at 0.5 and compare the independent and joint objectives. Account for changes in consumer surplus, profit, and total welfare separately.

Create an alternative parameter file with substitution set to zero and pass it using `--parameters`, saving results outside the released `results` folder with `--output`. Verify that the independent and joint objectives coincide. Next vary cost or the demand gap one object at a time. An input rejected by the interior-support restriction requires a model extension that explicitly handles quantity corners in the pricing problem.

## Assess Evidence and Justification

Read the [source review](../../01_Resources/37_Pricing_Systems_and_Competition/SOURCE_REVIEW.md). Classify the 2022 data announcement, the 2024 pricing clarification, the complaint's coordination allegation, and the original simulation by the claims each supports. Specify the contracts, pricing records, communications, costs, or adoption information that would change your assessment. Explain why the restaurant-availability data cannot substitute for those observations.

State a proposed pricing maxim and examine its treatment of customers' capacity to choose. Apply Confucian trustworthiness to the explanation of who controls prices and how customer-benefit claims are substantiated. Compare the ability to cancel a subscription with the availability of competing restaurant offers. A recommendation should distinguish empirical findings, legal status, and ethical reasons.

## AI-Assisted Coding

An LLM can explain the code, propose a change, and help inspect an error. Ask it to state the observation unit, probabilities, units, information timing, and changed parameter before generating code. Check the resulting calculation against the exact benchmark, consumer-utility calculation, and surplus identity. Describe material AI assistance accurately, and keep any applicable assignment-specific rules separate from this optional exercise.

## Source: 01_Resources/38_Digital_Usage_and_Inclusion/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# Source Review

## Article and Public Data

Mayana Pereira, Shane Greenstein, Raffaella Sadun, Prasanna Tambe, Lucia Ronchi Darre, Tammy Glazer, Allen Kim, Rahul Dodhia, and Juan Lavista Ferres, [Evidence and measures of the digital usage divide from 40 million Windows devices](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-78689-1), Nature Communications, November 9, 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-78689-1. The saved eight-page PDF is marked Article in Press. All eight pages and the thirteen-page supplement were reviewed on November 25, 2026.

The [Microsoft repository](https://github.com/microsoft/Consumption-of-Digital-Applications-Data-Set) contains the released indices, README, license, and standard repository documents. Commit `4024bc0938c4242f2429af94c5fec1e5a42113dc` and release tag `version` point to the inspected CSV. The release is also archived at [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/22084797), DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22084797. No original analysis code is included. Private telemetry, category-level observations, and the internal privacy computation are unavailable.

## Observation and Index Construction

The telemetry concerns consenting consumer Windows devices from October 2022 through March 2023. Virtual, test, and business devices are excluded. The device-month is the activity unit; each device receives a dominant postal code. Engagement uses recent interaction or an active-display keep-alive condition. Monthly category activity is capped at 9,000 minutes. No within-month task sequence is supplied. Browser use can include web-based email, documents, and other activities that a category label cannot distinguish.

MCI combines media and information categories; CCI combines content creation and computational categories. The supplement uses squared first-principal-component loadings for category weights, transformed minutes for device scores, and total category-group minutes for geographic aggregation. The public values are neither percent adoption nor probabilities. Recomputing PCA from the two public indices cannot recover the original category weights.

The OpenDP procedure uses private PCA and Laplace noise in aggregation; the supplement reports total epsilon 4.1 under device-level neighboring records. This privacy statement concerns incremental disclosure under a specified mechanism and does not establish representativeness or an absence of all inferential risk. Zero-device geographic entries are assigned zero activity/counts before noise in the described procedure; the released CSV has no device counts to identify those entries. Treating a very small score as evidence of observed inability would extend the measure beyond its support.

## Reproducibility Checks

| Object | Checked Result | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public CSV | 28,561 unique identifiers; no missing entries; 50 states and DC | Denominator for the course's release analysis |
| Main Figure 3 | 30,776 postal areas | A reported analytic sample whose relationship to the release is unresolved |
| Supplement prose | 28,199 in the information-sources discussion | A further reported count |
| Supplement Table 3 | 28,987 | Does not equal the release count |
| Supplement flow diagram | 35,177 initially; 31,299 after no-Census-match exclusion; 30,776 after missing predictors; 29,987 after household threshold | These steps do not reconcile all other counts |
| Equation S1 and Table 2 | Stated log2(1+minutes) fails to reproduce the three displayed MCI scores; natural log of positive minutes does reproduce two-decimal rounding | Alternative convention consistent with a toy table; original private transformation unresolved |

The supplement's flow uses a fewer-than-50-households exclusion, while another footnote describes a greater-than-30-households threshold. Preserve source locations and the actual release roster rather than inventing one reconciled screen. These documentation differences do not establish that every empirical finding is wrong.

The course's complete formula check uses the source's rounded weights, which sum to 0.996, and preserves the three displayed minute vectors. It compares conventions explicitly and leaves the upstream source unchanged. No source-provided notebook or private pipeline was executed.

## Census Context and Original Analyses

The course adds public 2017–2021 ACS income, education, and broadband estimates and 2021 Gazetteer internal points. [Census ZCTA guidance](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/zctas.html) distinguishes generalized area representations from USPS postal codes. Exact identifier matches support a transparent contextual comparison; they do not establish identical populations.

The [table-based Summary File](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/data/summary-file.2021.html) supplies B19013, B15003, and B28002. Official API metadata supplies variable definitions; direct summary-table downloads avoid an API-key requirement. [Census documentation of income boundary codes](https://www2.census.gov/adrm/PDB/2024/2024_PDB_Documentation.pdf) identifies 2,499 and 250,001 as open-ended intervals. The course excludes those 50 values from its income regression while preserving the records for usage-only comparisons.

The original examples assess the release, map Illinois internal points with fixed scales, estimate descriptive income projections, compare raw and standardized clusters, and check the supplement's numerical illustration. They reproduce their own computations. They do not reproduce the paper's full private analysis or observe customers' skills, willingness, welfare, AI adoption, or service outcomes.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Digital_Usage/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Data Dictionary

## Public Release

One row is a released postal area. `ZIP_CODE` is restored to five-character `zip`; `STATE` becomes `state`; `MEDIA AND INFORMATION INDEX` becomes `mci`; `CONTENT CREATION AND COMPUTATIONAL INDEX` becomes `cci`. Both outcomes are composite index units. Activity covers October 2022–March 2023. There are no individual identifiers, geographic device counts, original category inputs, or outcome labels. The original CSV remains byte-for-byte unchanged.

## Census Extract

`data/acs2021_zcta.csv` retains national ZCTAs from the 2021 five-year table-based ACS Summary File. `zcta` is a five-character identifier. Estimates cover 2017–2021. Column names use the Summary File convention `Bxxxxx_Eddd` for an estimate and `Bxxxxx_Mddd` for its supplied margin of error. The API metadata in [acs_variable_definitions.json](data/acs_variable_definitions.json) expresses the same estimate as `Bxxxxx_dddE`.

| Fields | Unit and Population | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B19013 E001/M001 | Median household income, 2021 inflation-adjusted dollars | E001 / 10,000 becomes `income_10k` after excluding boundary codes |
| B15003 E001/M001 | Population aged 25 or older | Education denominator |
| B15003 E022–E025 and corresponding M columns | Counts with bachelor's, master's, professional, and doctorate degrees | Sum of E022–E025 / E001 becomes `college_share` |
| B28002 E001/M001 | Households | Broadband denominator and sensitivity weights |
| B28002 E004/M004 | Households with broadband of any type | E004 / E001 becomes `broadband_share` |

Negative numeric sentinel values and nonnumeric unavailable entries become missing in the joined table. Raw extracts retain source values. Income values 2,499 and 250,001 denote open-ended intervals; `income_boundary` preserves this flag. Ratios require a positive denominator and an outcome between zero and one. `regression_eligible` requires all three regression covariates. No missing outcome is replaced with zero.

`data/zcta_coordinates.csv` contains Gazetteer `GEOID` as `zcta`, `INTPTLAT` as `latitude`, and `INTPTLONG` as `longitude`, in decimal degrees. They are internal points, not inferred device locations. The maps use fixed longitude/latitude axes; they are geographic point displays, without area or distance claims.

## Results

`joined_areas.csv` retains all release rows, raw Census estimates/margins, derived ratios, `census_match`, coordinates, and the regression flag. Identifier matches do not guarantee identical USPS and Census populations. `state_coverage.csv` counts released and regression-eligible areas by source state label.

`illinois_map.csv` adds `mci_z` and `cci_z`, each centered by its own Illinois mean and divided by its population standard deviation (`ddof=0`). All areas receive equal weight. `illinois_clusters.csv` adds standardized and raw-distance cluster assignments; labels are arbitrary across fits. `cluster_summary.csv` reports counts and original-unit means. `clustering.json` records k, starts, seed comparisons, scaling constants, standardized SSE, and adjusted Rand agreement.

`regressions.csv` reports outcome, specification, areas, income slope per $10,000, and in-sample residual RMSE in index units. `household_weight_sensitivity.csv` changes geographic weights to ACS household estimates. These weights are neither people nor observed Windows devices. No sampling interval, privacy-noise interval, causal effect, or out-of-sample accuracy is estimated.

`index_check.csv` reports the supplement's three illustrative devices, total group minutes, printed MCI, Equation S1 calculation, and alternative natural-log calculation. `index_check.json` compares equal-device and minute-weighted means of the displayed scores. The source's original private transform remains unresolved.

# Executed Comparisons

## Measurement and Geographic Coverage

The release has 28,561 distinct identifiers across the 50 states and DC; 2,214 leading zeros are restored. Every identifier matches the archived Census extracts. Fifty boundary-income values are flagged, yielding 28,511 common regression rows. All 1,253 Illinois areas have map coordinates and enter clustering; 1,252 enter the national regression sample. The equal-ZIP correlation of the two indices is 0.521531.

## Regression

| Specification | MCI per $10,000 | CCI per $10,000 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Income alone | 0.055213 | 0.048563 |
| Education and broadband | 0.002094 | -0.018209 |
| Controls and state intercepts | 0.001322 | -0.017497 |

Each row uses the same 28,511 areas and equal geographic weights. With ACS household weights and the two controls, the slopes are 0.004109 and -0.011857. Changing weights changes the projection. These comparisons do not estimate an income intervention or propagate ACS uncertainty, privacy noise, or spatial dependence.

## Illinois Clustering

Standardized three-group k-means gives groups of 94, 347, and 812 areas. Their mean (MCI, CCI) values are (1.9235, 1.4516), (2.7631, 2.2936), and (3.0573, 3.1167). Raw versus standardized partitions have adjusted Rand index 0.805038. The standardized partition is unchanged across tested seeds 1, 17, 534, and 2026 with thirty starts each. Computational stability is separate from validation as a measure of individual service needs.

## Index Construction

Equation S1 gives 6.4765, 4.4847, and 5.0689 for the supplement's illustrative devices. Natural logs of positive minutes, with zero contribution at zero, give 4.4603, 3.0887, and 3.4678, matching the displayed values to two decimals. The equal-device mean of displayed values is 3.673333; the minute-weighted mean is 3.630383. This check does not establish the transform used in the private pipeline.

# Digital Service, Geographic Evidence, and Customer Choice

A retailer plans to offer booking, discounts, and cancellation through an app. It wants to identify where assistance may help customers. Use the [released data and full programs](../../03_Data_and_Code/Digital_Usage/README.md) to assess which conclusions the geographic evidence supports. This exercise is public optional ungraded practice.

## 1. Define the Decision and Observation Unit

State the service decision, the customer task, and the information available before the firm acts. Distinguish a Windows device-month, a postal identifier, a Census area, and a customer. Explain why app-category minutes do not directly measure the ability to complete a cancellation request.

## 2. Assess the Release and Construct the Join

Run `assess_release.py`. Reconcile the raw count, restored leading zeros, matched identifiers, and regression eligibility using `assessment.json`. Inspect 01001, 60601, and 61801 as strings. Explain why the 50 open-ended income values remain in the released roster while leaving the common income-regression sample. Check that the education and broadband shares use different denominators.

Ask an AI assistant to suggest a join and then inspect its keys, cardinality assertion, unmatched-record handling, and income-code treatment. Verify one record against the archived source CSVs without relying on the assistant's explanation.

## 3. Evaluate the Geographic Display

Use `illinois_map.csv` and the two M2 maps. Compare MCI and CCI for one named area in original and standardized units. Explain what equal area weights and common z-score intervals hold fixed. Explain why a dense collection of points is not a count of residents, why the point is not a device location, and what a boundary or population-weighted display would change.

## 4. Compare Regressions on One Sample

Run `compare_models.py` to reproduce the positive simple CCI slope and negative adjusted slope, then explain how conditioning on education, broadband, and state intercepts changes the comparison. Assess sensitivity to household weights against the equal-area projection. Finally, formulate a causal question about an assistance offer and identify the additional evidence required to answer it.

## 5. Compare Geographic Groupings

Run `cluster_usage.py`. Verify that group counts sum to the Illinois roster and inspect original-unit group means. Explain the adjusted Rand index and the difference between scaling sensitivity and seed sensitivity. For an extension, compare k=2, 3, and 4 in a copy of the script; label this a new analysis and record outputs. Specify a held-out customer outcome before describing one grouping as more useful for service allocation.

## 6. Reproduce a Published Numerical Example

Run `verify_index.py`. Calculate one device score independently from the printed minutes and weights. Identify the log convention that matches displayed rounding, the convention stated in Equation S1, and the conclusion that remains unresolved. Reproduce the equal-device and minute-weighted means. Explain how a change in activity weights can change an area's score while each device's score remains fixed.

## 7. Justify the Marketing Practice

Compare an optional assistance offer with mandatory app completion for access to a benefit. Specify consent, customer-requested outcomes, correction of geographic classifications, usable alternatives, and failure costs. Apply the Kantian distinction between evidence and the additional premise authorizing a decision. Apply the Confucian concern with humane conduct and role responsibilities. Propose an assistance evaluation with an explicit eligible-customer denominator, assignment rule, outcomes, and observation period. Keep this proposed study separate from the executed geographic analyses.

## Source: 01_Resources/39_Statistical_Inference_and_AI/SOURCE_REVIEW.md

# Source Review: Fisher-R1

Reviewed November 25, 2026. Authors: Jiacheng Miao, Jin Mu, Guanhua Chen, and James Zou. The archived 22-page PDF was retrieved from the [arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07437). This selected Markdown companion preserves the methodological distinctions, central numbers, and figure meanings; it omits the complete mathematical training specification, bibliography, prompts, and biomedical examples.

## Question, Design, and Results

An agent receives a question and dataset, selects and executes an analysis, and reports a p-value and decision. P-Bench contains 425 tasks, split into 203 Easy and 222 Hard tasks. The public data card identifies economic and biomedical source families, derived variants, and 20 explicitly synthetic tasks. The benchmark should not be described as 425 independent, unmodified empirical studies.

The paper's Raw metric checks the reject/nonreject decision against a reference answer at alpha=0.05. Strict additionally requires the difference between two-sided normal-score transforms of the reported and reference p-values to be less than 0.5. This transformation is a scoring convention; it does not validate the underlying test. pass@1 averages individual-run accuracy across three runs, while pass@3 credits a task if any run succeeds. A user without a reference answer would still need a method for selecting among those runs.

Table 1 reports 65.8% Raw and 33.0% Strict pass@1 for Fisher-R1-14B on Hard tasks. The corresponding GPT-5.4 values are 58.3% and 30.5%. These scores describe the paper's task distribution, software, model versions, and scoring rules. They measure reference agreement, not rejection probabilities under a known null or calibration in a new marketing application.

Training uses synthetic executable tasks, supervised trajectories, and reinforcement learning. Table 3 examines one fixed rollout per task for the 7B backbone and trained agent. Operational failures fall from 43.5% to 8.5%; the paper attributes the largest gain to this reduction. Improvements in benchmark success therefore combine execution and analytical changes. The remaining errors include specification, method choice, and data handling.

## Figure Interpretations

Figure 1 compares a linear analysis influenced by extreme observations with a rank-based analysis. The course retains the need to inspect influential values and additionally asks whether each procedure answers the intended question. A rank association and a mean-based effect are different targets. Figures 2 and 6 trace question, data, executable reference analysis, and answer-key construction. Figure 3 describes task composition. Figure 4 separates supervised trajectories from reward-based training. Figure 5 compares prompt-embedding similarities across training and evaluation inputs; it assesses one form of overlap and does not establish the absence of all pretraining exposure. Figure 7 gives a synthetic simulation template.

## Repository Inspection

The inspected GitHub commit is `968dd38bea50102a313d7d36843aba564eabc33f`. The evaluation README requires Python 3.12, R 4.4, statistical R packages, model/tokenizer files, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. `run_benchmark.py` executes generated R in a persistent local subprocess and saves trajectories and parsed final answers. `evaluate.py` compares final reported p-values and decisions with the task keys. `verify_pbench.py` checks file availability, hashes, questions, and key/manifest consistency. These checks support integrity and reproducibility; statistical justification remains a separate question.

The training folder contains veRL-based training code and an R tool. Its commands expect model and training-data paths. No training or inference code was executed for the course review, and no model weights were downloaded. The released code does not include a license file in the inspected tree. It is linked, while the course Python implementations are original.

## Benchmark Limits and Course Adaptation

Matching a reference p-value does not independently establish inferential validity, and multiple defensible procedures can produce different values. The paper's evaluation concerns single frequentist hypotheses at a fixed threshold. It does not evaluate multiple-testing correction, sequential monitoring, Bayesian decisions, economic importance, or welfare. A reference test itself requires a specified sample, estimand, weights, and variance estimator.

The consumer-credit task asks about a joint null for 13 advertising-content coefficients. Its archived answer key contains only p=0.0431 and a reject decision. The reference specification has not been reconstructed here. Course materials use the question to examine the scope of an advertising claim without presenting a replicated result.

The implemented mHealth example checks a descriptive paired comparison. The original store simulation has a known sharp null, independent Gaussian stores, fixed equal store sizes, complete observations, and balanced assignment. It measures false-positive rates with two Welch calculations and preserves all prespecified repetitions. These examples implement the assessment principles without claiming to replicate Fisher-R1 or measure any assistant's performance.

# Statistical Inference and AI-Assisted Analysis

A manager needs uncertainty calculated for the comparison that informs the decision. These original programs reconstruct observed mHealth logging and simulate a store-randomized promotion. They distinguish a program that runs, a justified method, a faithfully reported number, and a supported managerial conclusion.

## Inputs and Commands

Use Python 3.12 with the pinned [requirements](requirements.txt). From the repository root:

```bash
python3 -m pip install -r 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/requirements.txt
python3 03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/download_data.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/mhealth_pairing.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/store_randomization.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/build_figures.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference -p 'test_*.py' -v
```

The downloader verifies the existing public mHealth release. Skip it when the release files are already present. The food-entry file is about 304 MB compressed; the program checks its hash and reads identifiers and dates in chunks. The simulation needs no external data. The figure builder writes two editable sources under `06_Lecture_Notes/figures`.

## Comparisons and Expected Results

- `mhealth_pairing.py` fixes the established cohort before May 2016, retains zero-log users, and counts distinct calendar days. The 340-user mean change is -5.123 percentage points. The paired standard error is 1.379 pp; the deliberately incorrect independent-day comparison gives 0.663 pp. Both reject zero at 5%, demonstrating that decision agreement can conceal a precision error. This is a descriptive change in logging.
- `store_randomization.py` generates 4,000 independent experiments at each within-store correlation, with 40 stores and 20 customers per store. The effect is zero for every customer. At correlation 0.3, the customer-row test rejects in 44.9% of experiments, compared with 4.7% using store means. The first experiment is retained without selecting on its result.
- `build_figures.py` draws assignment and outcome units and plots rejection fractions with Monte Carlo intervals. Counts and numerical values are in the [results](results/README.md).

The programs use Student/Welch approximations. The simulation comparison covers independent Gaussian stores, balanced assignment, equal customer counts, complete observation, and one prespecified hypothesis. Unequal sizes, few clusters, non-Gaussian shocks, spillovers, missing outcomes, sequential monitoring, and selection among outcomes require additional design choices. No AI model performance is measured by these reference calculations.

Complete code appears in M3 §3.18 and M6 §6.30. M1 §1.18 supplies the assessment protocol; M9 §9.24 examines advertising response and customer reasons. The [optional ungraded lab](../../07_Labs/Statistical_Inference/README.md) includes hand checks, method comparison, and an optional recorded AI exercise.

The [Fisher-R1 source review](../../01_Resources/39_Statistical_Inference_and_AI/README.md) motivates statistical assessment. Its code was inspected and linked, without copying or execution. These Python programs are original course implementations. The benchmark's consumer-credit question is discussion material; its reference p-value has not been independently reproduced. ## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Data Dictionary

## mHealth Input and Sample

Input: `../mHealth/data/food_entries.csv.gz`, verified against `../mHealth/manifest.json`. Only `Userid` and `Fancydate` are read. The cohort includes pseudonyms whose first four hexadecimal characters after the initial prefix represent an integer below 4096. Membership additionally requires an observed day before May 1, 2016. The retained dates are normalized to calendar days and duplicates are collapsed. No nutrient or weight values are used.

`mhealth_monthly.csv` has one row per month. `users` is the fixed roster; `logged_days` counts distinct user-days; `calendar_days` is users times days in that month; `users_without_logs` retains roster members without that month's entries. `logging_percent` is 100 times logged days divided by calendar days.

`mhealth_uncertainty.csv` has one row per uncertainty method. `estimate_pp`, `se_pp`, `ci_low_pp`, and `ci_high_pp` use percentage points. `p_value` is two-sided for zero mean change. `reference_df` is 339 for the approximate paired Student test and absent for the normal independent-day comparison. The latter intentionally omits dependence. `mhealth.json` records the source hash, roster rule, target, and interpretation.

## Synthetic Store Outcomes

`synthetic_store_customers.csv` retains repetition 0 at correlation 0.3. There are 40 stores, each with 20 customer rows. `store` identifies the assignment and shared-shock unit; `customer` is a within-store index. `assigned_promotion` is 0 or 1 and constant within store. `contribution_dollars` is synthetic net contribution for a customer, with Gaussian support allowing losses. Every potential treatment effect is zero.

`simulation.json` records seed 20261125, 4,000 experiments per correlation, 20 treated stores, mean contribution 100 dollars, marginal variance 800 dollars squared, correlations 0, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5, and alpha 0.05. New stores and customers are drawn in each experiment; common underlying draws and assignments are retained across correlations. Equal store sizes make store- and customer-average point estimates identical.

## Simulation Results

`null_calibration.csv` has one row per correlation and method. `rejections` counts p-values below 0.05; `rejection_rate` divides by `repetitions`. `mc_ci_low` and `mc_ci_high` are 95% Wilson intervals for that fraction. Effect estimates, empirical effect standard deviations, mean reported standard errors, and theoretical effect standard deviations use dollars. `design_effect` is the theoretical variance ratio to the independent-customer benchmark, `1 + (customers_per_store - 1) * rho`.

`first_experiment.csv` retains repetition 0 at every correlation and method. It includes the effect, standard error, Welch reference degrees of freedom, p-value, and effect confidence interval. Those intervals concern one experiment; the Wilson intervals in `null_calibration.csv` concern the Monte Carlo rejection fraction. Neither is a prediction interval for an individual customer.

## Statistical-Claim Examples

- `pvalue_summary.csv`: stores, true effect in dollars/customer, experiment count, rejection counts/fractions, analytical power, estimate dispersion, interval coverage, and conditional second-experiment rejection counts. `pvalue_bins.csv` uses equal-width 0.05 bins. `pvalue_first.csv` retains first draws; `pvalue_setup.json` fixes seed, sample, distribution, and effect.
- `campaign_decision.csv`: hypothetical independent customer counts, purchase proportions, lift as a probability, approximate 95% interval, fixed dollar margin/contact cost, break-even lift, and contribution per treated customer. Multiply probability differences by 100 for percentage points.
- `test_portfolio.csv` and `portfolio_sensitivity.csv`: specified test counts or proportions, size, power, expected false/true rejections, and their ratio. These are expected-count calculations.
- `equivalence_claims.csv`: hypothetical independent-arm sufficient statistics, mean differences in seconds, pooled standard errors/degrees of freedom, zero-null p-values, 90% intervals, two one-sided equivalence p-values, and a one-sided upper-bound decision. Bounds are illustrative and prespecified at ±5 seconds.
- `data_center_estimates.csv`: rounded coefficients transcribed from Rana et al. Tables 2, 4, and 7, source pages, original standard errors, scaling, units, samples, and normal-approximation inference. The residential reference scales both coefficient and SE by `100 * 456 / 6804`; developer estimates remain in dollars/MWh per percentage point. The sales slope is quarterly MWh per added MW.
- `data_center_power.csv` and `data_center_power_curve.csv`: externally specified positive price effects and two-sided 5% rejection probabilities, holding the published scaled SE fixed. `mde80` is a sensitivity threshold, not an upper effect bound.
- `data_center_sales_targets.csv`: hypothetical utilization of 25% or 50% over a full 2,190-hour quarter without displacement; resulting MWh per MW and fixed-SE power.
- `data_center_reporting_checks.csv`: descriptive observed-price difference, estimated/residual shares, reference exposure, and directly reported developer-equality p-value. No covariance is inferred.
- `data_center_incidence_illustration.csv`: two synthetic monthly allocations with 1,000 equal-use households, the number affected, their additional dollar bill, total revenue, and mean dollars/MWh. Neither scenario is measured household incidence.

## Inverse-Power Outputs

- `andrews_inverse_power.csv`: source case, fixed reported SE, units, test size, target power, required positive departure, and departure in SE units. Residential reference scaling follows Table 2; four-owner and sales cases retain their own slope units.
- `andrews_precision_scenarios.csv`: assumed SE multiplier, resulting SE in USD/MWh, and 80% detection threshold. Multipliers are illustrative sensitivity inputs, with no claim that they correct the original clustered SE.
- `andrews_directional_power.csv`: synthetic two-restriction Wald test with estimator covariance diag(0.25, 4), both outcomes in USD/MWh. A unit-length direction and target power determine the radius and two effect components.
- `logic_extrapolation.csv`: normalized synthetic load, linear and threshold price responses in USD/MWh, and an indicator for the assumed historical support. The functions agree throughout [0, 1] by construction; no sample is fitted.
- `logic_cost_ratios.csv`: hypothetical one-period total cost in USD, sales in MWh, and their ratio. The inputs establish counterexamples to a general inference and measure no actual utility.

No random seed is needed for these deterministic exports. The independent joint-power simulation in the test suite uses seed 20261126 and 100,000 draws; it validates the Gaussian calculation, not the paper's empirical design.

## Institutional Counterexamples

All `institutional_*.csv` inputs are synthetic. `institutional_bills.csv` records monthly revenue in USD, sales in MWh, and 1,000 matched customer-months. Its derived price, mean use, and mean bill satisfy the same-denominator accounting identity. No tariff or causal effect is estimated.

`institutional_donors.csv` has one row per imposed utility: completed, cancelled after investment, or unexposed. Operating additions are MW; initial/later prices and project-related increases are USD/MWh. Donor weights 0.75 and 0.25 sum to one. `institutional_comparisons.csv` reports treated and donor changes and their difference in USD/MWh. The no-project changes are stipulated equal. These are two-period comparisons, separate from the published within-utility regression.

`institutional_recovery.csv` uses annual USD for the revenue requirement, collectible developer contribution, and reuse offset; annual residential MWh for sales; and unitless recovery/allocation fractions in [0,1]. The derived USD/MWh increase follows a stated allocation rule. Upfront capital expenditures are not substituted for annual costs.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Inference/AGENTS.md

# Agent Guide for Statistical Inference

Read the root agent guide, this folder's README, data dictionary, and verification record. Preserve complete runnable code in M3 §3.18 and M6 §6.30 when editing either program; run `scripts/check_lecture_code.py` afterward.

- mHealth results describe observed logging within the fixed cohort. Days without an entry are zero recorded logging, not zero consumption. Preserve the initial roster, unique days, and paired users.
- The store experiment is synthetic, with zero effects, equal store sizes, independent Gaussian stores, and balanced store assignment. Each method receives the same outcomes. Do not select a dataset or method because its p-value is favorable.
- Monte Carlo rejection rates, benchmark agreement rates, and AI model performance are distinct quantities. The course programs measure the first; no model endpoint has been evaluated.
- The independent-day and customer-row methods are deliberate comparison procedures. Do not present their uncertainty as appropriate under the dependence they omit.
- The public credit-advertising task has a reference answer but no reconstructed reference specification here. Do not call it a verified empirical replication or infer borrower welfare from loan take-up.
- Preserve the source license distinctions. Upstream code is linked only; model and benchmark licenses do not establish a license for the GitHub code.
- Optional practice is ungraded. No assignment rules or permitted AI use can be inferred from this folder.

## Statistical Claims and the Recurring Electricity Case

Keep full code synchronized with M3 §3.19, M6 §§6.32–6.33, and M9 §9.25. Preserve source-table locations, units, clustered SEs, and the distinction between reference exposure and a mean of utility ratios. Power evaluates specified alternatives; it does not prove the true effect or explain nonsignificance uniquely. Minimum detectable effects and upper confidence bounds are different quantities.

Separate measured prices, household incidence, welfare, and agency. Retain positive findings and acknowledged limitations. Use the reported joint developer test; marginal SEs do not supply its covariance. The verified public communication is HBS coverage. Do not invent company posts, intent, or actual downstream harms. Keep instructor philosophy manuscripts and private notes outside the public repository.

## Logic and Inverse Power

Preserve the full M6 §6.34 and M9 §9.27 listings. Cite the inverse-power framework as (Andrews, 1989), DOI 10.2307/1913623, with the read 1986 Cowles version identified in the resource review. Preserve that source identity when retrieving related work. Distinguish a fixed-Wald sensitivity calculation from full-design power and uniform guarantees. Preserve covariance and units in directional comparisons. Synthetic counterexamples defeat general entailments; they do not establish empirical frequency, actual household harm, or author intention.

No operating addition does not establish no project exposure, but actual donor contamination and its effect remain unverified. Preserve the paper's discussion of realized payments and regulation. # Executed Statistical Comparisons

The mHealth tables describe observed May-to-June logging in the fixed 340-user cohort. The mean change is -5.123 pp; paired-user uncertainty gives a standard error of 1.379 pp, a Student interval of [-7.835, -2.411] pp, and p=0.000237. The independent-day comparison reports 0.663 pp and p=1.13e-14. These calculations share the same point estimate and differ in their treatment of dependence.

The store tables are synthetic. For 4,000 experiments at each correlation:

| Within-Store Correlation | Customer-Row Rejections | Store-Mean Rejections |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0.0 | 208 / 4,000 | 199 / 4,000 |
| 0.1 | 968 / 4,000 | 198 / 4,000 |
| 0.3 | 1,796 / 4,000 | 188 / 4,000 |
| 0.5 | 2,200 / 4,000 | 191 / 4,000 |

The first experiment at correlation 0.3 estimates $4.334 per customer. The customer-row p-value is 0.0287 and the store-mean p-value is 0.3446. Its full customer table is retained, and the dataset was not selected on its significance. Every customer has zero true effect in the simulation.

See the [dictionary](../DATA_DICTIONARY.md) for units, denominators, and interval definitions. No AI model output is included in these results.

## Statistical Claims and Decision Comparisons

The additional p-value simulation produces 32.515% rejection with 40 stores and 86.550% with 160 when the true effect is eight dollars. The hypothetical campaign has p=0.01868 and estimated contribution of minus $0.06 per treated customer. Equivalence examples distinguish an imprecise nonsignificant result from precise small effects and one-sided improvement.

The reported-table electricity calculation yields estimate $1.749/MWh, SE $1.059/MWh, two-sided 95% interval [-0.326, 3.825], and one-sided 95% upper bound $3.491/MWh at the stated reference exposure. Power is 15.675% for $1 and 47.167% for $2. The cloud-owner slope is reported separately in dollars/MWh per exposure percentage point. All inputs, denominators, and approximations are in the [data dictionary](../DATA_DICTIONARY.md). These are original calculations from reported summaries and hypothetical examples; no original utility-panel replication is claimed.

## Inverse Power and Counterexamples

For the residential reference precision, the positive departures giving 50%, 80%, 90%, and 95% power are 2.075, 2.967, 3.432, and 3.817 USD/MWh. The fixed test size is 5%. The four-owner 80% threshold is 0.448 USD/MWh per exposure pp; the sales threshold is 1,381 quarterly MWh per added MW. These thresholds use the inverse-power approach (Andrews, 1989) within a fixed Gaussian/Wald approximation.

In the synthetic joint test, two independent estimator SEs of 0.50 and 2.00 USD/MWh yield A-only and B-only 80% thresholds of 1.552 and 6.208. Equal increases of 1.506 on both outcomes also attain 80% joint-test power. The covariance is hypothetical.

The synthetic linear and threshold response functions agree throughout the assumed historical interval [0, 1], but give 4 and 14 USD/MWh at normalized load 2. Hypothetical totals of 1,000/10 and 1,100/11 both give 100 USD/MWh, while 1,000/8 gives 125. These constructions establish failures of general inference; they describe no actual utility.

## Institutional Counterexamples

The four `institutional_*.csv` files are synthetic. They preserve monthly bill denominators, MW versus MWh, three project states, fixed donor weights, and annual cost-recovery units. A USD 10/MWh completed-project increase and USD 6 weighted donor increase produce a USD 4 change difference. The unprotected annual-recovery scenario gives USD 8/MWh; enforceable contributions or disallowed recovery change that result. These files contain no observed utility or household records.
