**Reading focus:** Introduction and distinctions between construction and membership conditions.

Ask what establishes an institutional category and what qualifies something for membership. A valid tariff can help constitute a debt while remaining open to moral criticism.

**Access and scope:** Reference introduction and conceptual distinctions inspected; electricity example is an application.

## T19. Realism and Human Kinds

(Thomasson, 2003). *Philosophy and Phenomenological Research* 67(3), 580–609. [Publisher](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1933-1592.2003.tb00309.x) | [Public reading copy](https://joelvelasco.net/teaching/5330%28spring2021%29/thomasson03-human_kinds.pdf).

Read §§2–3, especially pp. 592–600. Intended features and the success of production help distinguish artifactual kinds. Apply this to the creation of a dataset, keeping accuracy of individual records and warrant for a broader claim separate. A schema's existence does not establish the truth of every entry or the adequacy of a welfare interpretation. ## Source: 01_Resources/46_Measurement_and_Disciplinary_History/README.md

# Measurement, Disciplinary Authority, and Marketing

An analyst chooses which customer outcomes a decision will recognize. Sales, retention, and estimated willingness to pay enter many models directly. The customer's authority to refuse a practice, the legitimacy of the firm's objective, and the distribution of power require further arguments. The history of economics and marketing helps explain how a particular division of analytical labor became influential. It also identifies alternatives that remained available within these disciplines.

## Cowles and the Role of Theory

The Cowles Commission adopted “Science is Measurement” at its founding in 1932. In 1952, it changed the motto to “Theory and Measurement.” The contemporary institutional history explains that measurement did not exhaust the scientific work the commission had come to undertake (Christ, 1952, pp. 61–62). Its later institutional account records the same change ([Cowles Foundation, n.d.](https://cowles.yale.edu/about-cowles)). The episode supports an argument about the authority of formal theory and quantitative evidence. Treating it as an unqualified commitment to whatever is immediately observable would misstate the history.

The critique of business-cycle measurement concerned the economic interpretation of observed regularities. Description required a structure connecting observations to economic relations (Koopmans, 1947). The methodological history also records an expanding role for pure theory alongside econometrics (Malinvaud, 1983). These developments challenged measurement without interpretation. Their contribution to causal analysis remains useful when examining whether electricity prices represent household burdens or whether observed purchases reveal consent.

The philosophical question concerns the boundary of that contribution. A theory can organize evidence while taking the firm's objective as given. Identification can establish a parameter within a model while leaving the justification of the modeled objective unresolved. These are contemporary applications of the historical record. Neither the motto nor the development of econometrics establishes that the institution deliberately rejected Kantian philosophy.

## Three Changes in Disciplinary Authority

| Historical Development | Evidence | Consequence for Marketing Dialectics |
|---|---|---|
| Separation of economic analysis from judgment about ends | Economics was defined as neutral among ends, with a distinction between factual propositions and ethical valuation (Robbins, 1935, pp. 24, 148–151). | An efficient means does not establish a justified end. The decision maker must supply and defend the end. |
| Quantitative science as an institutional priority | Foundation funding helped reshape business schools around academic disciplines, doctoral training, and scientific research (Khurana et al., 2011). | Research priorities can emerge from funding, training, and professional incentives. Measurement choices have an institutional history. |
| Marketing organized around managerial decisions | Historical accounts describe the managerial and scientific turn and the later fragmentation of scholarship (Wilkie and Moore, 2003, 2012). | A firm's decision problem can become the discipline's default frame, reducing the visibility of costs borne outside the firm. |

The separation of economics from virtue was historically contested. The same account that separates factual and ethical propositions encourages economists to think widely about ethical questions (Robbins, 1935, p. 150). A historical and conceptual account connects the technocratic ideal to assumptions about agreement on social purposes and the division of intellectual labor between economics and ethics (Schliesser, 2016). This supplies a more direct foundation for the philosophical critique than the original Cowles motto. It concerns whose reasons remain within the economist's professional task.

Marketing provides particularly useful evidence because the firm's standpoint became central to its teaching and research. The societal perspective lost prominence in parts of the mainstream while developing in specialized outlets. The change was reversible in some institutional settings: the 2007 marketing definition explicitly included society at large (Wilkie and Moore, 2012, pp. 61–65). The history supports an account of competing orientations and unequal disciplinary attention. The article's evidence does not isolate whether publication patterns arose from submissions, editorial decisions, or both.

## Quantification and Public Justification

Quantification can make decisions portable across organizations and credible to people who lack personal access to the decision maker. Its authority therefore has social and institutional foundations (Porter, 1995). An analysis of twentieth-century United States policymaking traces how efficiency, incentives, and competition became influential criteria across policy institutions, displacing some arguments framed around equality, rights, and constraints on corporate power (Berman, 2022, chapter 1).

For a pricing decision, this history motivates a concrete inquiry. Who selected profit or aggregate surplus as the objective? Which burdens disappear when the analysis moves to an average? Which claims require a measured effect before they receive attention? The historical account makes these choices available for criticism. A useful statistical estimate can coexist with an objection to the institution's chosen criterion.

## Phenomena and Noumena

The distinction between phenomena and noumena concerns the limits of theoretical knowledge and the standpoint from which objects are considered. A latent preference, an unobserved cost, and a missing household bill remain possible objects of empirical inquiry. Their present absence from a dataset does not make them noumena. The relevant Kantian application concerns the authority assigned to empirical knowledge when judging persons and permissible conduct. The existing [discussion of phenomena and noumena](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md) develops that distinction in §§9.41–9.43.

A defensible historical thesis is that influential institutions increasingly privileged questions answerable through formal models, measurement, and managerial choice. The stronger claim that economics and marketing uniformly abandoned noumenal questions requires evidence these histories do not supply. A history of consumer theory also challenges the familiar account in which psychology simply disappeared and later returned (Hands, 2010). An early behaviorist manifesto provides a clearer example of explicitly prioritizing prediction and control while setting introspection aside (Watson, 1913). Consciousness and Kantian noumena still refer to different philosophical problems.

## Evidence and Decisions

Identification, estimation, and inference acquired a central place in econometrics while statistical decision theory received less attention. A decision-theoretic account evaluates an analytical rule through its consequences across plausible states of the world, including states outside a convenient model (Manski, 2021, pp. 2828–2833). This provides a connection from disciplinary history to [evidentiary standards and asymmetric error costs](../47_Evidence_Standards_and_Error_Costs/README.md).

The resulting criticism concerns a transfer of authority. A standard designed to discipline a causal claim becomes a standard deciding whether a consumer deserves protection. That transfer requires a justification addressing the consequences of action and inaction. Statistical accuracy contributes to that justification; it does not settle the distribution of those consequences.

## Reading and Access Records

The [annotated readings](READINGS.md) and [catalog](catalog.json) contain 18 historical sources with inspection scope, versions, links, and access records. Nine PDFs are held under the local `readings/` directory. These source copies remain in Dropbox; GitHub publishes the original annotations and source links. Downloading a complete document does not imply that every page was inspected. The catalog identifies the passages or previews used. The linked error-cost collection records the decision-theory reading separately; the catalog counts overlap with other course collections and are not a unique-library total.

## Teaching Integration

[The lecture notes](../../06_Lecture_Notes/README.md#measurement-traditions-and-evidence-for-protection) integrate the argument across M1–M9, with full Python in M6 §6.44 and extended philosophy in M9 §§9.55–9.59. [Selected session discussions](../../05_Slides/SESSION_PLAN.md#evidence-standards-and-unequal-error-costs), the syllabus, and [optional practice](../../07_Labs/Evidence_Standards/README.md) connect the readings to pricing, household electricity, and prediction thresholds.

## Source: 01_Resources/47_Evidence_Standards_and_Error_Costs/README.md

# Evidentiary Standards, Consumer Harm, and Error Costs

A regulator must decide whether to investigate a pricing practice, require disclosure, impose temporary safeguards, or seek a legal remedy. The available evidence may suggest harm without identifying its exact causal magnitude. Requiring certainty before every action allocates the consequences of uncertainty to customers who remain exposed. That allocation is a substantive policy choice. Its justification depends on the seriousness of the suspected harm, the reliability of the evidence, the effects of the proposed action, and the people who bear each consequence.

## Rigor as an Institutional Standard

Conceptual engineering examines how conceptual resources organize inquiry and action, and how those resources should change. A concept can direct attention toward some features of a situation and authorize particular responses (Haslanger, 2022, pp. 1–4). Applied to analytics, this perspective asks what an institution allows the word *harm* to include, what it counts as *evidence*, and which responses it considers *rigorous*. The application to enforcement standards is an argument developed here, rather than a claim made in that philosophical source.

Suppose an institution recognizes harm only when an investigator produces a precisely identified average price effect. That rule excludes burdens arising through access, dependence, coercion, and the distribution of prices unless they can satisfy the same empirical requirement. If unresolved evidence then requires nonintervention, the rule also determines who bears uncertainty. A harmful firm can benefit from that arrangement even when each individual estimation procedure is implemented correctly. Establishing that a particular firm acted unlawfully requires evidence about its conduct and the applicable law. Establishing deliberate manipulation of the evidentiary rule requires additional institutional evidence.

The criticism becomes especially strong when the rule applies asymmetrically. A firm can introduce a practice on the basis of forecasts and expected profit, while those exposed to the practice must establish its harmful effects with substantially stronger evidence before receiving protection. Whether this asymmetry is justified depends on the consequences on both sides. Treating continuation of the practice as costless removes the consumers' losses from the decision before any calculation begins.

Inductive risk concerns the consequences of accepting or rejecting an uncertain claim. Where errors have important social consequences, judgments about their acceptability enter choices of methods, characterization of observations, and interpretation (Douglas, 2000). Values can guide the scrutiny required and the action taken. They do not supply missing observations or turn a desired conclusion into a finding.

## Type I and Type II Errors

Fix the null hypothesis as the absence of the specified harmful practice. A Type I error falsely flags harm when that null is true. A Type II error misses harm under a specified harmful alternative. Power is one minus the Type II error probability at that alternative. Reversing the null changes the labels, so the affected state and decision must accompany them.

For a simplified binary decision, expected loss across a specified population of cases is

$$R=(1-\pi)\alpha C_{FP}+\pi\beta C_{FN}.$$

Here, $\pi$ is the share of harmful cases in the population, $\alpha$ is the false-positive probability among harmless cases, $\beta$ is the false-negative probability among harmful cases, and $C_{FP}$ and $C_{FN}$ are the respective losses per error in common units. Correct decisions have zero loss in this illustration. A composite alternative requires averaging over harmful states or evaluating them separately. The equation is a decision model, not a legal burden of proof.

A small false-positive rate can coexist with large expected loss when missed harms are frequent, persistent, or severe. Conversely, an intervention with severe and irreversible consequences can make false positives especially costly. A conventional significance level fixes one error probability without specifying these consequences. An unbiased estimator likewise supplies no complete ranking of decisions: its variance, the policy response, and the losses from that response still matter.

The [complete Python example](../../03_Data_and_Code/Evidence_Standards/README.md) uses a synthetic signal with known distributions. It keeps those distributions fixed, compares one-percent and five-percent tests, and calculates the threshold minimizing expected loss under two opposing cost specifications. The output also separates an assumed posterior probability of harm from a p-value. The comparison measures the consequences of explicit decision rules; it supplies no estimate of misconduct in an actual market.

## The Antitrust Dispute About Error Costs

One influential defense of limited antitrust intervention argues that mistaken condemnation can persist through precedent, whereas market entry can correct some tolerated monopoly power (Easterbrook, 1984, pp. 2–4). The opposing critique examines assumptions about self-correction, entry, innovation, courts, and litigation that overstate false positives and understate false negatives (Baker, 2015, pp. 1–5). The disagreement concerns the economic and institutional content assigned to error costs. Decision theory itself does not require a presumption favoring firms.

The appropriate comparison must also identify the action. Opening an investigation, requiring relevant records, imposing a reversible safeguard, and awarding damages create different costs and evidentiary obligations. Legal burdens affect deterrence, beneficial conduct, and enforcement incentives as well as errors in an individual adjudication (Kaplow, 2012). A numerical loss threshold cannot simply replace the governing law.

Current United States merger guidance offers an example of evidence that extends beyond a precisely estimated price effect. It considers the totality of evidence, including documents, testimony, economic analysis, and structural presumptions; merger review addresses threats to competition in their incipiency ([DOJ and FTC, 2023, overview](https://www.justice.gov/atr/merger-guidelines/overview) and [§4.1](https://www.justice.gov/atr/merger-guidelines/tools/sources-of-evidence)). The guidelines describe agency practice and are not binding law. Their treatment of prospective mergers is distinct from the elements of a retrospective monopolization or damages claim. Positive markups, statutory price gouging, anticompetitive conduct, and moral wrong require different predicates. The [existing legal crosswalk](../16_AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/ANTITRUST_AND_REASONS.md) states those distinctions.

## Heterogeneity, Model Fit, and Market Power

Integrating over heterogeneous tastes constructs aggregate demand from individual choice probabilities. A representative Bayesian aggregate-share model assumes a distribution of preferences and common demand shocks, then uses the likelihood and priors to characterize parameter uncertainty (Jiang et al., 2007, §§2–3; published 2009). The [implementation documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/bayesm/html/rbayesBLP.html) makes the assumed normal heterogeneity and the additional instrumental-variable structure explicit. This is a specified model with restrictions. It does not permit an arbitrary explanation of every possible pattern.

The substantive concern arises when estimated differences in willingness to pay acquire a further interpretation as justified differences in treatment. A consumer with little ability to switch may appear price insensitive. An estimate of that response leaves open whether the relevant mechanism is preference, dependence, restricted access, or an objectionable feature of the market. A flexible demand fit can hide this interpretive choice when the analysis treats the estimated preference distribution as the complete account of consumer interests.

The direction of a markup conclusion is model dependent. For a single-product firm choosing an interior profit-maximizing price, differentiable demand and constant marginal cost imply $(p-c)/p=1/|\varepsilon|$, where $p$ is price, $c$ is marginal cost, and $\varepsilon$ is the own-price elasticity at the optimum. Lower elasticity implies a larger implied markup under those conditions. Integration over heterogeneity therefore has no general tendency to produce lower markups. In multiproduct settings, substitution patterns and ownership enter the pricing conditions as well.

Four points require separate assessment:

1. **Identification:** Which variation distinguishes tastes, common demand shocks, price endogeneity, and competing conduct models? Nonparametric identification results can help discriminate among oligopoly models under stated restrictions (Berry and Haile, 2010; published 2014).
2. **Prior Sensitivity:** How much precision comes from observations and how much from restrictions or priors? In partially identified models, a Bayesian credible set can remain inside the identified set even in large samples. Report the identified set and the conditional prior alongside posterior conclusions (Moon and Schorfheide, 2012).
3. **Institutional Content:** What do the outside option, switching costs, available products, and cost records represent? Which mechanisms are absent from the model? Assess alternative specifications against institutional evidence, rather than allowing good fit to settle their interpretation.
4. **Decision Consequences:** How does each plausible specification change the action and its distribution of losses? Sensitivity analysis that relaxes an instrument's exclusion restriction provides a concrete way to reason with imperfect assumptions (Conley et al., 2012).

These distinctions support a demanding critique of how models are used. A blanket claim that Bayesian methods or identification necessarily prevent enforcement is inconsistent with the methods and their possible applications. The testable concern is whether a particular specification or institutional standard excludes relevant harm, obscures consequential uncertainty, or places unjustified burdens on the people seeking protection.

## An Argument for Protection Under Uncertainty

**Ontological premise.** A person's dependence, financial burden, or loss of authority can exist whether or not the analyst has a variable that adequately represents it. A missing measure does not remove the underlying interest. Empirically unobserved interests and Kantian noumena remain distinct concepts.

**Epistemic premise.** Credible institutional mechanisms, documents, testimony, and descriptive patterns can support concern while leaving causal magnitude unresolved. The strength of that concern depends on the source quality, alternative explanations, timing, and the actual exposure. A non-significant estimate does not establish harmlessness.

**Normative premise.** People have reasons to reject an institutional rule that exposes them to serious, avoidable burdens merely because others cannot meet a demanding identification requirement. The competing reasons include mistaken restriction, livelihood, useful innovation, procedural fairness, and the costs of collecting evidence. Contractualist assessment compares principles through the objections affected individuals could reasonably raise (Scanlon, 1998, chapter 5).

**Action conclusion.** When credible evidence indicates serious exposure and a feasible intervention has smaller, proportionate, and reversible costs, acting before precise causal identification can be justified. Relevant actions include obtaining records, limiting exposure temporarily, and requiring a review as evidence improves. An accusation or punitive remedy remains subject to its separate factual and legal requirements. A low-cost response to a credible threat requires a different justification from a severe sanction imposed on an uncertain attribution.

Expected-loss calculations make the distribution of error costs visible. A contractualist assessment also asks whether a particular person's serious burden is defensible; summing small benefits to others does not automatically answer that objection. The moral importance of a consequence cannot be inferred from how readily it fits into a common monetary unit.

## Household Electricity and Targeted Pricing

For household electricity, an average revenue-per-kWh result concerns a different object from a household's bill, consumption sacrifice, disconnection risk, or exposure to future infrastructure charges. The [existing institutional assessment](../44_Bad_Controls_and_Project_Exposure/CASE_ASSESSMENT.md) identifies mechanisms and records needed to evaluate phantom projects, investment timing, and comparison-group exposure. The [data assessment](../45_Data_Truth_and_Norms/ELECTRICITY_ASSESSMENT.md) documents what is collected and where access or linkage remains incomplete. These distinctions can justify further inquiry without establishing the causal effect of a particular project.

For targeted pricing, prediction of willingness to pay helps a firm select offers. It does not establish that each person's limited alternatives supply a reasonable justification for charging more. Evidence about dependency, suppressed alternatives, and targeting rules bears directly on that question. Consumers should not disappear from moral consideration because the analyst can estimate their demand more readily than their freedom to refuse.

# Evidence Thresholds and the Costs of Error

A consumer-protection office must choose when a statistical signal should trigger a protective action. A strict threshold reduces unnecessary intervention and can leave more harmful cases untreated. The appropriate comparison depends on the consequences of both decisions.

## Synthetic Setup

Each observation is one hypothetical case. Ten percent of cases have the specified harm. Before the decision, the office observes a standardized signal $Z$. Harmless cases have $Z\sim N(0,1)$; harmful cases have $Z\sim N(2,1)$. These are two stipulated states, and the harmful signal shift is fixed at two standard deviations. The rule intervenes when $Z>c$, where $c$ is the threshold. No data from a firm or a research paper enter the calculation.

Correct decisions have zero loss. An unnecessary intervention creates loss $C_{FP}$ and a missed harmful case creates loss $C_{FN}$, in comparable illustrative units per case. The first scenario sets these losses to 1 and 20; the second reverses them. The signal distributions, case prevalence, and available actions remain fixed.

The normal distribution supplies exact error probabilities:

$$\alpha(c)=1-\Phi(c),\qquad \beta(c)=\Phi(c-2).$$

Here, $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The false-positive probability conditions on harmless cases; the false-negative probability conditions on harmful cases. The population expected loss is

$$R(c)=0.9\alpha(c)C_{FP}+0.1\beta(c)C_{FN}.$$

Differentiating this expression and equating its two weighted density terms gives the loss-minimizing threshold

$$c^*=1+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{0.9C_{FP}}{0.1C_{FN}}\right).$$

This solution uses the two normal states, positive costs, zero losses for correct decisions, and the specified prevalence. These conditions make the likelihood ratio increase with the signal, so a single threshold implements the optimum. Different states, residual harm after intervention, or costs of all actions require a revised loss model.

## Results

| Error Costs $(C_{FP},C_{FN})$ | Rule | False-Positive Probability | False-Negative Probability | Expected Loss per Case |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| (1, 20) | One-percent test | 0.0100 | 0.6279 | 1.2648 |
| (1, 20) | Five-percent test | 0.0500 | 0.3612 | 0.7675 |
| (1, 20) | Minimum expected loss | 0.2740 | 0.0809 | 0.4083 |
| (20, 1) | One-percent test | 0.0100 | 0.6279 | 0.2428 |
| (20, 1) | Five-percent test | 0.0500 | 0.3612 | 0.9361 |
| (20, 1) | Minimum expected loss | 0.0002 | 0.9448 | 0.0974 |

When a missed harm costs twenty times an unnecessary intervention, the five-percent test has about 1.88 times the expected loss of the loss-minimizing rule. Reversing the cost ratio favors a much stricter threshold. These results establish that a significance convention alone does not determine a justified action. The assumed losses need their own substantive and moral defense.

![Expected loss across thresholds with the signal distributions fixed and missed harm costing twenty times mistaken intervention. The minimum is near 0.601; conventional five-percent and one-percent thresholds create higher loss under these assumptions.](figures/error_costs.png)

The plotted population contains 10% harmful cases. The curve uses the first cost scenario and the two known normal distributions. Every point is an exact expected loss, rather than a sample estimate or confidence bound. The [underlying table](results/risk_curve.csv) supplies both error probabilities and both cost scenarios at each threshold. The [editable TikZ source](figures/error_costs.tex) uses Illinois blue and orange with distinct marker shapes.

## Posterior Probability and a P-Value

If $q$ denotes the posterior probability of harm under an explicit probability model, intervention has expected loss $(1-q)C_{FP}$ and inaction has expected loss $qC_{FN}$. The preferred action changes when $q>C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$. With costs 1 and 20, that posterior threshold is $1/21$. A p-value is calculated conditional on the null and cannot be substituted for $q$. The program checks that the posterior odds implied by the synthetic normal model at $c^*$ equal the cost ratio.

## Interpretation and Practice

For a temporary, inexpensive safeguard, a high cost of missed harm may be defensible. A severe penalty requires accounting for much greater costs of mistaken attribution and the applicable legal standard. Neither a 27.4% false-positive rate nor the numerical cost ratio is a recommended enforcement rule. Both are consequences of the stated synthetic decision problem.

Change the prevalence, harmful signal shift, and the two costs separately. Explain whose losses each value represents and whether they are reversible. Then consider a person's serious objection that aggregate expected loss does not capture. The [philosophical guide](../../01_Resources/47_Evidence_Standards_and_Error_Costs/README.md) connects this comparison to inductive risk, contractualist reasoning, and institutional standards of evidence.

Python 3.8 or later and its standard library are sufficient. No random draws, seed, network access, packages, or external datasets are required. Outputs are written beside the script under `results/`. `decision_rules.csv` has one row per scenario and rule; `risk_curve.csv` has one row per threshold; `summary.json` records assumptions and checks. Each error-rate denominator is its own underlying state population. Expected loss uses the full case population.

Executed on November 27, 2026. Probability symmetry, a boundary value, equal-cost symmetry, an independent dense-grid comparison, and posterior-odds agreement passed. The figure was compiled from the saved numerical tables and inspected for readability. The [verification record](VERIFICATION.md) lists artifact checks.

Python source: `03_Data_and_Code/Evidence_Standards/error_costs.py`

```python
"""Exact synthetic error probabilities and decision losses; standard library only."""

from csv import DictWriter
from math import isclose, log
from pathlib import Path
from statistics import NormalDist
import json


NORMAL = NormalDist()
PREVALENCE = 0.10
SIGNAL_SHIFT = 2.0
OUTPUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "results"


def error_rates(cutoff, shift=SIGNAL_SHIFT):
    """Flag harm when Z > cutoff; Z is N(0,1) or N(shift,1)."""
    false_positive = NORMAL.cdf(-cutoff)
    false_negative = NORMAL.cdf(cutoff - shift)
    return false_positive, false_negative


def expected_loss(cutoff, false_positive_cost, false_negative_cost,
                  prevalence=PREVALENCE, shift=SIGNAL_SHIFT):
    alpha, beta = error_rates(cutoff, shift)
    return ((1 - prevalence) * alpha * false_positive_cost
            + prevalence * beta * false_negative_cost)


def optimal_cutoff(false_positive_cost, false_negative_cost,
                   prevalence=PREVALENCE, shift=SIGNAL_SHIFT):
    """Minimize loss for two normal states with equal variance and positive shift."""
    if not 0 < prevalence < 1 or shift <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Use a prevalence in (0,1) and a positive signal shift.")
    if min(false_positive_cost, false_negative_cost) <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Error costs must be positive.")
    odds = ((1 - prevalence) * false_positive_cost
            / (prevalence * false_negative_cost))
    return shift / 2 + log(odds) / shift


def write_csv(path, records):
    with path.open("w", newline="") as handle:
        writer = DictWriter(handle, fieldnames=list(records[0]))
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(records)


def verify_calculations():
    # Symmetry gives an independent benchmark at the midpoint of the signals.
    alpha, beta = error_rates(SIGNAL_SHIFT / 2)
    assert isclose(alpha, beta, abs_tol=1e-12)
    assert isclose(error_rates(0)[0], 0.5, abs_tol=1e-12)
    assert isclose(optimal_cutoff(1, 1, prevalence=0.5), 1.0)
    # Check the analytical optimum against a separately enumerated dense grid.
    grid = [i / 1000 for i in range(-1000, 6001)]
    for fp, fn in [(1, 20), (20, 1)]:
        optimum = optimal_cutoff(fp, fn)
        grid_optimum = min(grid, key=lambda c: expected_loss(c, fp, fn))
        assert abs(optimum - grid_optimum) <= 0.00051
        assert expected_loss(optimum, fp, fn) <= expected_loss(grid_optimum, fp, fn) + 1e-12
    # Posterior odds at the optimum equal the specified loss ratio.
    cutoff = optimal_cutoff(1, 20)
    posterior_odds = (PREVALENCE / (1 - PREVALENCE)
                      * NORMAL.pdf(cutoff - SIGNAL_SHIFT) / NORMAL.pdf(cutoff))
    assert isclose(posterior_odds, 1 / 20, rel_tol=1e-12)
    return "Passed: symmetry, probability boundary, equal-cost benchmark, grid optima, posterior odds."


def main():
    verification = verify_calculations()
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    scenarios = [("Missed harm costs 20", 1.0, 20.0),
                 ("Mistaken intervention costs 20", 20.0, 1.0)]
    rows = []
    for scenario, fp, fn in scenarios:
        rules = [("One-percent test", NORMAL.inv_cdf(0.99)),
                 ("Five-percent test", NORMAL.inv_cdf(0.95)),
                 ("Minimum expected loss", optimal_cutoff(fp, fn))]
        for rule, cutoff in rules:
            alpha, beta = error_rates(cutoff)
            rows.append({
                "scenario": scenario, "rule": rule, "cutoff": cutoff,
                "prevalence": PREVALENCE, "signal_shift": SIGNAL_SHIFT,
                "false_positive_cost": fp, "false_negative_cost": fn,
                "false_positive_rate": alpha, "false_negative_rate": beta,
                "power": 1 - beta,
                "expected_loss": expected_loss(cutoff, fp, fn),
            })
    write_csv(OUTPUT / "decision_rules.csv", rows)
    write_csv(OUTPUT / "figure_points.csv", rows[:3])
    commands = {"PrevalencePercent": 100 * PREVALENCE, "SignalShift": SIGNAL_SHIFT}
    for prefix, row in zip(["One", "Five", "Optimal"], rows[:3]):
        commands[prefix + "Cutoff"] = row["cutoff"]
        commands[prefix + "Loss"] = row["expected_loss"]
    (OUTPUT / "figure_values.tex").write_text("\n".join(
        "\\newcommand{\\" + name + "}{" + f"{value:.12f}" + "}"
        for name, value in commands.items()) + "\n")
    curve = []
    for index in range(161):
        cutoff = index / 40
        alpha, beta = error_rates(cutoff)
        curve.append({
            "cutoff": cutoff, "false_positive_rate": alpha,
            "false_negative_rate": beta,
            "missed_harm_cost_20": expected_loss(cutoff, 1, 20),
            "mistaken_intervention_cost_20": expected_loss(cutoff, 20, 1),
        })
    write_csv(OUTPUT / "risk_curve.csv", curve)
    summary = {
        "data_status": "Synthetic known distributions; no estimated market effects.",
        "unit": "One hypothetical case before observing its signal.",
        "null": "No specified harm; Z ~ N(0,1).",
        "alternative": "Specified harm; Z ~ N(2,1).",
        "prevalence": PREVALENCE,
        "loss_units": "Illustrative comparable loss units per case.",
        "correct_decision_loss": 0,
        "verification": verification,
        "rules": rows,
    }
    (OUTPUT / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(verification)
    for row in rows:
        print(f"{row['scenario']} | {row['rule']}: "
              f"alpha={row['false_positive_rate']:.4f}, "
              f"beta={row['false_negative_rate']:.4f}, "
              f"loss={row['expected_loss']:.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Scope

The program calculates probabilities and losses from two stipulated normal distributions. It estimates no causal effect, demand system, market prevalence, or actual enforcement loss. Both cost scenarios use the same population share and signal distributions. Correct decisions have zero loss.

- Expected loss at each analytical optimum no greater than at the grid minimum.

# Evidence Standards, Error Costs, and Reasonable Protection

By Nathan Yang

This is optional ungraded practice. An authority must decide whether to obtain records, limit exposure temporarily, or seek a remedy for a suspected harmful practice. The exercise separates the evidence about harm from the reasons for the particular action.

# Synthetic sensitivity: the signal separation remains two standard deviations.
for prevalence in (0.01, 0.10, 0.30):
    cutoff = optimal_cutoff(1, 20, prevalence=prevalence)
    alpha, beta = error_rates(cutoff)

# Subscription Records and Their Intended Uses

The records are synthetic. All six accounts were subscribed at the start of January 2027. Four accounts submitted cancellation requests before the cutoff, 00:00 UTC on February 1. One request was completed; three remained pending. No new subscription or other closure occurs in this constructed history.

| Quantity | Numerator | Denominator | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Retained accounts | 5 | 6 initial accounts | 83.33% |
| Pending requests | 3 | 4 submitted requests | 75% |
| Retained accounts with pending requests | 3 | 5 retained accounts | 60% |

`retention_v1.csv` contains subscription status. `assessment_v2.csv` adds submitted and completed request indicators. Projecting V2 onto the V1 columns reproduces V1 exactly. `assessment_v2_reordered.csv` changes only row order. Under the declared identity rule, the two V2 files contain the same records despite different byte hashes.

`manifest.json` records the cutoff, population, unit, intended uses, release relationship, identity rule, and file hashes. `summary.json` records counts and fractions. A hash verifies a file's bytes against a reference; it supplies no evidence that the records describe real events. The synthetic example establishes coexistence of the two descriptive results. It identifies neither a causal effect of cancellation procedures nor the prevalence of obstructed cancellation in any company.

## Source: 01_Resources/45_Data_Truth_and_Norms/05_Restricted_Research/README.md

# Confidentiality, Research Independence, and Public Claims

The research decision concerns whether access to a valuable dataset justifies the conditions attached to it. Distinguish an agreement that protects records from one that governs permissible questions or publication. The actual terms and their implementation determine the constraint. The label NDA alone supplies little information about those terms.

## Readings and Scope

| Source | Reading Focus | Application |
|---|---|---|
| T20: (Mello et al., 2005), [Academic Medical Centers' Standards for Clinical-Trial Agreements with Industry](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa044115) | Survey of medical-school administrators responsible for agreements; sponsor participation and data-sharing provisions | Evidence that contracts allocate consequential control. The study's setting does not establish prevalence in marketing. Abstract and publisher results inspected; full-text access blocked. |
| T21: (ICMJE, n.d.), [Disclosure of Financial and Non-Financial Relationships and Activities, and Conflicts of Interest](https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/roles-and-responsibilities/author-responsibilities--conflicts-of-interest.html) | Independent access, interpretation, and publication; disclosure of sponsor roles and restrictions | Professional benchmark for medical journals. The marketing application is a normative comparison. |
| T22: (American Economic Association, 2026), [Data and Code Availability Policy](https://www.aeaweb.org/journals/data/data-code-policy) | Documented exceptions for nonpublic data, public code, preservation, source information, access statements, and editorial exceptions | AEA policy compliance and unrestricted independent verification are different assessments. |

Policies checked November 27, 2026. These professional standards are distinct from the legal enforceability of a particular agreement. Catalog IDs refer to `45_Data_Truth_and_Norms/catalog.json`.

## Artifactual Interpretation

The file's schema and contents form one part of the research object. Its governed use concerns who may inspect it, which analyses are permitted, who can correct it, and which results can become public. Shared norms can help constitute recognized artifacts without making each object publicly accessible (Thomasson, 2014, §5.4). Applying this distinction to research asks how a contract and professional practice shape what the published paper represents.

A restriction on identifiers can protect people. A restriction on questions can limit which burdens receive scrutiny. A discretionary publication right can select the visible literature after an otherwise valid analysis. These mechanisms differ, and an allegation that one operated in a named study requires evidence. Unknown restrictions leave uncertainty about the reporting process; they do not reveal an unpublished effect.

## Teaching Application

[M9 §§9.63–9.65](../../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md) compares three hypothetical agreements using the same six-account synthetic history. Students distinguish confidentiality review, restricted research purpose, and discretionary sponsor approval. The [optional practice](../../../07_Labs/Data_Truth_and_Norms/README.md) asks whether NDA-governed research ought to exist, separating the decision to conduct a study from publication and public reliance.

A defensible answer addresses affected people's reasons, privacy, the value of knowledge, the risk of selective reassurance, and feasible alternative terms. It identifies conditions for proceeding, renegotiating, or declining. A researcher can have a reason to forgo a publication when the governing arrangement prevents adequate justification to the people affected by its use.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/README.md

# Heterogeneity and Consumer Protection

A firm can fit heterogeneous responses accurately while leaving the source of those responses unresolved. This example reanalyzes released retail-account data and constructs two explanations with exactly the same likelihood. It connects model fit to the evidence and reasons required before a consumer complaint can be dismissed.

## Data and Provenance

The `bayesm` 3.1-7 package attributes its `cheese` dataset to the trade-promotion study (Boatwright et al., 1999). The released file has 5,555 weekly observations for 88 retailer–market accounts, with Borden unit sales, price in US dollars, and display activity. All released rows and columns are retained. The upstream R object, documentation, package description, GPL license, conversion script, pinned commit, and hashes accompany the CSV. See [PROVENANCE.json](PROVENANCE.json) and the [data dictionary](DATA_DICTIONARY.md).

This is a reanalysis of a public dataset attributed to the study. The January 1999 preprint describes 77 accounts and a Kraft application with additional variables; the public package describes 88 accounts and Borden sales. The mapping is unresolved. The exercise therefore makes no claim to reproduce a published table or the paper's constrained hierarchical sampler. The package provides a concrete research-data example with an explicit replication boundary.

## Run the Example

Python 3 with NumPy, pandas, and SciPy is required. The provided CSV permits execution without R. To reproduce the extraction from the original object, run `Rscript 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/convert_data.R` from the repository root.

```sh
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/heterogeneity_reanalysis.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/test_reanalysis.py
```

The program runs account regressions of log unit sales on log price, an intercept, and display where display varies. It then integrates account coefficients under one- and two-component normal distributions, fitting their parameters by marginal maximum likelihood. The resulting conditional distributions are empirical Bayes. First-stage standard errors use an iid Gaussian working model; temporal dependence and uncertainty in fitted hyperparameters remain outside this calculation. These restrictions preclude using the reported precision as a validated measure of uncertainty about causal demand or conduct.

## Results and Interpretation

The one-component and two-component log likelihoods are -128.629 and -124.520. Their BIC values are 266.213 and 271.427, respectively, so BIC favors the simpler model despite the extra in-sample fit. Mean conditional account slopes are -2.138 and -2.151. The two positive OLS slopes become negative conditional means in both integrated models. This shrinkage illustrates how a distributional model changes the interpretation of noisy account estimates; it establishes no consumer benefit or injury.

The constructed mechanism decomposes the observed response as a latent taste component plus an imposed restriction component. Shifting the latent distribution offsets the imposed restriction exactly. Every account's marginal likelihood remains unchanged at restriction values 0, 0.25, 0.5, and 1. These values are synthetic explanatory scenarios applied to the fitted response distribution. They are not measured switching costs or findings of misconduct.

If a constructed harmless and harmful state generate the same observed-data distribution, any rule with a five-percent false-flag rate under the harmless state also flags only five percent under the harmful state. Its missed-harm rate is 95% in that construction. This is an identification result, not an estimated error rate for these retailers or a general property of Bayesian models. Additional observations capable of distinguishing the mechanisms can change the result.

## Decision and Philosophical Questions

The public record supports a comparison of response models. A conclusion about price discrimination, wrongdoing, or permissible conduct requires further economic and normative premises. Consumers with credible concerns about serious exposure may reasonably demand records or proportionate protection before investigators identify every aspect of heterogeneity. The argument compares their reasons with the burdens of the proposed response, including those of other customers and affected workers [(Scanlon, 1998, pp. 191–196)](https://e-edu.nbu.bg/pluginfile.php/314831/mod_resource/content/0/scanlon_5.1-3.pdf).

[M4 §4.31](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md) contains the derivation and complete Python. [M9 §§9.57.1–9.57.4](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md) distinguishes model-relative possibility, evidential support, and permission. [Optional practice](../../07_Labs/Evidence_Standards/README.md) asks students to defend a lower threshold for a specified protective action while preserving the assumptions needed for a factual allegation.

## Outputs and Verification

The [results guide](results/README.md) identifies each table and denominator. [VERIFICATION.md](VERIFICATION.md) records numerical checks, source fidelity, and the replication boundary. No upstream estimation code is executed. The course program is an original adaptation; source data and documentation retain the package's license and attribution.

## Precision and Missed Harm

Run `python3 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/harm_elasticity.py` for the separate synthetic example in M6 §6.46. Partial pooling narrows posterior standard deviation from 1 to 0.5345 and lowers population-average MSE from 1 to 0.2857, while detection of the harmed group falls from 63.88% to 14.07% under a fixed one-sided posterior-credibility rule. Actual false-flag rates fall from 5% to 0.1045%. The harmed subgroup's MSE increases to 2.1224.

This is a precision comparison, with a population that includes ten percent harmed groups and a normal working prior. It is not bias reduction within the harmed group or an empirical harm finding in the retail data. The positive precision elasticity is 0.3999 at the pooled endpoint. Matching the actual false-positive rates recovers the same detection because the score transformation preserves information. These checks identify the joint role of pooling and the institutional decision rule.

The source algebra is (Gelman et al., 2012, pp. 196–198), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.618213). The consumer population, harms, loss function, and elasticity are original course constructions. M9 §9.57.5 connects the result to reasonable protection and the data-center reassurance critique.

## Method Correspondence

The [method crosswalk](METHOD_CROSSWALK.md) traces the hierarchical loop to `runiregG`, derives the matrix posterior, and verifies the scalar conditional identity numerically. Source files and hashes are retained; no upstream sampler was executed. The known-harm example changes this conditional update and the associated decision threshold, with full hyperparameter uncertainty outside its scope.

## Statistical Virtues and Ontological Scope

[M9 §§9.66–9.69](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md#966-statistical-virtues-and-ontological-laziness) evaluates the choice of object and error criterion behind the comparison. The population MSE, a harmed group's burden, and the reasons for protection have distinct roles. The [philosophical reading guide](../../01_Resources/48_Statistical_Virtues_and_Ontology/README.md) connects this distinction to abstraction, value capture, and justification. The calculation and its conditional scope are unchanged.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/DATA_DICTIONARY.md

# Released Retail-Account Data

The unit is a released weekly observation for a retailer–market account. There are 5,555 rows across 88 accounts. The file supplies neither a date column nor household identifiers, purchases, incomes, contract terms, marginal costs, or welfare outcomes. Row order is preserved without assigning calendar dates.

| Field | Meaning and Units |
| --- | --- |
| `RETAILER` | Public retailer–market account label; grouping unit |
| `VOLUME` | Unit sales of the released Borden sliced-cheese product |
| `DISP` | Released display measure in [0,1], described as percent ACV in the upstream documentation; retained in its fractional scale |
| `PRICE` | Average price in US dollars |

`log(VOLUME)` and `log(PRICE)` use natural logarithms. The price coefficient is a conditional log-sales/log-price association. Display enters in its released scale. Two accounts have constant display and therefore use an intercept and log price only. Every account remains in the analysis; no observations are removed. Each account receives one contribution to the second-stage likelihood, with its own first-stage sampling variance. The reported mean account coefficient gives accounts equal weight.

The independent-error assumption is a working model. Missing dates limit assessment of temporal dependence; prices and promotions can also respond to demand conditions. The exercise makes conditional comparisons under these restrictions and does not treat the fitted coefficients as identified causal elasticities.

## Synthetic Precision Inputs

The precision calculation uses no rows from `cheese.csv`. It specifies independent normal group signals with SD one, zero burden for 90% of equal-sized groups, and burden two for 10%. One burden unit is $10 per person-month. The normal working prior is centered on zero; its variance determines the retained data weight. Monetary loss uses 10,000 consumers, the ten-percent harmful share, and 12 months of $20 burden when harm is missed. These inputs define an illustration rather than observations.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/METHOD_CROSSWALK.md

# Hierarchical Regression, Pooling, and Missed Harm

## The Documented Method

The `cheese.Rd` example prepares account-specific regressions for `rhierLinearModel`. The package documentation identifies the hierarchical regression model and its author (Rossi, 2025, bayesm 3.1-7). The maintained source separates the hierarchical loop from the conditional coefficient draw. The file `rhierLinearModel_rcpp_loop.cpp` forms the prior precision from `Vbeta`, constructs the prior mean `Z * Delta`, and calls `runiregG` in `utilityFunctions.cpp`. The latter adds data precision and prior precision before drawing each regression coefficient vector. These GPL source files are saved under `upstream/`, with pinned hashes in `PROVENANCE.json`. They were inspected, not executed.

## The Exact Conditional Update

For regression $j$, let $y_j=X_j\beta_j+e_j$, with $e_j\sim N(0,v_jI)$, and let $\beta_j\sim N(\mu_j,V)$, where $\mu_j=Z_j\Delta$. Conditional on $v_j$, $V$, and $\Delta$, the posterior covariance and mean are

$$C_j=(X_j'X_j/v_j+V^{-1})^{-1},\qquad
m_j=C_j(X_j'y_j/v_j+V^{-1}\mu_j).$$

The source computes this covariance through a Cholesky factor and this mean through the precision-weighted right-hand side. The course's `conditional_update` computes the same normal conditional moments without drawing random values. Setting $X'X=1$, $X'y=2$, $v=1$, $\mu=0$, and $V=0.4$ gives $C=2/7$ and $m=4/7$. These equal $w\sigma^2$ and $wY$ in the precision example. The connection is an exact scalar conditional specialization of the documented update, rather than a verbal analogy.

## The Decision That Produces the Loss

The known-harm simulation holds the population, raw observations, and follow-up horizon fixed. It substitutes the pooled conditional posterior for the unpooled estimate and applies a one-sided 95% posterior lower-bound rule. Relative to the unpooled benchmark, detection falls by 49.81 percentage points and synthetic missed-harm loss increases by $119,538 across the specified 10,000 consumers and 12 months. This difference is caused by the estimator-and-decision-rule change in the constructed experiment. Average MSE nevertheless falls by 71.43%, and reported posterior SD falls by 46.55%.

The source implementation supplies the pooling mechanism. The synthetic harmful population, fixed hyperparameters, centered prior, protection rule, and dollar losses are additional course assumptions. The normal working prior approximates the two-point population. The result does not establish an observed injury in the cheese data or the published trade-promotion application. Full hierarchical sampling also updates the mean, covariance, and residual variances. Integrating uncertainty in those quantities can change intervals and decisions, so conditional precision must not be reported as the full sampler's uncertainty.

The mechanism matters when a low pooled mean, weak group-specific information, and a demanding posterior rule make a minority burden difficult to flag. More heterogeneous prior dispersion weakens the pooling; unrestricted claims that adding heterogeneity always suppresses harm are unsupported. The criticism instead identifies a particular operation in the method and the institutional use that makes its missed detections costly.

## Sources

- (Rossi, 2025), [hierarchical model documentation at the pinned version](https://github.com/cran/bayesm/blob/453ae30857cf09a0c537f4deab64ed193493c8c9/man/rhierLinearModel.Rd).
- (Kim, 2014; bayesm 3.1-7), [hierarchical loop](https://github.com/cran/bayesm/blob/453ae30857cf09a0c537f4deab64ed193493c8c9/src/rhierLinearModel_rcpp_loop.cpp) and [conditional update](https://github.com/cran/bayesm/blob/453ae30857cf09a0c537f4deab64ed193493c8c9/src/utilityFunctions.cpp). Preserve the implementation contributor's attribution separately from the package author's model documentation.
- (Boatwright et al., 1999), [study attributed by the public data documentation](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1999.10473859). The public package and preprint sample differ.
- (Gelman et al., 2012, pp. 196–198), [partial-pooling algebra](https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.618213).

# Statistical Virtues and Ontological Adequacy

A statistical procedure can answer its chosen question well while leaving the object of a broader claim inadequately represented. The criticism of ontological laziness identifies the substitution, the omitted relation, and its consequence for the decision. It applies to arguments and uses of results; it supplies no diagnosis of a researcher’s motives.

The teaching material is in [M1 §1.24, M6 §6.46.6, and M9 §§9.66–9.69](../../06_Lecture_Notes/README.md), Sessions 1 and 14, and the [optional argument exercise](../../07_Labs/Philosophical_Arguments/README.md#statistical-virtues-and-the-missing-object). The existing [hierarchical-method example](../../03_Data_and_Code/Heterogeneity_and_Consumer_Protection/METHOD_CROSSWALK.md) supplies the exact statistical connection and its synthetic scope.

## Reading Sequence

Begin with V01 on abstraction, V02 on ontology and knowledge, V04 on records and explanatory objects, V10 on metric-driven changes in values, and V11 on justification to affected people. Use V06 and V09 to examine criticism and error consequences. V14 supplies a serious empiricist reply. V07–V08 supply institutional history; their annotations are based on publisher accounts. These readings disagree about realism, knowledge, and justification. Each argument supports a specified premise; the collection preserves these disagreements.

## Catalog and Access

The 16 records in [catalog.json](catalog.json) use IDs V01–V16 local to this folder and overlap with earlier course collections. Their counts are not unique additions to the full library. Each record states the inspected passage and the application. Five newly retrieved source copies remain in the ignored `readings/` directory in Dropbox. Public teaching files contain original analysis, citations, and links. The published V10 article carries CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; the saved copy is an author preprint and is kept local. The Gutenberg endpoint for V01 and the journal PDF endpoint for V10 were unavailable during retrieval.

[Source and course verification](VERIFICATION.md) records the checks on the catalog, generated documents, code listings, and lesson.

## Source: 01_Resources/49_Online_Engagement_and_Agency/README.md

# Marketing Research, Online Engagement, and Agency

A platform can retain a person by serving a purpose the person endorses or by making departure harder. Marketing publications help explain how sequences, rewards, and records sustain activity. The critical question is whether the commercial use respects the person's purposes and authority to stop.

This collection contains ten marketing and consumer-research papers, one economics paper, three company documents, and one regulatory notice. It is a focused selection of mechanisms and documented applications, with no claim to estimate their prevalence across the literature. The [catalog](catalog.json) records author metadata, inspected passages, access limits, and local retrieval hashes. IDs E01–E15 refer to this collection only.

## Evidence and Interpretation

| Claim | Evidence Required | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A feature can change repeated behavior | Experiment or an adequately supported empirical design | E01–E05 |
| A related feature was deployed | Product evidence identifying the feature and date | E08, E13, E14 |
| A company uses the research in its rationale | Explicit citation or other documented connection | E12 cites E02 |
| A feature caused unwanted continuation or harm | Relevant user outcomes, comparison, and population | Requires more than a retention effect |
| A firm ought to change the design | Supported factual premises, a defended principle, and feasible alternatives | M9 §§9.74–9.75 |

A corporate citation leaves the consequence question open. A deployed feature does not establish that an academic paper originated it. High use alone distinguishes neither enjoyment from compulsion nor an economic habit model from a clinical diagnosis. The notes preserve these distinctions while allowing proportionate protection before every uncertainty is resolved.

## Marketing and Consumer-Research Readings

| ID and Source | Reading Question |
| --- | --- |
| E01: [Down a Rabbit Hole](https://doi.org/10.1177/00222437211055403) (Woolley and Sharif, 2022), *Journal of Marketing Research* | Does a sequence shape the preference the platform later predicts? Inspect interruptions, identical-content satiation, and delayed choice alongside continuation. |
| E02: [On or Off Track](https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucac029) (Silverman and Barasch, 2023), *Journal of Consumer Research* | When does a record become a goal? Distinguish intact-versus-broken comparisons from inconsistent comparisons against no log. |
| E03: [The Fun and Function of Uncertainty](https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucy062) (Shen et al., 2019), *Journal of Consumer Research* | Does repetition among participants conceal reduced initial entry? Keep the immediate-resolution boundary and denominator. |
| E04: [The Motivating-Uncertainty Effect](https://doi.org/10.1086/679418) (Shen et al., 2015), *Journal of Consumer Research* | How does attention to reward pursuit change the interpretation of effort? Annotation uses the abstract and opening. |
| E05: [The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected](https://doi.org/10.1509/jmkr.43.1.39) (Kivetz et al., 2006), *Journal of Marketing Research* | Who determines the goal toward which activity accelerates? The study includes online music ratings and coffee loyalty. |
| E06: [Binge Watching and Advertising](https://doi.org/10.1509/jm.15.0258) (Schweidel and Moe, 2016), *Journal of Marketing* | What does a model of viewing and ad response leave outside its commercial objective? Publisher abstract reviewed. |
| E07: [Driving Mobile App User Engagement Through Gamification](https://doi.org/10.1177/00222437241275927) (Paschmann et al., 2025), *Journal of Marketing Research* | Whose value is measured? Inspect provider-serving survey activity, the flow proxy, returning-user restriction, and counterfactual status. |
| E08: [Game Over?](https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0345) (Blanchard and Palazzolo, 2025), *Marketing Science* | Does behavior persist after an incentive stops? Publisher abstract and disclosures reviewed; the NDA preserves adverse publication. |
| E09: [Wait for Free](https://doi.org/10.1177/00222437241270194) (Choi et al., 2025), *Journal of Marketing Research* | When does paid immediacy preserve meaningful choice? Publisher abstract reviewed; free waiting remains a consequential benefit. |
| E10: [Leveraging Rational Addiction Theory to Reduce Mobile Usage](https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429251405841) (Somasundaram et al., 2025), *Journal of Marketing* | How can habit insights serve a reduction goal? Accepted abstract distinguishes fixed targets from proportional incentives. |

The issue year is used for E01–E09. E02 appeared online in 2022; E07–E09 appeared online in 2024. E10 uses its 2025 online publication year. These dates matter when reconstructing a connection to company practice.

| E14: [Binge-Viewing Ad Launch](https://press.hulu.com/pressrelease/hulu-launches-new-ad-experience-designed-to-connect-brands-with-binge-watchers/) (Hulu, 2019) | Documents a commercial reward for continued viewing. It establishes neither adoption of E06 nor a measured harmful effect. |

Its preliminary findings leave the investigation's outcome open; no final liability determination is asserted. |

## Philosophical Assessment

Repeated activity can become an ontologically inadequate substitute for the person whose interests supposedly justify the design. The criticism must identify the omitted relation: a stopping instruction, a learning purpose, a spending boundary, or a burden on someone outside the retained sample. An analyst can estimate the chosen outcome precisely while leaving that omission intact.

Kantian respect concerns the person's authority to set ends. Contractualist reasoning compares objections to principles governing the design, including a feasible alternative and the interests of users who want extended access. Value capture concerns the possibility that a simplified goal displaces deliberation about what matters. These are applications of the philosophical arguments in M9 §§9.41, 9.47, and 9.67; the empirical papers do not themselves prove the normative conclusions.

# Chicago Price Theory and Moral Justification

A price-theory model can explain how people respond to constraints and how costs move through markets. A recommendation also requires a principle governing the terms imposed on the people affected. The critical question is where a conditional economic result receives more moral authority than its premises support.

The [13-record catalog](catalog.json) separates analytical price theory, normative law-and-economics arguments, and philosophical criticism. Seven newly downloaded PDFs remain local to Dropbox. Three primary texts are reused from existing collections. The advertising paper, market-limits article, and competition essay are annotated from their inspected abstracts or summaries; full texts were not obtained. No unique-resource total should be calculated by adding these records to overlapping course collections.

## Reading Sequence

| --- | --- | --- |

| C02 | [The Methodology of Positive Economics](https://edisciplinas.usp.br/pluginfile.php/8853288/mod_resource/content/1/FriedmanEssaysonPositiveEconomics%20%281%29.pdf), section I (Friedman, 1953) | Why can common predictions leave disagreement about what ought to be done? |
| C03 | [A Theory of Rational Addiction](https://doi.org/10.1086/261558), pp. 675–677 (Becker and Murphy, 1988) | Does consistency over time answer whether the firm respects a person's stopping purpose? |
| C04 | [A Simple Theory of Advertising as a Good or Bad](https://doi.org/10.2307/2118455), publisher abstract (Becker and Murphy, 1993) | Which utility and market conditions enter the welfare interpretation? |

## Moral Objections and Required Premises

| Proposed Inference | Consequential Missing Premise | Course Application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Higher willingness to pay gives priority | Purchasing power provides a defensible basis for this allocation | Synthetic budget exchange; M4 §4.32 and M9 §9.77 |
| Predictable continued use proves endorsement | The user can understand, refuse, and revise the purpose | Engagement research and stopping controls; §9.78 |
| Aggregate gains justify uncompensated losses | The affected person's objection is answered, or a justified alternative is unavailable | Synthetic compensation; §9.79 |
| Bargaining will resolve the household burden | Affected people possess workable information, rights, and negotiating capacity | Electricity commitments and canceled projects; §9.80 |
| Uncertain harm warrants waiting | The cost and duration of waiting are defensible relative to a feasible response | Hierarchical detection example and antitrust error costs; §9.81 |

These are conditional criticisms of arguments and actions. The readings contain important disagreements: positive prediction is expressly distinguished from normative judgment; transaction-cost analysis considers institutional alternatives; the antitrust argument recognizes interim losses and beneficial anticartel enforcement. School affiliation supplies no evidence of a particular author's intention or a firm's violation. The course's moral conclusions require supported factual premises, a defended principle, and comparison with a feasible alternative.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Price_Theory_and_Justification/README.md

# Prices, Budgets, and Justification

A manager ranks customers by willingness to pay. A project sponsor argues that aggregate gains justify an uncompensated loss. These synthetic comparisons separate the numerical calculation from the principle needed to justify the action.

## Inputs and Units

The first comparison has two people, A and B, with one-period budgets of $100 and $1,000 and the same specified service increment of 0.2 in logarithmic utility. Exchanging budgets holds that increment and the functional form fixed. Reservation prices solve the indifference equation in M9 §9.77. These are constructed preferences, with no estimate of actual need, autonomy, or interpersonal welfare.

The separate project comparison has one firm gaining $140 and 100 residents each losing $1 over the same period. The alternative pays each resident $1. Transfers have zero resource cost in this illustration; no uncertainty, other affected party, or nonfinancial consequence is included. Aggregate dollar changes are accounting sums, with no interpersonal utility interpretation.

## Reproduction

Run from the repository root with Python 3 and its standard library:

```sh
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Price_Theory_and_Justification/compare_valuations.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Price_Theory_and_Justification/verify_comparisons.py
```

The program saves [results.json](results.json) beside its source. Expected reservation prices are $18.13 and $181.27; exchanging budgets reverses their owners. Both project policies have a $40 aggregate dollar gain, while the number of residents with dollar losses changes from 100 to zero. The verification evaluates the utility equation directly, checks the budget reversal, and reconciles firm and household changes with the saved file. There is no seed or network dependency.

## Interpretation and Provenance

The calculations are original teaching examples. They implement no particular author's estimated model and use no replication microdata. The [reading guide](../../01_Resources/50_Chicago_Price_Theory_and_Moral_Justification/README.md) links the valuation, compensation, and moral arguments. [M9 §§9.76–9.82](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md) includes the complete program and explains why these calculations leave the choice of principle open. [Optional practice](../../07_Labs/Scanlon_Pricing/README.md#price-theory-and-moral-permission) asks students to defend that principle and answer its strongest objection.

# Modern Power Analysis and Evidence About Harm

A public assurance about household costs requires evidence excluding a relevant burden. Power against a zero-effect null, evidence of equivalence, and a valid causal design answer different questions. These readings extend the inverse-power framework (Andrews, 1989) already used in the course.

The [catalog](catalog.json) contains 11 source records published or circulated in 2018–2026. Ten full reference files are saved locally in Dropbox, with their versions, hashes, and inspected passages recorded. The newest DID power article was inspected through its publisher abstract; its restricted full text was not obtained. A retrieved file does not imply that every proof or application was read. Original source copies remain outside public Git.

## Design Power

| Source | Contribution | Information Required for the Electricity Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Panel Data and Experimental Design](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2020.102458) (Burlig et al., 2020) | Power with nonconstant serial correlation; 2019 working-paper version saved | Outcome covariance, pre/post periods, assignment, and the relationship to the actual estimator |
| [Power With Variation in Treatment Timing](https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986211070625) (Schochet, 2022) | Staggered timing, clustering, unequal intervals, and covariates; 2021 author version saved | Exposure timing, cluster structure, repeated measurements, and a chosen effect |
| [Computing Statistical Power for DID](https://doi.org/10.1177/0193841X251380898) (Hedberg and Hedges, 2026) | Design-specific power and minimum detectable effects; first online in 2025 | Exact analysis and variance inputs; formulas were not inspected or implemented |

These formulas do not automatically describe a synthetic-control gap regression with repeated cumulative treatment. A full-design calculation must preserve the actual exposure process and the estimated comparison. Neither the observation count nor an assumed SE multiplier supplies that reconstruction.

## Equivalence and Identification

| Source | Contribution | Course Application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Pretest With Caution](https://doi.org/10.1257/aeri.20210236) (Roth, 2022) | Tests can miss consequential pre-trends; selecting on a passed test can distort inference | Assess the power of a design diagnostic before treating it as support for the counterfactual |
| [Equivalence of Pre-Trends](https://doi.org/10.1080/07350015.2024.2308121) (Dette and Schumann, 2024) | Tests small departures explicitly; contains a scalar folded-normal construction | Adapt the scalar test to reported price summaries; do not call it a joint pre-trend replication |
| [A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdad018) (Rambachan and Roth, 2023) | Inference under specified classes of trend violations | Identify the coefficient vector, covariance, target, and restrictions needed before using HonestDiD |
| [Optimal Inference in Regression Models](https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA14434) (Armstrong and Kolesár, 2018) | Confidence bounds account for worst-case bias within a stated model class | Derive an elementary scalar upper bound with an imposed bias allowance |

The folded-normal calculation uses an established scalar testing construction discussed in the modern equivalence paper. Its availability illustrates how a different test can answer the intended small-effect question. Its date does not establish its applicability to a particular empirical design.

## Cluster and Synthetic-Control Uncertainty

| Source | Contribution | Additional Inputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cluster-Robust Inference](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2022.04.001) (MacKinnon et al., 2023) | Leverage, finite-sample reliability, and bootstrap procedures | Regressors, residuals, cluster structure, and influence |
| [Prediction Intervals for Synthetic Controls](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2021.1979561) (Cattaneo et al., 2021) | Uncertainty from estimated weights and post-treatment prediction errors | Donor and treated panels, constraints, and error models |
| [Staggered Synthetic-Control Inference](https://titiunik.github.io/files/publications/CattaneoFengPalombaTitiunik2025-RESTAT.pdf) (Cattaneo et al., 2025a) | Multiple treated units and simultaneous prediction; March 2025 manuscript saved | Adoption timing, a defined prediction target, and joint dependence |
| [scpi](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v113i01) (Cattaneo et al., 2025b) | Python, R, and Stata implementation | Correct input preparation and maintained prediction assumptions; software was not executed |

## Worked Critique

[M6 §§6.47–6.51](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md) displays the price comparisons that undermine broad reassurance. The [Python example](../../03_Data_and_Code/Modern_Power/README.md) reproduces the six price comparisons and three imposed bias scenarios discussed in the notes. These scalar approximations use rounded reported estimates and already-clustered SEs. They are not full-panel or synthetic-control replications.

At the paper's residential reference exposure, the one-sided 95% upper bound is $3.491/MWh. Illustrative margins of $1, $2, and $3/MWh are not excluded by the one-sided margin test, TOST, or the scalar folded-normal test. The four-owner estimate also leaves the displayed positive margins unresolved. These are teaching comparisons, with no claim that the chosen margins are validated household tolerances. The source and claim assessment is [here](../41_Statistical_Claims_and_Decisions/CLAIM_ASSESSMENT.md).

The conclusion concerns unsupported reassurance. A sufficiently informative design can establish a bounded small-effect claim. [M9 §9.83](../../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M09_Marketing_Dialectics.md) connects this distinction to truthful public communication and reasons owed to exposed people. [Optional practice](../../07_Labs/Statistical_Inference/README.md#modern-power-and-harm-bounds) asks students to specify the missing premise and the feasible response. The [verification record](VERIFICATION.md) identifies completed checks.

## Source: 03_Data_and_Code/Modern_Power/README.md

# Power, Equivalence, and Harm Bounds

The electricity-price case asks whether an insignificant coefficient supports reassurance about household costs. These calculations compare zero-null power with tests of specified positive margins and two forms of scalar equivalence. A separate sensitivity calculation allows a bounded bias.

## Inputs and Interpretation

The inputs are rounded coefficients and utility-clustered SEs from the course's [unchanged 42-page source](../../01_Resources/41_Statistical_Claims_and_Decisions/RanaKapsNetessine_WorkingPaper2026.pdf) (Rana et al., 2026):

| Case | Coefficient and SE | Source | Units and Targets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Residential reference | 0.261 and 0.158, both scaled by 100(456/6804) | Table 2, column 4, p. 23 | USD/MWh at a 6.702-point reference exposure; targets 1, 2, 3 |
| Four-owner slope | 0.158 and 0.160 | Table 4, column 4, p. 26 | USD/MWh per exposure percentage point; targets 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 |

The price samples contain 41 treated utilities and 627 post-anchor observations. No utility records are reconstructed. The reference exposure is a ratio of reported means. The subgroup slope is not multiplied by that overall ratio. Price margins are illustrative rather than validated tolerances or originally prespecified tests.

All sampling calculations use a fixed Gaussian approximation with the reported clustered SE. The source study's positive findings remain part of the interpretation. No observed-power calculation substitutes the estimated coefficient for an assumed true effect. No additional clustering multiplier is imposed.

## Reproduction

Python 3 and SciPy are required. NumPy supports independent verification. Verified locally with Python 3.13.5, SciPy 1.15.3, and NumPy 2.1.3.

```sh
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Modern_Power/harm_bounds.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Modern_Power/verify_harm_bounds.py
python3 03_Data_and_Code/Modern_Power/build_figure.py
```

The program writes [results.json](results.json). The figure builder writes the editable TikZ source used in M6. No seed, network call, downloaded code, or participant microdata is used. Complete source appears in M6 §6.51.

## Output Fields

`cases` retains the estimate, SE, units, source cell, p-value against zero, and one-sided 95% upper bound. Each `comparisons` entry contains the chosen margin, zero-null power at that margin, the one-sided margin-test p-value, TOST and folded-normal p-values and decisions, and the folded-normal critical value. `bounded_bias` records imposed bias allowances and their resulting upper bounds, in USD/MWh. These allowances are sensitivity inputs, with no estimate of actual bias or full HonestDiD implementation.

All six displayed price margins fail the three margin tests. The result concerns these price comparisons and their assumptions. It does not establish that every valid method must fail at every possible margin.

Verification uses numerical quadrature, SciPy's independent folded-normal distribution implementation, boundary-size checks, unit rescaling, interval/test duality, and an informative synthetic case that must establish equivalence. These checks validate the probability calculations, not the original identifying design. Read the [modern-method guide](../../01_Resources/51_Modern_Power_and_Harm_Bounds/README.md) for methods requiring additional data and the [optional exercise](../../07_Labs/Statistical_Inference/README.md#modern-power-and-harm-bounds) for the interpretation task.
