### additional:karpathy-vibe-coding-post-2025 | There's a new kind of coding I call 'vibe coding' (X post)

Source URL: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383

Modules: AI, M1

Priority: core

Focus: The 2 February 2025 post that coined 'vibe coding': you give in to the vibes, accept AI-generated changes without reading the diffs, and let the model, Cursor Composer in his case, write the code.

Teaching Suggestion: Opening reading for the AI module; students compare Karpathy's throwaway-project framing with the standard required for analysis code they will submit.

Cautions: URL cited in the Wikipedia 'Vibe coding' article and in Simon Willison's March 2025 post, which also quotes the text in full. x.com may require login to view, so link Willison's post as a backup.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:willison-not-all-ai-programming-is-vibe-coding | Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding (but vibe coding rocks)

Source URL: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Mar/19/vibe-coding/

Modules: AI, M1

Priority: core

Focus: Argues that vibe coding means not reviewing the code. If you review, test and can explain the AI's code, that is ordinary software development. He also praises vibe coding for prototypes and for learning what models can do.

Teaching Suggestion: Required reading paired with Karpathy's post; it supplies the course rule that anything submitted must be code you can explain.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:willison-using-llms-for-code | Here's how I use LLMs to help me write code

Source URL: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Mar/11/using-llms-for-code/

Modules: AI, M1

Priority: core

Focus: Practical advice: treat LLMs as overconfident pair programmers; account for training cut-offs and prefer well-known libraries; manage context; ask for options before committing; be specific; 'test everything' (if you haven't seen it run, it isn't working); vibe-code to learn but not for production.

Teaching Suggestion: First-week reading that sets norms for the course: AI writes the draft, the student verifies.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:willison-vibe-engineering | Vibe engineering

Source URL: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Oct/7/vibe-engineering/

Modules: AI, WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: Coins 'vibe engineering' (7 October 2025) for experienced engineers who use coding agents while staying accountable for quality. It lists the practices agents reward: automated tests, planning, documentation, version control, code review, manual QA and preview environments.

Teaching Suggestion: Basis for the course's 'vibe engineering' standards: map each practice to a requirement in the team project, such as tests, a README, Git history and peer review.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:willison-agentic-engineering-patterns | Agentic Engineering Patterns (guide)

Source URL: https://simonwillison.net/guides/agentic-engineering-patterns/what-is-agentic-engineering/

Modules: AI, WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: A growing guide to working with coding agents. Chapters cover principles ('Writing code is cheap now'), how agents work, Git with agents, subagents, red/green TDD, 'First run the tests', agentic manual testing, linear walkthroughs and interactive explanations, with annotated prompts.

Teaching Suggestion: Link chapters from the wiki as just-in-time references, for example red/green TDD before the regression lab and linear walkthroughs whenever students must explain AI-written code.

Cautions: Page last updated around 15 March 2026. Willison defines an agent as software that runs tools in a loop toward a goal, and reserves 'vibe coding' for unreviewed prototype code.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:willison-vibe-coding-agentic-engineering-closer-2026 | Vibe coding and agentic engineering are getting closer than I'd like

### additional:osmani-70-percent-problem | The 70% problem: Hard truths about AI-assisted coding

Source URL: https://addyo.substack.com/p/the-70-problem-hard-truths-about

Modules: AI, M1

Priority: core

Focus: Argues that AI tools quickly get non-experts about 70% of the way, but the last 30% (edge cases, debugging, maintainability) needs engineering knowledge. Juniors and seniors get very different value as a result.

Teaching Suggestion: Assigned reading framing why the course still teaches the analysis underneath; pair with Prather et al. (2024) on novices.

Cautions: The URL came from a linking page (ipspace.net, December 2024); the Substack page itself wasn't fetched. Published December 2024. Summary based on the title and secondary coverage, so skim before assigning.

### additional:sarkar-drosos-vibe-coding-ppig-2025 | Vibe coding: programming through conversation with artificial intelligence

Modules: AI

### additional:bockeler-to-vibe-or-not | To vibe or not to vibe

Source URL: https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/to-vibe-or-not-vibe.html

Modules: AI, M1

Priority: core

Focus: Whether AI code needs review depends on three things: how likely the AI is to be wrong, how bad an error would be, and how easily you would notice it. Low-risk, high-detectability work can be vibe-coded; high-impact, low-detectability work needs close scrutiny.

Teaching Suggestion: Turn the three factors into a one-page rubric students apply to each analysis step. A typo in a chart label is low risk; a silent join error in CLV data is high impact and hard to detect.

Cautions: Published 23 September 2025.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:mollick-speaking-things-into-existence | Speaking things into existence: Expertise in a vibe-filled world of work

### additional:michels-vibe-coding-state-of-the-art-review-2026 | Vibe Coding: Practice, Performance, Productivity, and Risk - A State-of-the-Art Review

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20446

Modules: AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Cross-disciplinary review from August 2026 (software engineering, HCI, labor economics, security, education). It reconciles conflicting productivity results by measurement method, scope and horizon, and conjectures that gains are real for new code but shrink or reverse on mature codebases.

Teaching Suggestion: Instructor background for an evidence lecture; its 'new code vs. mature codebase' conjecture is a good discussion question.

Cautions: Recent preprint, not peer reviewed. Its HTML version didn't expose the reference list in this pass.

### additional:koren-bekes-vibe-coding-kills-open-source | Vibe Coding Kills Open Source

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15494

Modules: AI, M8

Priority: optional

Focus: Economic model with entry and quality choice. Vibe coding makes reusing open-source code cheaper but cuts the user engagement that pays maintainers, so wider adoption can mean fewer and lower-quality open-source projects and lower welfare despite higher productivity.

Teaching Suggestion: Case for the 'Current Topics' module on platform and ecosystem externalities of AI tools; Békés also co-wrote a widely used data analysis textbook.

Cautions: Submitted 21 January 2026.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:peng-2023-copilot-rct | The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590

Modules: AI, M6, M8

Priority: core

Focus: Controlled experiment in which developers with GitHub Copilot finished an HTTP server in JavaScript 55.8% faster than the control group.

Teaching Suggestion: Classic early RCT; use in M6 as a worked example of a two-arm experiment and of what a narrow, well-specified task can and cannot tell us.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:cui-2025-three-field-experiments | The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers

Source URL: https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/fpi/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535

Modules: AI, M6, M8

Priority: core

Focus: Three randomized field experiments (Microsoft, Accenture, an anonymous Fortune 100 firm; 4,867 developers) find a 26.08% (SE 10.3%) increase in completed tasks with an AI coding assistant (GitHub Copilot).

Teaching Suggestion: Academic anchor in Management Science for M6 (field experiments, staggered rollout, pooling estimates) and the AI module's evidence page.

Cautions: The INFORMS page didn't show volume or issue, so check the final citation. SSRN version: https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4945566. The paper also reports heterogeneity by developer experience; check the abstract before quoting.

Rights or Access: open

---

### additional:metr-2025-early-ai-os-developer-rct | Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

Source URL: https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/

Modules: AI, M1, M6, M8

Priority: core

Focus: RCT with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 real issues in their own large repositories. Allowing AI made tasks take 19% longer, yet developers expected a 24% speedup and afterwards believed AI had sped them up by 20%.

Teaching Suggestion: Centerpiece case on perception vs. measurement; students contrast it with Cui et al. and discuss task, population and tool differences.

Cautions: METR now flags these results as out of date; always pair with the February 2026 update.

Rights or Access: open

---

### additional:metr-2026-uplift-update | We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design

Source URL: https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/

Modules: AI, M6

Priority: core

Focus: Late-2025 follow-up (57 developers, 800+ tasks). Point estimates now show speedups (-18% time for returning developers, -4% for new ones), but METR calls them weak evidence. Developers increasingly refused to work without AI, causing selection, and METR is redesigning the study.

Teaching Suggestion: Excellent M6 teaching case on selection, attrition and non-compliance when the treatment becomes indispensable; pair with the 2025 study.

Cautions: Published 24 February 2026. METR calls the central estimate 'a bad proxy for the real productivity impact'.

Rights or Access: open

---

### additional:metr-time-horizons-2025 | Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

Source URL: https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/

Modules: AI, M3

Priority: recommended

Focus: Introduces the '50% time horizon', the length of tasks (in human-expert time) that agents complete with 50% reliability, and finds it doubled roughly every 7 months over six years.

Teaching Suggestion: M3 tie-in: students fit the log-linear trend themselves; also frames why the tools change mid-semester.

Cautions: METR says the static March 2025 figures are dated. Current methodology (Time Horizon 1.1, January 2026) is at https://metr.org/time-horizons/

Rights or Access: open

### additional:paradis-2024-google-enterprise-rct | How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12944

Modules: AI, M6

Priority: recommended

Focus: RCT with 96 Google engineers on an enterprise-grade task: AI features cut time on task by about 21%, with a wide confidence interval, and gains were larger for developers who spend more hours a day coding.

Teaching Suggestion: Third data point beside Peng and METR for an in-class 'meta-analysis by hand' exercise.

Rights or Access: open

---

### additional:dellacqua-2023-jagged-frontier | Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality

Source URL: https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4573321

Modules: AI, M1, M6, M8

Priority: core

Focus: Preregistered experiment with BCG consultants: GPT-4 improved speed and quality on tasks inside the AI 'frontier' but reduced correctness on a task just outside it. Introduces 'centaur' and 'cyborg' work styles.

Teaching Suggestion: Core business-school reading on why AI help is uneven; students map which Marketing Analytics tasks sit inside or outside the frontier.

Cautions: The SSRN page wouldn't load directly; URL and PDF come from search results. Author list as given in Shen & Tamkin (2026). A later journal version couldn't be confirmed.

Rights or Access: open

---

### additional:brynjolfsson-li-raymond-generative-ai-at-work | Generative AI at Work

Source URL: https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/generative-ai-at-work

Modules: AI, M6, M8

Priority: core

Focus: Staggered rollout of an AI assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents raised issues resolved per hour by about 15% on average. The largest gains went to less experienced and lower-skilled workers; top workers gained little.

Teaching Suggestion: Economics anchor for the heterogeneity theme (who gains from AI); useful in M6 as a staggered-adoption design.

Cautions: Customer support, not coding. Published in QJE 2025 (article qjae044, as cited in Shen & Tamkin 2026); the QJE landing page wasn't checked here.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:daniotti-2025-who-is-using-ai-to-code | Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08945

Modules: AI, M7, M8

Priority: recommended

Cautions: Published 30 August 2024. Links to research on AI detection and to the Bastani SSRN paper.

Source URL: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-sandboxing

Modules: AI

### additional:claude-code-data-usage | Claude Code data usage (training, retention, telemetry)

Source URL: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage

Modules: AI, M2

Priority: core

Focus: Free, Pro and Max (consumer) accounts choose whether their data trains future models. With the setting on, retention is 5 years; with it off, 30 days. Team, Enterprise and API (commercial) data is not used for training by default, and standard retention is 30 days. Local transcripts are stored in plaintext under ~/.claude/projects/ for 30 days.

Teaching Suggestion: Use it on the data-privacy wiki page to show why personal accounts differ from institutional ones, and have students check their claude.ai privacy setting before using course or client data.

Cautions: Transcripts sent with /feedback are retained for 5 years. Telemetry can be disabled with environment variables. Point out to students that local plaintext transcripts can contain any data the agent has read.

### additional:mcp-docs | What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? (official docs)

Source URL: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro

Modules: AI

Priority: core

Focus: MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external data, tools and workflows, described as 'a USB-C port for AI applications'. Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor and others support it. The docs cover building servers and clients and MCP Apps. The current docs version is dated 2026-07-28.

Teaching Suggestion: Concept page: show how an agent could query a course SQL database or Google Drive through MCP instead of students pasting data into chat.

Cautions: Anthropic's launch post (November 25, 2024): https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol. Claude Code MCP setup: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp. Security: the MCP Security Best Practices page (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/security_best_practices.md, fetched) covers confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF and local-server compromise; its local-server section is a good warning against installing random MCP servers. Governance: the Agentic AI Foundation (https://aaif.io, fetched) hosts MCP, AGENTS.md, Agent Skills, A2A, goose and others.

### additional:agents-md | AGENTS.md: a simple, open format for guiding coding agents

Source URL: https://agents.md

Modules: AI

Priority: core

Focus: AGENTS.md is a plain-Markdown 'README for agents' with no required fields. Codex, Jules, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code, GitHub Copilot coding agent, Windsurf, Zed, Aider and others read it. The Agentic AI Foundation now stewards it.

Teaching Suggestion: Have each team commit an AGENTS.md (with a CLAUDE.md that points to it) so the project works the same whether a teammate uses Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or Cursor.

Cautions: Repo: https://github.com/agentsmd/agents.md (link from the site). Codex docs on how AGENTS.md files are discovered and merged: https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/agent-configuration/agents-md. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md (see claude-code-memory-claude-md).

Rights or Access: open

### additional:willison-lethal-trifecta | The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication

Source URL: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/

Modules: AI

Priority: core

Focus: An agent that combines access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally can be steered by prompt injection into leaking data. Guardrails help only partly, so avoid giving one agent all three.

Teaching Suggestion: The single most teachable security concept. Students check their own setup (for example customer CSV + web browsing + MCP email = all three) against it.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:greshake-indirect-prompt-injection | Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173

Modules: AI, M8

Priority: optional

Focus: The foundational paper on indirect prompt injection. Instructions hidden in content an LLM retrieves can hijack the application, causing data theft, worming and contamination of information ecosystems. Demonstrated against Bing Chat and code-completion engines.

Teaching Suggestion: Academic citation for the security page, and for M5's point that scraped social-media text may itself contain injected instructions.

Cautions: The arXiv page lists no venue. The paper is widely cited as appearing at ACM AISec 2023, which I did not verify here.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:perry-insecure-code-ai-assistants | Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622

Modules: AI, M6

Priority: recommended

Focus: In a user study, participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code yet were more confident it was secure. Participants who trusted the AI less and refined their prompts more produced fewer vulnerabilities.

Teaching Suggestion: Evidence for the course norm 'confidence is not correctness'. Pair it with an in-class exercise assessing AI-generated code.

Cautions: The arXiv page shows the ACM DOI but not the venue name. CCS 2023 is inferred from the DOI and should be confirmed before citing.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:mcbroken-api-lab | Lab: collecting public data from an API (McBroken, McDonald's ice-cream machines)

Source URL: https://github.com/nene88991999/BADM534-Marketing-Analytics/tree/main/01_Resources/02_M2_Customer_Data_and_Visualization/mcbroken_api_lab

Modules: M2, M6

Priority: core

Focus: Executed notebook plus two scripts. fetch_mcbroken.py calls https://mcbroken.com/markers.json (one GeoJSON feature per store, gzip, undocumented), checks status, decompresses, flattens to a DataFrame and saves a timestamped copy, with a fallback to a public-domain GitHub archive. build_panel.py walks that archive's 60,000-commit git history and writes daily (one year) and weekly (six years) panels by country, US state and store. Includes a GitHub Actions template for students to build their own daily snapshots.

Teaching Suggestion: M2 session on data collection: HTTP requests, headers, status codes, JSON to table, polite scraping, and git scraping as a cheap way to build a time series. Exercise 1 has students assess AI-written request code (timeout, User-Agent, status check, gzip, raw copy). Exercise 5 previews M6 with a right-to-repair event study (US Copyright Office exemption, late Oct 2024).

Cautions: Measurement caveats are in the README: is_broken means the McDonald's app refused an ice-cream order (also fires when a store is closed); the denominator is stores checked in that hour and the checking cadence changed over the years. Raw JSON is not redistributed; derived aggregates and one snapshot are.

Rights or Access: open

Teaching Suggestion: Flagship M6 experiment dataset: estimate effects by arm, explore heterogeneous effects and build uplift targeting policies. sklift.datasets.fetch_hillstrom() loads it in one line.

Cautions: The original 2008 post is on blog.minethatdata.com; a direct file URL was not verified. scikit-uplift also has loaders for the Criteo, X5 RetailHero, Lenta and MegaFon uplift datasets: https://www.uplift-modeling.com/en/latest/api/datasets/index.html

### additional:reddit-data-access | Reddit Data API and Reddit for Researchers access rules

Modules: M5

Priority: recommended

Focus: Reddit's policy: the Data API is rate-limited and bulk export is restricted. Academic research must go through the Reddit for Researchers program, and content may not be used for model training without Reddit's consent.

Teaching Suggestion: Required policy reading for M5 social-media analysis. It explains why students should not scrape Reddit or use the API for research projects, and how research access works.

Don't plan student projects on Reddit data without lead time.

Teaching Suggestion: Opening reading for M8 (or M5); pairs with M6 ad-measurement papers: what exactly is being bought?

Rights or Access: paid

### additional:wu-2019-blind-spot-attention-economy | Blind Spot: The Attention Economy and the Law

Source URL: https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/2029/

Modules: M8, M5

Priority: core

Focus: Attention is a scarce resource; 'attention brokers' offer free services and sell access to audiences, and antitrust and consumer-protection authorities have struggled to analyse these markets because users pay no money. Distinguishes voluntary exchange from captive exposure.

Teaching Suggestion: Pre-reading for the M8 session; class point that ad load and interstitial questions are a price paid in time.

### additional:ftc-act-s5-deception-unfairness | FTC Act Section 5 (15 U.S.C. 45) and the FTC Policy Statement on Deception

Source URL: https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/ftc-policy-statement-deception

Modules: M8, M3

Priority: core

Focus: The general US prohibition of unfair or deceptive acts. Deception: a representation or omission likely to mislead a reasonable consumer that is material. Unfairness (15 U.S.C. 45(n)): substantial injury, not reasonably avoidable, not outweighed by benefits. Objective claims require prior substantiation. Since AMG Capital (2021) money comes mainly through rule violations (civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation at 2025 levels, unchanged for 2026).

Teaching Suggestion: Legal backbone slide for M8; the substantiation point for M3 (claims built on regressions).

Teaching Suggestion: M5 fake-review incentives.

### additional:miller-sahni-strulov-shlain-sophisticated-inertia | Sophisticated Consumers with Inertia: Long-Term Implications from a Large-Scale Field Experiment

Source URL: https://bfi.uchicago.edu/working-paper/sophisticated-consumers-with-inertia-long-term-implications-from-a-large-scale-field-experiment/

Modules: M4, M6, M8

Priority: core

Focus: Large field experiment randomising auto-renewal: auto-renewal raises short-run revenue through inertia, but many consumers anticipate their inertia and decline auto-renewal offers or delay subscribing; after a year revenue is about equal and auto-renewal has fewer subscribers.

Teaching Suggestion: Shows the business case against subscription traps (M4 CLV, M6).

### additional:egan-russel-shi-yao-2026-competition-generative-ai | Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand

Source URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35953

Modules: M8, M4, M6, M7

Priority: core

Focus: Card transactions for 174 million US consumers measure paid adoption of generative-AI services: about 2.9% paying by April 2026, skewed young and high-income; almost all on plans of $30 or less; multihoming common but falling; annual retention 20-45%; switching rising around model releases. A structural demand and supply model finds high price sensitivity, loyalty to AI rather than to providers, and rising substitutability that limits pricing power.

Teaching Suggestion: Anchor reading for an M8 session on competition in AI, and the source of the measurements reproduced on the synthetic panel in genai_demand_lab. Pairs with the Fradkin OpenRouter paper for the API side.

Cautions: NBER working papers are paywalled for non-subscribers; UIUC has access. The PDF could not be fetched from the workspace, so the entry rests on the NBER abstract page. Fiserv appears in the author disclosures, not as a stated data source.

Rights or Access: paid

Focus: Uses CDNOW to build an RFM summary with clv.utils.rfm_summary and a train/test split, fits BG/NBD by MAP and MCMC, and computes P(alive) and expected purchases. It then checks the Gamma-Gamma independence assumption, fits Gamma-Gamma and computes discounted CLV with uncertainty intervals.

Teaching Suggestion: Main CLV lab notebook. Sibling notebooks cover Pareto/NBD, MBG/NBD, standalone Gamma-Gamma and sBG with cohorts and covariates for subscription settings.

Cautions: BG/NBD: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/bg_nbd.html. Pareto/NBD: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/pareto_nbd.html. Gamma-Gamma: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/gamma_gamma.html. sBG: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/sbg.html. The quickstart doesn't mention migrating from lifetimes. The rfm_summary definitions of frequency and recency differ from standard RFM scoring, which is worth flagging to students.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:gelman-loken-forking-paths | The garden of forking paths: Why multiple comparisons can be a problem, even when there is no 'fishing expedition' or 'p-hacking' and the research hypothesis was posited ahead of time

Source URL: https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/unpublished/p_hacking.pdf

Modules: M3, M6, AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Shows that data-dependent analysis choices (exclusions, codings, subgroups, interactions) invalidate p-values even without deliberate fishing. Remedies include preregistration, replication and multilevel modeling.

Teaching Suggestion: Framing reading for 'vibe coding' risks. AI agents make it nearly free to try dozens of specifications, so students should log every specification an AI tool ran and report all of them.

Cautions: The link redirects from stat.columbia.edu to sites.stat.columbia.edu; the final URL is used here.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:korkames-stanley-stremersch-2026-ad-elasticity | Meta-Analysis of Advertising Effectiveness: New Insights from Improved Bias Corrections

Source URL: https://pure.eur.nl/en/publications/meta-analysis-of-advertising-effectiveness-new-insights-from-impr/

Modules: M3, M6

Priority: recommended

Focus: Meta-analysis of 538 B2C own-brand advertising elasticities. Modern publication-bias corrections cut the mean effect more than fivefold (short-term about 0.0008, long-term about 0.03), in line with RCT evidence, and internet advertising shows the highest elasticity.

Its repository title differs from the published JMR title 'How Well Does Advertising Work?'.

### additional:digital-twins-funhouse-mirrors | Digital Twins as Funhouse Mirrors: Five Key Distortions

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19088

Modules: M4, M8, AI

Priority: core

Focus: Mega-study of 19 preregistered studies and 164 outcomes. Digital twins built from 500+ answers per person beat a generic LLM only slightly and correlate weakly with real answers (mean r = 0.20). Five distortions are documented: insufficient individuation, stereotyping, representation bias, ideological bias and hyper-rationality.

Teaching Suggestion: The most current large-scale validation (2025-26) of synthetic respondents. Use it as the critical counterweight in the synthetic-conjoint activity.

Cautions: A more optimistic 2025 counterpoint is Maier et al., 'LLMs Reproduce Human Purchase Intent via Semantic Similarity Elicitation of Likert Ratings' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338). Its free-text-plus-embedding method reached about 90% of human test-retest reliability on 57 personal-care surveys. Some of its authors work in industry (Wiecki is, from recollection, at PyMC Labs).

### additional:overgoor-knight-bart-2025-llm-annotated-regressors | Correcting Toward the Wrong Target: LLM-Annotated Regressors Under Noisy Human Benchmarks

### additional:cheng-mayya-sedoc-silicon-llm-annotation | To Err Is Human; To Annotate, SILICON? Toward Robust Reproducibility in LLM Annotation

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14461

Modules: M5, AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Shows how LLM-based annotation becomes irreproducible when proprietary models are retired, and proposes the SILICON workflow: decompose measurement error, choose open-weight backup models, and route low-confidence labels to auxiliary models.

Teaching Suggestion: Reading for the 'non-reproducibility' failure mode. Supports a course rule that teams log the model version, prompt, temperature and date, and keep an open-weight fallback.

Cautions: Preprint by business-school (NYU Stern) authors; no journal ref listed.

### additional:gilardi-2023-chatgpt-outperforms-crowd-workers | ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks

Source URL: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2305016120

Modules: M5, AI

Priority: core

Focus: On 2,382 tweets, zero-shot ChatGPT beat MTurk crowd workers on four of five annotation tasks, had higher intercoder agreement than crowd workers and trained annotators, and cost under a third of a cent per annotation (about 20 times cheaper).

Teaching Suggestion: Short core reading that motivates LLM labeling. Pair it with Reiss (2023) and Baumann et al. (2025) for the cautionary side.

Cautions: DOI and license confirmed via Crossref. arXiv version: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15056. Results are for ChatGPT as of early 2023, so newer models differ.

### additional:ludwig-mullainathan-rambachan-llm-econometric-framework | Large Language Models: An Applied Econometric Framework

Source URL: https://nber.org/papers/w33344

Modules: M5, M3, AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Distinguishes prediction uses of LLMs, which need no training leakage, from estimation or measurement uses. For measurement, valid inference requires a small validation sample, because otherwise arbitrary choices such as the model or prompt can change results a lot.

Teaching Suggestion: Instructor anchor for the module's validation rule: every LLM-coded variable needs a human-labeled validation subsample. Assign a simplified slide version to students.

Cautions: The NBER page is open. Was presented at the NBER SI 2026 ML session (conference PDF seen in search).

### additional:egami-2023-design-based-supervised-learning | Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large Language Models

### additional:reiss-2023-chatgpt-reliability-cautionary | Testing the Reliability of ChatGPT for Text Annotation and Classification: A Cautionary Remark

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11085

Modules: M5, AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Repeated runs and small prompt or setting changes produce inconsistent ChatGPT classifications, so unsupervised use without validation against human labels is not advisable.

(2023), 'Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation', https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00176 (fetched).

### additional:baumann-2025-llm-hacking | Large Language Model Hacking: Quantifying the Hidden Risks of Using LLMs for Text Annotation

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08825v2

Modules: M5, M6, AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Across many replicated hypotheses, about 31% of tests using state-of-the-art LLM annotations reached incorrect conclusions, and the risk is highest near significance thresholds. Human annotations were the best safeguard of the 21 mitigations tested.

Teaching Suggestion: Key cautionary reading. It links naturally to M6 on p-hacking: changing models or prompts until results look significant is a form of p-hacking.

Cautions: Preprint (v2, Oct 2025); no journal ref yet.

Focus: Explains how to randomize a nudge (e.g., a banner) when the feature itself can't be withheld, and then use IV to estimate the complier effect. Covers monotonicity, exclusion and relevance, with practical trade-offs.

Teaching Suggestion: The best business-facing intro to IV for this audience. Pair with a linearmodels IV2SLS exercise on simulated nudge data.

Rights or Access: open

Modules: M6

### additional:lewis-rao-2015-qje | The Unfavorable Economics of Measuring the Returns to Advertising

### additional:sklearn-common-pitfalls | scikit-learn User Guide 12: Common pitfalls and recommended practices

Source URL: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html

Modules: M7, AI

Priority: core

Focus: Short worked examples of inconsistent preprocessing, data leakage (for example feature selection on the full data inflates accuracy from 0.5 to about 0.76 on pure noise) and random_state control, with Pipeline as the fix.

Teaching Suggestion: Suggested reading before students let an AI assistant write an ML pipeline. Use it as an assessment checklist: 'find the leakage in this AI-generated notebook'.

Cautions: These are exactly the bugs LLM-written notebooks often contain: fit_transform before the train/test split, and feature selection on the full data.

Rights or Access: open

Priority: recommended

Focus: Q-learning pricing algorithms in simulated oligopolies learn to sustain supra-competitive prices with punishment strategies, without communicating.

Teaching Suggestion: Background for the algorithmic-pricing discussion (RealPage-style cases). Present the key figure and intuition rather than assigning the full paper.

Cautions: Empirical complement: Brown & MacKay (2023), 'Competition in Pricing Algorithms', AEJ: Microeconomics 15(2): 109-56, doi 10.1257/mic.20210158 (aeaweb page verified). It shows that simple rival-responsive pricing algorithms at online retailers can raise prices.

Rights or Access: library

Source URL: https://jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/10302

Priority: optional

Focus: Introduces oversampling of rare classes by interpolating synthetic minority examples, a standard tool for churn and response models where positives are rare.

### additional:zielnicki-2025-value-personalized-recs-netflix | The Value of Personalized Recommendations: Evidence from Netflix

Source URL: https://www.ifo.de/en/cesifo/publications/2026/working-paper/value-personalized-recommendations-evidence-netflix

Modules: M7, M4

Priority: core

Focus: Uses Netflix viewership and recommendation exposure to estimate a discrete-choice model under conditional exogeneity of exposure. A randomized perturbation supplies diversion evidence for model validation. Model-based replacement with matrix factorization or popularity-based recommendation lowers engagement by about 4% or 12%, respectively.

Teaching Suggestion: The 'why firms invest in recommenders' anchor for M7. It pairs naturally with the MBA 542 synthetic Netflix viewing data.

Cautions: The supplied PDF is dated June 9, 2026, despite 2025 in its filename. Results are model-based engagement counterfactuals, not direct experimental effects of full replacement or measures of consumer welfare. Abstract and identification discussion checked locally.

Rights or Access: open

Modules: M7, M6

Priority: optional

Focus: Studies a temporary ranking boost for celebrity sleep-reminder videos in a randomized platform campaign. The analyzed active-user panel shows increased late-night and overall usage, with persistence after the campaign. The authors relate persistence to training signals and policy updates generated by the intervention.

Teaching Suggestion: Recent example for the M6/M7 discussion of spillovers and unintended outcomes in platform experiments.

Cautions: Local Sections 4.2–4.3 and Table 6 checked. The analyzed panel contains 200,000 users active on the first experiment day. Reported 14.75% and 2.18% figures are relative assignment effects on usage. Mechanism attribution and sample inclusion require separate attention.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:cosley-2003-is-seeing-believing | Is Seeing Believing? How Recommender Interfaces Affect Users' Opinions

Source URL: https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/is-seeing-believing-how-recommender-interfaces-affect-users-opini/

Modules: M7, M6

Priority: optional

Focus: Classic experiment in which showing users (sometimes manipulated) predicted ratings pulls their own re-ratings toward the displayed value: recommender interfaces anchor opinions.

Teaching Suggestion: Short classic that pairs with Adomavicius et al. (2019) in this folder; useful for discussing how recommenders contaminate the ratings they learn from.

Source URL: https://doi.org/10.1111/1756-2171.12481

Modules: M7, M8

### additional:berke-2024-cscw-amazon-data-sharing-experiment | Insights from an experiment crowdsourcing data from thousands of US Amazon users: the importance of transparency, money, and data use

Source URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13172

Modules: M8, M6

Priority: recommended

Focus: Randomised experiment embedded in the data-collection tool behind Open e-commerce 1.0: showing people their own data raises willingness to share it, sharing rises linearly with the payment offered, real money moves people more than hypothetical money (a field test of the privacy paradox), and willingness differs by demographic group.

Teaching Suggestion: M8 privacy session: a field experiment on what consumers' data is worth to them, from the same people whose purchases students can analyse. Also an M6 example of an experiment built into a product flow.

### additional:github-pages-limits | GitHub Pages limits

Source URL: https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/github-pages-limits

Modules: WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: Official GitHub Pages limits: a published site can be at most 1 GB, and the source repo should stay under 1 GB. Soft limits are 100 GB/month of bandwidth and 10 builds/hour (custom GitHub Actions builds are exempt), and deployments time out after 10 minutes. Pages is not meant for commercial or sensitive-transaction sites.

Teaching Suggestion: Instructor-only planning: keep the wiki's datasets and media under these caps, host large data elsewhere (GitHub Releases, Box, Hugging Face), and never collect passwords or student data on the site.

Cautions: Rate-limited requests get HTTP 429. Custom domains use a CNAME record for a subdomain or A/ALIAS/ANAME for an apex domain; verify the domain first to prevent takeover (https://docs.github.com/en/pages/configuring-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site/about-custom-domains-and-github-pages, fetched). A campus subdomain such as *.illinois.edu would need campus DNS cooperation; that is my inference, not from GitHub's docs.

Rights or Access: open

Modules: WIKI

### additional:quarto | Quarto

It also made opt-in (express) cookie consent the default, added screen-reader labels for videos, and added experimental PDF/UA output. Release posts now live on opensource.posit.co. Cautions: Status on 2026-10-23: pre-0.1 (the site is built with zensical 0.0.70). A 'dependable release line' starting with 0.1 is scheduled for 2026-11-05. Only a subset of MkDocs plugins is supported. An October 2026 update says the planned Rust Markdown parser has been replaced by a Python-Markdown-compatible one. Announcement: https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/blog/2025/11/05/zensical/. It has no notebook-execution story comparable to Quarto or MyST.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:pyodide | Pyodide changelog

Source URL: https://pyodide.org/en/stable/project/changelog.html

Modules: WIKI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Pyodide, CPython compiled to WebAssembly, is the engine under quarto-live, JupyterLite, marimo WASM and PyScript. The 314.x line (314.0.0 on 2026-06-09) runs Python 3.14, and 314.0.7 (2026-09-14) is the latest release.

Teaching Suggestion: Instructor-only reference for which Python version and package builds students get in any in-browser cell.

Cautions: Version numbers jumped from 0.x (0.28 shipped Python 3.13) to 314.x. The changelog announces no policy, so the link to the Python version is my inference. 0.29.5 and 0.27.8 got Node 26 fixes in September 2026. Pure-Python wheels install through micropip.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:pyodide-packages | Packages built in Pyodide

Source URL: https://pyodide.org/en/stable/usage/packages-in-pyodide.html

Modules: WIKI, M2, M3, M4, M7

Priority: core

Focus: List of compiled packages shipped with Pyodide 314.0.7, including pandas 3.0.2, scikit-learn 1.8.0, statsmodels 0.14.6, scipy 1.18.0, matplotlib 3.10.8 and numpy 2.4.6. Seaborn is not on the built-in list.

Teaching Suggestion: Check before writing in-browser exercises: the core M2–M7 stack (pandas wrangling, statsmodels OLS/logit, scikit-learn clustering and prediction) runs in the browser.

Cautions: Trade-offs: the first page load downloads the runtime and packages. marimo's docs cite a 2 GB memory cap and no true threading or multiprocessing under WASM. Packages with compiled code that are not on this list (for example PyTorch) generally won't install. Seaborn is pure Python and should install through micropip (not tested). pandas 3.0 is a major release, so syntax can differ from older tutorials and from whatever pandas version Colab ships; check version parity before mixing Colab and in-browser cells.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:jupyterlite | JupyterLite documentation

Source URL: https://jupyterlite.readthedocs.io/en/stable/

Modules: WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: A JupyterLab and Notebook distribution that runs entirely in the browser, with Pyodide or Xeus Python kernels in Web Workers. It deploys as a static site with no server.

Teaching Suggestion: Give students a full notebook interface from a wiki link (for example a 'Try it' button on each module) with no accounts or installs.

Cautions: The docs were labeled 0.8.6 when fetched, while their compatibility table listed jupyterlite-core 0.7.0 (bundling JupyterLab 4.5 and Notebook 7.5); confirm the current version before pinning. Only the last two releases are supported. Not every JupyterLab feature works. Student files are kept in browser storage, so test how work persists before relying on it for assignments.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:jupyterlite-demo-template | jupyterlite/demo: template for deploying JupyterLite to GitHub Pages

Source URL: https://github.com/jupyterlite/demo

Modules: WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: Template repo that builds a JupyterLite site and deploys it to GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions. Notebooks go in the content folder, and kernels and extensions are listed in requirements.txt.

Teaching Suggestion: Use as the template for a Marketing Analytics 'lab' subsite that holds the module notebooks and is linked from the wiki.

Cautions: Deploy guide (https://jupyterlite.readthedocs.io/en/stable/quickstart/deploy.html, fetched): click 'Use this template', enable Actions, set workflow permissions to read/write and the Pages source to GitHub Actions. For pre-installed packages, use the xeus-python demo with an environment.yml. Live demo at jupyterlite.github.io/demo. Requires Firefox 90+ or Chromium 89+.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:marimo-wasm | marimo WebAssembly notebooks

Source URL: https://docs.marimo.io/guides/wasm/

Modules: WIKI, M4

Priority: core

Focus: marimo's reactive notebooks can run entirely in the browser through Pyodide. numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas and matplotlib are pre-installed, and other pure-Python wheels install automatically on import.

Teaching Suggestion: Build reactive demos (for example sliders driving a CLV or conjoint simulator), export them as static HTML, and embed them in wiki pages.

Cautions: Export with 'marimo export html-wasm notebook.py -o out --mode run' for a read-only app or '--mode edit' for an editable notebook. The export must be served over HTTP, not opened from file://, and Pyodide and packages load from a CDN. Run 'marimo check --select MW' to catch incompatible packages (https://docs.marimo.io/guides/exporting/webassembly_html/, fetched). Limits: 2 GB memory, emulated concurrency, no PDB. marimo islands, which embed single reactive cells in any HTML page, are still a 'Preview' feature (https://docs.marimo.io/guides/island_example/, fetched).

Rights or Access: open

### additional:marimo-ai-notebook | marimo: reactive Python notebook (GitHub repository)

Source URL: https://github.com/marimo-team/marimo

Modules: WIKI, AI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Open-source reactive Python notebook stored as plain .py files. It has a built-in AI assistant that sees in-memory variables, Copilot completion, bring-your-own-key or local models, and 'marimo pair' for working alongside Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode.

Teaching Suggestion: Option for in-class vibe-coding activities: notebooks diff cleanly in Git and work with coding agents, and the same files export to WASM pages for the wiki.

Cautions: 22.3k stars when fetched. The latest release number was not visible on the fetched page.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:binder-thebe | Binder (mybinder.org) user guidelines

Source URL: https://mybinder.readthedocs.io/en/latest/about/user-guidelines.html

Modules: WIKI

Priority: optional

Focus: Free service that launches a GitHub repo of notebooks in a temporary cloud Jupyter session. Sessions get 1–2 GB of RAM, shut down after 10 minutes idle, last up to about 6 hours, and are capped at 100 simultaneous users per repository.

Teaching Suggestion: Fallback 'Launch Binder' button for notebooks that need packages Pyodide lacks. The 100-user cap and slow cold starts make it unreliable for a whole class at once.

Cautions: The mybinder.org homepage says the service is 'currently in testing'. Thebe (https://github.com/jupyter-book/thebe, BSD-3-Clause, fetched) turns static code cells into runnable ones backed by a Jupyter server, or by JupyterLite through thebe-lite. Thebe 0.9.0 is still in development, and Jupyter Book 2 does not yet support editable Thebe cells.

Rights or Access: open

### additional:colab-github-badge | Using Google Colab with GitHub (colab-github-demo notebook)

Modules: WIKI, M1

### additional:pagefind | Pagefind

Source URL: https://pagefind.app/

Modules: WIKI

Priority: recommended

Focus: Static search library that indexes the built HTML from any site generator and serves a chunked index. It claims a total payload under 300 kB for a full-text search of a 10,000-page site. The current version is 1.5.2.

Teaching Suggestion: Adds search to a plain-HTML or mixed-tool wiki; it is also Starlight's default search.

Cautions: Repo: https://github.com/pagefind/pagefind (MIT). Lunr.js (https://github.com/olivernn/lunr.js, MIT, fetched) is the older in-browser alternative; it shows 105 open issues and recent activity could not be confirmed. Quarto and Jupyter Book 2 have built-in search, so Pagefind matters mainly for plain-HTML builds.

### additional:wcag-overview | WCAG 2 Overview

Modules: WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: W3C overview of WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 and the A, AA and AAA conformance levels. W3C recommends WCAG 2.2, which is backward compatible with 2.1 and is also published as ISO/IEC 40500:2025.

Teaching Suggestion: Instructor-only reference for setting the wiki's accessibility target.

Cautions: WCAG 2.1 was last updated 2025-05-06, and WCAG 3 is still an early draft. UIUC's own standard requires 2.2 AA for internally built web content (see uiuc-minimum-digital-accessibility-standards).

### additional:ada-title-ii-web-rule | ADA.gov fact sheet: Title II rule on web content and mobile app accessibility

Source URL: https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/

Modules: WIKI

Priority: core

Focus: The DOJ's ADA Title II rule requires web content from state and local governments, including public universities, to meet WCAG 2.1 AA. An April 2026 interim final rule moved compliance to 2027-04-26 for entities serving 50,000+ people and 2028-04-26 for smaller ones.

Teaching Suggestion: Instructor-only: a public-university course wiki should meet WCAG 2.1 AA by April 2027 at the latest.

Cautions: The exceptions for archived content and individualized password-protected documents are narrow and don't cover public HTML course pages. This is a summary, not legal advice. The page title shown here is paraphrased.

Rights or Access: open

Modules: WIKI

Focus: Campus standard under the Digital Accessibility Policy (HR-86). Internally developed web content must meet the most recent recommended WCAG, currently 2.2 AA, use WAI-ARIA 1.2, and work with major browsers and screen readers. Course content and training materials are explicitly in scope.
